Title: Building security review into your SDLC with Codex Security
Context: Threat models, repository security policies, and architecture documents make that knowledge available
Full Text:
As AI accelerates the SDLC, it’s putting pressure on security workflows. Security teams need to prevent insecure code from being committed in the first place, but manual security reviews for PRs can’t scale at the same pace that agents are producing and revising code.

Application security programs have followed the pace of human development: a design review before implementation, a manual pass on the riskiest pull requests, and periodic work to triage vulnerability backlogs. To keep up, we must now deploy agentic security workflows that match the speed of agentic SDLC.

This post presents four principles for agentic security workflows, then shares how to build and run those workflows through Codex Security and our CLI.

Four principles for agentic security workflows

Expanding security review capacity requires a clear basis for evaluating changes and a clear way for teams to assess the results. We recommend four principles for integrating security agents into development:

Give agents system-specific context

Agents need to understand the application’s assets, trust boundaries, and security requirements to evaluate a change. Threat models, repository security policies, and architecture documents make that knowledge available. Regularly reviewing these artifacts and keeping them current gives agents a reliable foundation for their investigations.

Integrate review into development

Security feedback should reach developers while changes are still in progress. Connect reviews to local work, pull requests, and CI workflows, with clear triggers for when they should run. This makes security review a consistent part of the development process.

Set review scope and reporting thresholds deliberately

Review scope should reflect the change and the components it could affect. A diff scan, a component assessment, and a full repository scan serve different purposes. Reporting thresholds should also reflect risk, giving sensitive areas such as authentication and billing appropriate attention.

Make findings inspectable

Reviewers need enough information to evaluate a finding and determine what action to take. Reports should explain the relevant code locations, reasoning, severity, confidence, and remediation guidance. They should also identify what was reviewed, excluded, or deferred so teams can understand the investigation’s limits.

Seeding context for security reviews

Differences among threat models, AGENTS.md, SECURITY.md, and knowledge bases

AGENTS.md keeps shared engineering instructions that establish consistent expectations. SECURITY.md tells Codex how your organization wants that reality evaluated and reported. A threat model describes the security reality of the system. They overlap, but the threat model is usually one part of the broader policy.

For example, a threat model would include details about assets, entry points, attacker-controlled inputs, trust boundaries, authentication assumptions, privileged operations, and risky components. Commit it as a separate file, docs/security/threat-model.md, so Codex Security can reference it during pull request reviews and security scans.

<!-- docs/security/threat-model.md --> # Threat Model The public API accepts untrusted JSON and file uploads. Requests cross from the internet-facing API into internal billing and identity services. Attackers are unauthenticated users or compromised tenant accounts. Protect tenant data, billing mutations, and service credentials.

The SECURITY.md file tells Codex how your organization wants that reality evaluated and reported.

<!-- SECURITY.md --> # Security Policy ## Security Invariants - Every billing mutation must be authorized for the active tenant. - Uploaded content must be parsed within explicit size and resource limits. - Service credentials must never be returned to clients. ## Reportable Findings Report realistic violations of tenant isolation, authentication bypass, unsafe parsing, secret exposure, or unauthorized billing mutations. ## Severity Context Cross-tenant access is Critical. Single-tenant unauthorized mutation is High. ## Out of Scope Development-only tools that cannot be included in production builds.

Finally, a knowledge base supplies supporting documents to particular scans. This can include architecture documents, policies, additional threat models, or operational context that the CLI scanner should consider. Here’s an example of a Markdown architecture document you can pass to the CLI when running a security scan against a codebase.

<!-- docs/security/payment-service-context.md --> # Payment Service Security Context ## Purpose The payment service creates charges, issues refunds, and stores references to payment-provider customers. It does not store full card numbers or CVVs. ## Deployment and Exposure - `POST /api/payments` is internet-facing through the API gateway. - `POST /internal/refunds` is reachable only from the support service. - Background workers consume messages from the `payment-events` queue. - The service runs with access to the payment-provider API and billing database. ## Authentication and Authorization - Public endpoints use JWTs issued by the identity service. - The API gateway validates signatures, issuer, and expiration. - This service remains responsible for tenant authorization. - Internal requests use workload identity; network location alone is not trusted. - Refunds above £1,000 require a previously recorded approval. ## Trust Boundaries 1. Internet client → API gateway 2. API gateway → payment service 3. Payment service → payment provider 4. Payment service → billing database 5. Message producers → `payment-events` consumer Inputs crossing any of these boundaries must be treated as untrusted unless the receiving component performs the documented validation. ## Sensitive Assets and Operations - Payment-provider API credentials - Customer-to-provider identifier mappings - Charge creation - Refund issuance - Webhook signature secrets - Tenant billing history ## Important Data Flows ### Creating a charge 1. The API receives an authenticated request containing an order identifier. 2. The service retrieves the order using both tenant ID and order ID. 3. The service calculates the amount from server-side order data. 4. The service creates the provider charge with an idempotency key. 5. The resulting provider identifier is stored in the billing database. Client-supplied amounts must never be passed directly to the provider. ### Processing a webhook 1. The raw request body is retained. 2. The provider signature is verified over the raw bytes. 3. The event timestamp must be within five minutes. 4. Duplicate event IDs are ignored. 5. State changes occur only after all validation succeeds. ## Relevant Code - `src/http/payments.ts`: public payment endpoints - `src/http/refunds.ts`: refund endpoints - `src/webhooks/provider.ts`: webhook validation - `src/workers/payment-events.ts`: asynchronous event processing - `src/auth/tenant.ts`: tenant authorization - `src/provider/client.ts`: provider API wrapper ## Security Assumptions - The identity service is trusted to authenticate users, but not to authorize access to payment records. - Queue publishers may be compromised; consumers must validate message content. - API-gateway authentication does not replace service-level tenant checks. - Provider webhook payloads are attacker-controlled until signature validation completes. ## Known Limitations - Legacy refunds created before 2025 do not have idempotency keys. - Webhook replay protection is local to one region. - The development payment-provider emulator does not validate signatures.

It can be supplied to the scan using the following command:

npx @openai/codex-security scan . \ --knowledge-base docs/security/payment-service-context.md

Putting it all together, a useful arrangement could look like the following:

SECURITY.md docs/security/ ├── threat-model.md ├── architecture.md ├── payment-service-context.md ├── authentication.md └── deployment-boundaries.md

Seeding a threat model

Committing a threat model is a core component of informing how Codex should conduct security reviews. You can initialize a threat model by invoking the threat model skill within Codex and committing it.

Generate a Threat Model of this repository that covers entry points and untrusted inputs, sensitive data paths, and privileged actions.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

You can invoke the threat model skill through Codex by simply typing $threat-model. Once a threat model has been created, commit it to the repository under /docs/security and then link to the threat model within the Codex Cloud settings for the selected repo. If a threat model is not specified, Codex will regenerate the threat model for every security review.

When generating a threat model, pay particular attention to assumptions that the code alone can’t establish, such as compensating controls and responsibilities shared with other services.

Want an even better example? Look at the trust model for Backstage, an open-source framework for building an internal developer portal. A generated model might treat its authentication and catalog plugins as isolated because they run on separate hosts. However, Backstage’s threat model explains that this separation does not establish a security boundary if the catalog plugin can still access the authentication plugin’s database.

Correcting the model allows a review to inspect deployment configuration and access grants to determine whether another plugin can read or modify authentication data. This turns an architectural assumption into a requirement. Changes to database access, shared caches, or plugin placement should trigger another review of that boundary.

Lastly, don’t forget to revisit the threat model when entry points, trust boundaries, or privileged operations change. Those are useful triggers for keeping the review context aligned with the application.

Seeding a SECURITY.md

You can use the $define-security-policy skill to generate a seeded security policy within the repository.

Define Security Policy for the Northstar Bank API. Here are key policies that should be included: Authentication and Authorization: - Every non-public endpoint must authenticate the caller. - Sessions and tokens must be validated for issuer, audience, signature, expiry, revocation, and intended authentication context. - Authentication failures must fail closed. - Sensitive operations must require recent or stronger authentication where appropriate. - Password-reset, account-recovery, MFA, and identity-linking flows must not permit account takeover.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

A strong security policy should include thorough details about how the application operates. Here’s an example of what to ask Codex to include in SECURITY.md:

<!-- SECURITY.md --> ### Authentication and Authorization - Every non-public endpoint must authenticate the caller. - Sessions and tokens must be validated for issuer, audience, signature, expiry, revocation, and intended authentication context. - Authentication failures must fail closed. - Sensitive operations must require recent or stronger authentication where appropriate. - Password-reset, account-recovery, MFA, and identity-linking flows must not permit account takeover. - Authentication secrets and tokens must never appear in logs, URLs, analytics, or error responses. - Authorization must occur before every read, mutation, transaction, export, or administrative action. - Possession of a valid account or resource identifier never proves authorization. - Customer, account, and tenant isolation must hold across list, detail, search, bulk, export, and indirect-reference endpoints. - Server-side authorization must not rely on client-supplied roles, ownership fields, prices, balances, or approval state. - Administrative and service-to-service permissions must use least privilege. - Failures allowing cross-customer access are reportable even when only one endpoint is affected. ### Transaction and ledger integrity - Transactions must be authorized against the authenticated customer and eligible source account. - Amounts, currencies, destinations, fees, limits, and approval state must be validated server-side. - Transaction requests must be protected against replay, duplication, race conditions, and idempotency-key confusion. - Balance checks and ledger updates must be atomic. - Posted ledger entries must be immutable or corrected through auditable compensating entries. - High-risk transactions must enforce applicable limits, step-up authentication, approval, or fraud controls. - No failure path may produce an ambiguous transaction state without reconciliation. ### Data protection - Sensitive data must be encrypted in transit and at rest using approved controls. - Secret material must come from an approved secret-management system rather than source code or ordinary configuration files. - Logs, traces, metrics, support tooling, and security artifacts must exclude credentials and minimize personal and financial data. - Data exports and backups must receive equivalent authorization and protection to primary data. - Error responses must not expose internals, sensitive records, credentials, or authorization details. - Retention and deletion behavior must follow the system’s approved data-governance requirements. ### Input and output handling - Treat headers, paths, query parameters, bodies, uploaded files, webhook payloads, third-party responses, and stored customer content as untrusted. - Apply schema, type, range, length, and format validation before security-sensitive use. - Database access must use parameterized queries. - Outbound requests must restrict destinations, protocols, redirects, DNS behavior, and response sizes. - Parsers, uploads, decompression, and serialization must be bounded against resource exhaustion. - Customer-controlled content must be safely encoded for its output context.

Let’s take a look at Apache Superset, an open-source business intelligence web application, as an example. The application connects to databases and lets users explore data, run SQL in SQL Lab, and build and share charts and dashboards. The security policy within their open-source repo establishes detailed context concerning roles and capabilities, as well as how async execution and realtime notifications operate. For example, the policy defines:

Asynchronous execution paths do not create a separate data-access capability. A background task is a continuation of an already-authorized action, such as reading chart data or executing SQL through SQL Lab. The initiating route, command, or scheduler must enforce the same route-level and object-level checks the synchronous path would enforce before it creates the task, and the worker must execute under the initiating principal’s effective identity when row-level security, impersonation, embedded guest-token scope, or similar controls affect the result.

This makes vulnerability reporting more precise because it defines what must remain true as execution moves from a request into a background worker. A reviewer can trace the initiating user, the requested resource, the authorization checks before task creation, and the identity used during execution. As a result, reports from both security researchers and agents can test the policy requirement, the code paths that could violate it, the attacker’s starting permissions, and the resulting unauthorized capability.

Codex Security

Once context is established, you should choose a review workflow that works with your team’s existing development process. Local review gives a developer feedback before a PR is opened. Automatic PR review provides a consistent team checkpoint. The CLI supports workflows that need explicit targets, saved artifacts, or custom CI integration.

You can also use multiple workflows. However, you should start with one workflow, inspect its results on a change the team understands, and then expand once the review is producing evidence people can use.

Codex Security Review in GitHub Cloud

The fastest way to automate security reviews in GitHub Cloud is through the Security Review feature within ChatGPT. This is available through the same product surface as Codex Code Reviews available within your organization at https://chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/settings/code-review.

Codex Security Review goes deeper than Code Review on security-specific risks by analyzing the pull request diff, supporting repository context, and configured threat models or security guidance.

Difference between Code Review and Security Review

Code Review is a broad engineering review that assesses code quality. For example, Code Review asks: “Could this change break the product or introduce a serious engineering problem?” It reviews issues such as incorrect control flow, data corruption or loss, compatibility regressions, or incorrect API behavior. The intended users for Code Review are software developers within the organization.

Codex Security is a specialized, deeper assessment of security risks in the same PR changes. Security Review is for both software developers responsible for remediating vulnerabilities, as well as application security engineers responsible for securing CI/CD pipelines and source code. It assesses issues such as authentication and authorization bypasses, cross-tenant access, injection and unsafe parsing, or sensitive data exposure.

Configuring security reviews

There are two options for configuring security reviews. The auto-review reporting determines which findings Codex posts to the PR when Security Review runs automatically. It is defaulted to High, so only High and Critical findings are posted.

The option for manual review controls which findings Codex posts after someone explicitly requests a Security Review. It is defaulted to Medium, so Medium, High, and Critical findings are posted.

When configured, posted vulnerabilities will surface within the PR.

It’s best to choose automatic reporting thresholds around what the team is prepared to investigate consistently. For a targeted investigation, use the manual review settings to surface the additional detail relevant to that question.

Setting path overrides

Path-based reporting overrides the minimum severity published to the GitHub PR. Given that a repository’s risk is rarely uniform, this feature can tailor the risk threshold for more critical paths, such as:

Lowering the threshold for authentication, authorization, payments, cryptography, CI workflows, or infrastructure.

Keeping a higher threshold for lower-risk or especially noisy areas.

You can modify the path overrides within the Codex Cloud settings for the selected repo. In this example below, we have established that src/** should have auto reviews for low vulnerabilities or higher. Changes to GitHub workflows or dependencies will enforce reporting for medium vulnerabilities.

A practical starting point is to identify the application’s sensitive operations and map them to paths with their owners. For the payment service example at the beginning of this post, that includes tenant authorization and billing mutations. I would review those paths with the team that owns them and choose a reporting threshold that reflects the consequence of a missed issue.

Going back to our Apache Superset example, I would keep a High repository-wide reporting threshold, but lower it for these paths:

Repository-relative path prefix

Minimum severity to report

Why it deserves additional attention

superset/security/

Low

Path contains code for central authorization, guest tokens, password recovery, and session invalidation

superset/row_level_security/

Low

Path controls the policies determining which data rows users can access

superset/sqllab/ and superset/commands/sql_lab/

Medium

Path focuses on SQL execution, query authorization, result retrieval, and exports

superset/embedded/

Medium

Path focuses on boundaries for dashboards embedded in other applications

If these settings were applied, then Codex Security Review would only report High vulnerabilities for all paths except those stated above. In those paths, Low and Medium would be reported given the additional sensitivity of the code.

Codex Security Review in Codex Desktop

For a more interactive experience reviewing PRs or uncommitted changes, you can also execute reviews through the security tab within Codex.

Alternatively, you can prompt Codex within the repository project of Codex by invoking the skill.

Please run a Security Diff Scan on the changes in the current branch.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

This workflow is most useful when the implementation is still fresh in your mind and you can investigate a finding immediately. If the review points to an authorization assumption, you can inspect the caller and the affected operation before the change moves into a separate review queue.

Codex Security Review in the CLI

Reviewing uncommitted local work

You can use the CLI to review uncommitted local work with seeded context about the repository and security policies.

Run the examples in the same shell from your Git checkout. They assume your security policy is in SECURITY.md and your supporting documents are in docs/security/. The setup creates a temporary directory for scan results.

northstar_repo="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" northstar_kb="$northstar_repo/docs/security" northstar_results="$(mktemp -d)"

npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --working-tree \ --base HEAD \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/working-tree"

This reviews staged and unstaged changes relative to HEAD.

Before starting, be sure to confirm that the working tree contains the change you intend to assess. Unrelated edits broaden the investigation and can make it harder to connect the findings to the question that prompted the review.

Reviewing PRs or branch commits

Another option is to review a PR or branch for security issues. Check out the branch to review and fetch its target branch. This example uses origin/main.

northstar_pr_base="$(git -C "$northstar_repo" merge-base origin/main HEAD)" npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --diff "$northstar_pr_base" \ --head HEAD \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/branch"

Note that a diff scan evaluates the proposed changes and does not scan the entire repository. Once complete, the output directory will contain the following files:

report.md: readable review

scan-manifest.json: confirms the exact base, head, target, and artifacts

findings.json: presents the severity, confidence, locations, and remediation

coverage.json: identifies the reviewed surfaces, exclusions, deferred work, and completeness

Scanning monorepos

In a monorepo, a change to a shared library can affect multiple services. Codex should receive enough context to review those interactions, while CI determines which components and checks are required.

Repository context

Keep shared engineering instructions in AGENTS.md and security expectations in SECURITY.md. A typical repository could look like this:

monorepo/ ├── AGENTS.md ├── SECURITY.md ├── docs/security/ │ ├── architecture.md │ └── threat-model.md ├── packages/auth/ └── services/ ├── billing/ └── reporting/

Use existing ownership and build metadata to connect each component to its dependencies, consumers, and tests. For example, a change to packages/auth may require reviewing both services even when their files are unchanged. This scope mapping is maintained by your organization; it is not automatically configured by adding Codex.

Component assessment

Large repositories may not always require scanning the entire codebase for each PR. One option is to use a path scan when a monorepo contains separate services or packages. Repeat --path to assess a shared library and its consumers together.

npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --path packages/auth \ --path services/billing \ --path services/reporting \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/paths"

This scans only the selected paths rather than the entire repository.

PR and diff scanning

For a PR, use its exact base and head commit hashes from authenticated GitHub metadata. Both revisions and their history must be available in the checkout. The following example reuses the variables above and saves the diff results separately:

BASE_SHA="<full PR base commit SHA>" HEAD_SHA="<full PR head commit SHA>" BASE_REVISION="$( git -C "$northstar_repo" merge-base "$BASE_SHA" "$HEAD_SHA" )" || exit npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --diff "$BASE_REVISION" \ --head "$HEAD_SHA" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --auth chatgpt \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/pr"

A diff scan focuses on the proposed changes. If a shared-library change requires broader consumer review, also run the component assessment against a clean checkout of that PR’s head revision. Keep the results distinct: --diff and --path are separate scan modes and cannot be combined.

Scanning alerts from GitHub

You can also assess code scanning alerts from the default branch using the Codex Security CLI.

northstar_github_repository="example/northstar" northstar_github_alerts="$northstar_results/github-alerts.json" # Import all open alerts as complete JSON. npx @openai/codex-security import github "$northstar_github_repository" \ --format json \ > "$northstar_github_alerts" # Or import a selected subset. npx @openai/codex-security import github "$northstar_github_repository" \ --github-alert 12 \ --github-alert 18 \ --format json \ > "$northstar_github_alerts" # Run from the corresponding local repository; imported contents are data. cd "$northstar_repo" npx @openai/codex-security validate "$northstar_github_alerts"

GitHub Actions workflows

Instead of enforcing security reviews through Codex, it is also possible to create custom workflows that run the Codex Security CLI. We’ve packaged this workflow to easily be used as a GitHub Action.

# .github/workflows/codex-security-repository.yml name: Codex Security review on: workflow_dispatch: schedule: - cron: "23 7 * * 1" # Mondays at 07:23 UTC permissions: contents: read jobs: security: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - name: Set up the Ubuntu sandbox run: | sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install --yes bubblewrap apparmor-profiles sudo apparmor_parser -r /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 with: persist-credentials: false - uses: openai/codex-security@3f61e5150981a5087c32e4395bbaa8ce5ce0c3e3 # action-v0.3.0 with: model: gpt-5.6-sol effort: high env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY }}

These workflows can also be applied to other source code management tools like GitLab, BitBucket, or Jenkins. Take a look at our documentation page to learn more: Run Codex Security in CI.

Managing supply chain risk in CI/CD

You can also leverage the Codex Security CLI to assess dependencies in the codebase, such as when a new dependency is introduced or a version is bumped.

This is extremely useful in preventing vulnerable packages from presenting supply chain risk – you can achieve this by deploying the Codex Security CLI as commands within custom workflows.

Validating Dependabot alerts

Codex Security provides a skill for validating existing third-party vulnerabilities, including Dependabot, for reachability and exploitability. You can invoke the skill directly in the UI or through the CLI.

Use Triage Finding to import and triage Dependabot vulnerabilities against this repository.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

Codex will triage each of the Dependabot alerts and subsequently present a ledger of each presented risk with a reason why the alert was validated or not.

Looking at Apache Superset again, we can take its documentation toolchain to identify a security advisory related to it (such as webpack-dev-server advisory).

Using Codex, we can trace the dependency through Docusaurus, check the resolved version, and follow the development, build, and deployment paths to establish where the affected functionality could run. The reviewed lockfile selected version 5.2.6, which the advisory identifies as patched.

Codex’s analysis therefore supported a specific conclusion: the advisory did not affect the version selected by that documentation revision. Before closing a corresponding Dependabot alert, we would reconcile its reported version and revision with this evidence and verify the installed dependency.

Running scans when package versions change

It is also possible to run security scans against the latest version of a dependency when the version is changed.

# .github/workflows/codex-security-dependency.yml name: Codex Security dependency scan on: pull_request: paths: - package.json - package-lock.json permissions: contents: read jobs: scan: name: Scan dependency changes if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 timeout-minutes: 45 steps: - name: Set up the Ubuntu sandbox run: | sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install --yes bubblewrap apparmor-profiles sudo apparmor_parser -r /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict - name: Set up Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7 with: node-version: "26" - name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@5fda3b95a4ea91299a34e894583c3862153e4b97 # v7 with: python-version: "3.14" - name: Install Codex Security run: | set -euo pipefail npm install \ --prefix "$RUNNER_TEMP/codex-security" \ --ignore-scripts \ --no-audit \ --no-fund \ @openai/codex-security - name: Verify Codex Security env: CODEX_SECURITY_BIN: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security/node_modules/.bin/codex-security run: | set -euo pipefail test -x "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" --version - name: Check out the pull request uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} fetch-depth: 0 persist-credentials: false - name: Install project dependencies run: | set -euo pipefail npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund - name: Run full repository scan env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY }} CODEX_SECURITY_BIN: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security/node_modules/.bin/codex-security CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-state SCAN_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-results run: | set -euo pipefail "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" scan . \ --auth api-key \ --output-dir "$SCAN_DIR" \ --fail-on-severity high \ --json > "$RUNNER_TEMP/codex-security.json" - name: Preserve scan results if: always() uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7 with: name: codex-security-dependency-results path: | ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-results ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security.json if-no-files-found: warn retention-days: 7

Wrapping up

As agents contribute more code, security teams must carve the right scaffolding for agentic systems to reason across the codebase for application security reviews and enforce gates when insecure code could be committed.

Start with a few critical repositories, commit your threat models and security policies, then review the pull requests to assess how accurately agents are reasoning against enterprise context and the codebase. When you begin to feel confident in the quality of the results, begin to expand into a broader number of repositories or pipelines as you expand agentic security coverage in the SDLC.

Full Text:
BLUF: Debian and Ubuntu dropped a config directive in the rsyslogd package in early 2023.

As any of my FOR577 students will tell you, I'm a fan of ISO-8601 (ok, RFC 3339, too, see below). They'll probably also tell you I'm a firm believer in UTC||GTFO especially on servers (also true, and I've made stickers to prove it). I was also asked recently why the syslog timestamps in newer Ubuntu and Debian systems changed to ISO-8601 (well, probably actually RFC 3339, but I won't got down that rabbithole in this handler's diary) timestamps from the historical Mmm dd hh:mm:ss format we've known since the 1980s. I had noticed the same, a few years ago, but never really paid attention to it. Given the question from a student, I decided to do a little research on the subject and this diary is the result.

To back up some, the syslog protocol and syslogd were originally the creation of Eric Allman in 1983 because he needed a way to debug sendmail[1]. They became part of BSD 4.2 that same year. BSD 4.2 also happened to be my introduction to Unix in 1983. Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2 major branches of Unix at the time. System V adopted the protocol and routing interfaces but built the daemon on top of System V internals.

The first effort to develop the protocol into an actual standard was an IETF draft in Oct 2000 that evolved into RFC 3164[2] in 2001, by which time the protocol was actually already 18 years old. This is the syslog message format we've all come to know so well over the years. Meanwhile, around 2005, rsyslogd added the option of outputing RFC 3339 timestamps. In 2009, RFC 3164 was superceded by RFC 5424[3] which defined the timestamp to be of the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss]Z or YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss](+/-)hh:mm. Despite the new RFC, the default setting even for rsyslogd in most Linux distros continued to be to write messages to the log files in the older format (referred to as the BSD format, as specified in the title of RFC 3164), by setting a directive in /etc/rsyslog.conf (the RSYSLOG_TraditionalFileFormat directive).

That brings us to 2023, with the release of Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 23.04 (not a LTS release) both distros stopped installing rsyslogd by default and defaulted to the systemd journal for logging and removed the directive from the default config file for those who did install it.. Many system administrators continue to install rsyslogd because they had infrastructure in place for forwarding syslog to central log servers and/or SIEMs. These are the folks most likely to have noticed the format change. Meanwhile, Fedora and Alma (and presumably the rest of the RedHat family) have left the directive in place when the package is installed.

From a Ubuntu 24.04 system:

From a Fedora 44 system:

Meanwhile you can get either one with journalctl by setting the output format to either short (BSD format) or short-iso-precise (ISO format).

Also, note that rsyslogd is not the only option for a syslog server. I've been using syslog-ng as the syslog server on my home log collector since about 2000. In syslog-ng, the new 'ISO' timestamps can be enabled by setting the following two options in syslog-ng.conf: ts-format(iso) and frac-digits(6). Since I have just been upgrading my central log server for years, I haven't done a fresh install lately, so I'm not sure if that is the default. I had to explicitly add it to my config.

References:

1. The History of Centralized Logging

2. RFC 3164: The BSD Syslog Protocol

3. RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol

Title: Your Endpoint Protection Works. So Why Add EDR?
Context: Your endpoint protection is doing exactly what you bought it to do: stop malware, ransomware, and other threats before they can harm your business
Full Text:
Your endpoint protection is doing exactly what you bought it to do: stop malware, ransomware, and other threats before they can harm your business.

So why add Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)?

Because prevention and detection solve different parts of the same problem. Endpoint protection blocks threats. EDR helps you recognize, understand, and respond to suspicious activity that may indicate an attack underway.

For lean IT teams, that visibility is increasingly valuable as AI helps attackers rapidly discover and leverage new vulnerabilities and launch more convincing attacks targeting your people.

If Endpoint Protection Works, What Does EDR Add?

EDR adds the context needed to understand suspicious activity across your endpoints and act before it becomes a larger incident. Individual actions can appear harmless when viewed separately. EDR correlates endpoint activity, connecting those signals into an incident your team can investigate. It helps answer:

Where did the activity begin?

Which endpoints and users are involved?

How is the activity progressing?

What action should we take?

EDR helps explain what happened and guides next steps.

Why Does AI Make EDR More Important?

AI makes EDR more critical because it helps attackers increase the speed, volume, and sophistication of their activity.

According to the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 52.6% of surveyed IT and cybersecurity professionals believe AI is helping attackers more than defenders. AI can help threat actors improve phishing, vary malicious code and accelerate reconnaissance.

This does not make endpoint protection ineffective. It increases the likelihood of activity requiring investigation. A compromised account, unusual command sequence or misused legitimate tool may not present a simple “malware blocked” moment. Your team needs context to determine whether it is routine, risky, or part of an attack.

Is EDR Too Complex for a Small Security Team?

EDR is not too complex for a lean team if correlation, investigation guidance, and response are built into the endpoint security platform the team already uses.

In GravityZone Business Security Enterprise, EPP and EDR capabilities are integrated within the same platform. GravityZone automatically correlates attacks across endpoints. By automatically consolidating incidents into a unified, larger incident, it accelerates response and streamlines workflows.

Incident insights and response recommendations simplify investigation, so your team gains more security context without starting over with a separate security environment. This leads to better security outcomes because faster understanding gives attackers less time to establish persistence, steal data, or disrupt operations.

Is EDR Worth the Investment for a Small or Mid-Sized Business?

EDR is worth considering when the financial and operational impact of a serious incident could exceed the cost of strengthening security before one occurs.

Smaller organizations have fewer specialists and less capacity to absorb downtime. The question is whether the existing team has enough information to recognize and contain suspicious activity when prevention cannot provide the full story.

Security expectations are changing, and organizations must keep up. Customers, business partners, cyber insurers, and regulators increasingly ask organizations to demonstrate they can detect and respond to threats, not simply block them. EDR adds the visibility and investigation detail to achieve that.

Your endpoint protection works. Adding EDR helps ensure that when something unusual happens, your team can see the larger picture and respond before a suspicious event becomes a business-wide incident.

What are three reasons to add EDR to EPP?

Title: Perplexity and Intelligence

Full Text: Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Title: Six Things Every Exec Believes About Recovery, Until They’re Wrong
The Outages Are Just Getting Started
Context: Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”

Title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS
Context: Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is...
Full Text:
Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete."

The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen.

It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature.

Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

"The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy."

The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk.

Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android).

"However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said.

"Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system."

Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data.

Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users -

Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience

Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing

The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup.

On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications.

In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post.

"We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said.

"In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents."

Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings.

Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

Today we are joined by Prince Chaddha, ProjectDiscovery researcher, discussing how abliterated models can get you pwned. Title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
Context: 6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month
Full Text: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline. Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry. The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well. The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight. Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs. Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies. PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability. The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range. Another tricky day for PHP devs For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles. As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves. “In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote. Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®

Title: What’s Really Behind the Recent Tech Outages?
Context: Some vulnerabilities found with AI can be exploited by attackers and others are addressed before they pose a real risk
Full Text:
What’s Really Behind the Recent Tech Outages?

November 20, 2026

By the GuidePoint Research and Intelligence Team (GRIT)

BLOG

5 min.

Following a string of highly visible tech outages, from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), many people are asking the same question. Kim Nash at The Wall Street Journal put it simply: how do we make sense of all this?

It’s tempting to assume a coordinated cyberattack. So far, the evidence points elsewhere: increased attention on ordinary outages, alongside a growing volume of technical changes as organizations work to patch vulnerabilities that artificial intelligence (AI) is helping them discover.

TL;DR – The recent tech outages don’t appear connected and none has been tied to a cyberattack so far.

Key takeaways:

Outages are common. Heightened media attention can make routine downtime feel like a trend.

AI is helping organizations find more vulnerabilities faster, which means more patches.

Every patch is a change and every change can introduce risk.

Organizations may be working through years of technical debt as vulnerabilities are discovered.

What Happened During the Recent Tech Outages?

It started on November 12, when Microsoft 365 went down. Outlook, Teams and other services were disrupted for much of the business day and into the evening. Microsoft traced the problem to an issue from an earlier network capacity upgrade and said a cyberattack was not to blame.

The next day, the FAA halted departing flights across the country, only the third nationwide ground stop in U.S. history. Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed. The FAA blamed an equipment issue during an upgrade to the telecommunications network that connects air traffic control facilities. Over the same few days, a widely used human resources (HR) and payroll platform, several major U.S. banks and a major airline also had outages. In each case, the organizations involved pointed to technical problems.

While outages are common across every industry, they’re rarely noticed. However, the recent string of outages, ranging from a few hours of downtime on a highly visible system to nationwide disruptions, have drawn national media attention. These stories have led to widspread speculation, which can be a natural response. When several major services go down within days of each other, it’s easy to assume there’s a connection, even when there isn’t one.

That doesn’t make these tech outages trivial. Many businesses depend on the same handful of platforms, so a disruption at one provider can reach organizations far from the source.

Why Are There So Many More Patches?

AI has made vulnerability discovery trivial for anyone willing to spend the tokens. In May, one major security vendor fixed 75 flaws, compared with its usual five per month.

Some vulnerabilities found with AI can be exploited by attackers and others are addressed before they pose a real risk. Either way, organizations are facing more remediation work than they are accustomed to and much of that work ends in a patch.

Why Do More Changes Mean More Outages?

Every patch is a change to a production system and every change carries some risk of causing an unforeseen issue. That risk grows with the number of changes and the number of underlying systems involved. When those systems support other businesses, even small issues can have a much wider impact.

Other kinds of change carry the same risk. Microsoft traced its outage to an earlier network upgrade and the FAA blamed an equipment issue during a network upgrade. Neither has been described as a security patch, but both show how routine changes to large, interconnected systems can have outsized effects.

Is the Holiday Code Freeze Making It Worse?

Many organizations freeze changes before the holidays to protect peak traffic. That can push teams to fit more changes than usual into the weeks before the freeze. Every organization handles its change windows differently, but this timing could be adding to the problem.

When Will Things Settle Down?

In GRIT’s view, the number of vulnerabilities waiting to be discovered is likely finite. AI is surfacing years of technical debt in a short period. Once major organizations work through it, the pace of change and the disruptions that can come with it, may return to relative normalcy.

What Should Security Leaders Do Now?

Check the root cause before you escalate. Not every outage is a cyberattack, so build a triage step into your incident process and tell your executives what is known and what is still unknown.

Treat every patch as a change. Test it, schedule it and have a rollback plan ready.

Plan patching around your holiday freeze so you don’t rush untested changes.

Know which outside platforms your business depends on and what happens when one goes down.

Have an outage communications plan ready. When a service goes down, early and honest updates help you keep the trust of customers and employees.

What the Recent Tech Outages Tell Us

The recent tech outages are a reminder of how much businesses depend on a small number of shared platforms, especially as vulnerability discovery accelerates and change becomes more frequent.

Managing vulnerabilities and minimizing disruption takes more than keeping up with patches. Organizations need a clear understanding of their exposure, a reliable testing process and a plan for responding when a critical system goes down.

Talk with our team about strengthening your vulnerability management and incident response programs.

FAQs

Can a security patch cause an outage?

None has been tied to a cyberattack so far. Microsoft said its outage was not a cyberattack and other affected organizations have pointed to technical problems.

Can a security patch cause an outage?

Yes. Every patch changes a production system and any change can cause unexpected issues in complex, connected environments.

Why are there more patches right now?

AI tools are helping vendors and researchers find far more vulnerabilities and many of them need a fix.

How can organizations reduce outage risk from patching?

A structured patch management process with testing, scheduling and rollback plans reduces the chance of disruption.

What should security leaders communicate during an outage?

Share what is known, what is unknown and what steps are underway. Early, honest updates maintain trust with customers and leadership.

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
Context: Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent...
Full Text: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers. First the flood, then the dams While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®

Executive Summary

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap out-of-bounds write in HotSpot’s AVX-512 Base64 decoder on x86-64. Calif reported it and showed pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Nobody has reported exploitation in the wild as of November 17, 2026. CISA issued an alert that same day, urging everyone to patch now.

Your Java4Shell Response Plan

If you can’t patch today, start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart it.

You’re only exposed on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM64 isn’t affected.

Tip for Qualys customers: you can apply the step 2 flag with TruRisk Eliminate, targeting only the hosts that need it and rolling it back in one click.

Oracle shipped the fixed builds on November 17, 2026. October’s builds are still vulnerable.

How the Java4Shell Attack Chain Works

This is a typical Java4Shell attack chain:

The attacker needs a Base64 decode value they can control. Vulnerability discoverers were able to reach this pre-authentication condition via authentication in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after login in Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. A Java client that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server is exposed too.

The attacker then sends valid decodes until the server compiler compiles the fast path, then the bad input: 64 valid characters and one =, or 128 and one = on older 17 builds.

The target must pass the gates in the source. The JVM must see avx512_vbmi and avx512bw with UseAVX=3, the intrinsic must be on, and on 17u the input must be longer than 128 characters.

The stub’s tail handling goes wrong. The next section walks through it.

On a fixed build, or with the intrinsic off, nothing happens. Otherwise, 62 or 63 bytes land past the destination array on the Java heap.

Vulnerability researchers mentioned that they groomed the heap (G1 regions, thread-local allocation buffers) to turn that write into code execution. Unsuccessful exploitation will lead to a denial-of-service condition on the endpoint.

This remote code execution chain has only been mentioned as achieved by the vulnerability researchers. Nobody has reported it in the wild yet.

Tracing Java4Shell to Its Root Cause

Based on the jdk17u source at the fix commit, HotSpot generates the stub in generate_base64_decodeBlock (it shows up as implDecode at runtime), and C2 calls it from java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0 once that method is hot. JDK-8268276 added the AVX-512 decoder in JDK 18 and JDK-8296735 backported it to 17.0.6, so 17.0.5 and older are clean.

The whole vector decoder sits inside if (VM_Version::supports_avx512_vbmi() && VM_Version::supports_avx512bw()). Without both features HotSpot only builds the scalar 4-character loop, which is fine. 17u has no AVX2 decoder; the AVX2 tables in that file are for encoding. MIME input goes straight to the scalar loop. Basic and URL input take the vector path once it’s longer than 128 characters.

The vector code decodes 64 characters a pass, and L_finalBit handles the last 1 to 63. Before the fix, a tail of 1 to 3 characters ending in = gave an output size of 0, and the padding step subtracted 1 from it. The output mask then came from bzhiq with an index of -1. bzhiq only reads the low 8 bits of the index, so -1 became 255, nothing got cleared and the mask stayed all ones. The final masked store wrote a full 64 bytes where it should have written none.

The exact trigger condition on 17u follows from the control flow. The input must be longer than 128 characters and go through the basic or URL decoder, since MIME goes to the scalar loop. Inputs of 256 characters or more run through 256-character passes, then everything runs through 64-character passes, so the tail left at L_finalBit is the length modulo 64. Every character in those passes must be valid Base64; a = or any other bad character inside a pass makes the stub exit early and hand the rest to Java. The tail must be 1 to 3 characters ending in =, and any non-padding character in it must also be valid. Put together, the bad lengths are 64k + 1 to 64k + 3 for k of 2 or more: 129 to 131, 193 to 195, 257 to 259 and so on. Legitimate padded Base64 always has a length that’s a multiple of 4, so none of these inputs is valid anyway. Unpadded values such as JWT segments can have other lengths, but they never end in =. That makes length modulo 64 plus a trailing = a tighter hunting signal than “not a multiple of 4”.

The fix, JDK-8393212, adds four lines at L_finalBit: if fewer than 4 characters remain, jump to L_bruteForce, the scalar path. The commit title is “Base64 optimization improvements”, which tells you nothing.

The fix closes the underflow and causes no other change. The new check runs before the stub computes either the input mask or the output size. With 4 or more characters left, the output size starts at (length / 4) × 3, which is at least 3. Padding takes off at most 2, so the size stays at 1 or more and bzhiq always gets a valid index. A tail made only of = fails the validity check and drops to the scalar loop. Tails of 1 to 3 characters never reach the vector code at all. I checked memory safety only. I didn’t check whether the stub decodes every odd-length tail of 4 to 63 characters correctly, and the fix doesn’t touch that logic.

No CWE is assigned yet. I’d file it as an integer underflow (CWE-191) that causes an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Windows x64 gets the same vector code; the function only differs in how it reads its arguments there. I’ve only read the 17u source. Calif’s shorter trigger on newer lines suggests a lower threshold than 128 characters there, but I haven’t confirmed it.

Confirm Exposure From Inside the Java Runtime

A JVM is exposed only when all four of these conditions are true:

It runs on an x86-64 CPU with avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2. That covers Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire, Emerald and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Skylake-SP and Cascade Lake have AVX-512 but no VBMI.

It’s OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or 18 to 27, below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack counts too, because it ships a 17-based VM.

UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics=true, which are the defaults on those CPUs.

Attacker input reaches the basic or URL decoder in java.util.Base64. Basic auth and JWT parsing do this before login.

A quiet service isn’t safe. The attacker warms up C2 with valid decodes first.

The OS doesn’t change the bug. Windows x64 gets the same generated code as Linux, though only Linux has public testing.

I wouldn’t rely on /proc/cpuinfo. It doesn’t exist outside Linux, and an empty result looks like “not affected”. Ask the JVM what it sees instead, on any OS: java -Xlog:os+cpu -version 2>&1 | grep -oE ‘avx512f|avx512bw|avx512_vbmi|bmi2’ | sort -u java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E ‘ (UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics) ‘

All four flags, UseAVX = 3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics = true mean that runtime is exposed. Run the check with each java binary on the host, since each runtime reports its own settings.

Turn the intrinsic off with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart the JVM. With that flag HotSpot never generates the stub, which I confirmed in the source and on a live JVM. Oracle hasn’t published it as a workaround.

Control

Impact

Trade-off

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Base64 decoding falls back to plain Java and runs slower. No one has published a number

Also stops it, since the VBMI decoder never gets built, but it drops every AVX-512 optimization. ARM64 JVMs won’t start with it

Migration work, and a reschedule back onto a VBMI node re-exposes you

Skip -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock. Upwind reports it fails unless you also pass -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions.

CISA’s alert also suggests validating Base64 at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Boundary validation helps if it rejects padded input whose length isn’t a multiple of 4 before the decoder runs. Size limits won’t: the trigger is 65 characters on newer lines, shorter than most Basic-auth and JWT values. Limiting unauthenticated access works, but it means network ACLs or a VPN in front, because the vulnerable decode happens before login.

Mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate

For Qualys customers, the Java4Shell mitigation is available now with TruRisk Eliminate on Linux and Windows hosts, linked to QIDs such as 389494. As additional QIDs are released for different operating systems, we will test them and add support. The Cloud Agent runs it on the hosts you pick. Before it changes anything, it checks that the host has an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime, so hosts that can’t hit the bug are left alone. On the hosts that can, it adds -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and keeps whatever value was already there.

The setting takes effect when each JVM restarts, so plan restarts with the application owners. Windows services pick it up after a host reboot. After the change, the agent reports every running Java process with its effective setting, worked out in the order HotSpot applies options. A JVM it can’t read shows up as unknown, so you know where to look instead of assuming it’s covered.

Rollback is one click in the console and restores the previous value. The mitigation doesn’t reach containers; set the flag in the image or pod spec for those. Treat it as a bridge to the patched builds, since Oracle hasn’t published the flag as a workaround.

Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?Java4Shell is a heap out-of-bounds write in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM on x86-64. A malformed Base64 value can make the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of an array on the Java heap. Researchers turned that into pre-authentication remote code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

Which Java versions are affected by Java4Shell?OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, and versions 18 to 27, are affected below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack is also affected because it uses a 17-based VM. Oracle released the fixed builds on November 17, 2026: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1 and 8u513-perf. Vendor builds that include fix JDK-8393212 are also safe. Java 8 standard and Java 11 are not affected.

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 17, 2026. Remote code execution has only been demonstrated by researchers. CISA issued an alert the same day urging organizations to patch now.

How do I know if my Java runtime is exposed to Java4Shell?A Java runtime is exposed only when all four conditions are true. It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. It’s an affected version. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics are on, which are the defaults on those CPUs. And attacker input reaches the Basic or URL Base64 decoder. Check by asking each Java binary what it sees, not by reading /proc/cpuinfo. ARM64 is not affected.

How can I close the Java4Shell vulnerability if I can’t patch yet?You can mitigate it by starting the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restarting it. With this flag, HotSpot never generates the vulnerable code. Oracle hasn’t published it as an official workaround, so treat it as a bridge until you can patch.

How do I mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate?Apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics with TruRisk Eliminate through the Qualys Cloud Agent. It automatically targets only Linux and Windows hosts that have an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime. It keeps existing JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS values, reports the effective setting for every running Java process and offers one-click rollback.
