Full Text: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim. "As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said. The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders." Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy. "It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. "Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience." Smart specs can't shake the hate When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees. "Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time. Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces. Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time. Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas. On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning. With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general. A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children. There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy. A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament. The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

Title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 47 (2026)
Context: The Bad | Autonomous AI-Powered Pentesting Tool “ARTEX” Abused to Launch Global Cyberattacks A FLASH advisory from the FBI went out this past week, warning that threat actors...
Full Text:
The Good | Italian Officials Extradite “8-Digits” Ransomware Affiliate & U.S. Courts Sentence SMS Attacker to Prison

Italian authorities have extradited a Kazakh national, Roman Khlynovskiy, to the United States to face charges for orchestrating attacks against the American healthcare and education sectors. Prosecutors allege that Khlynovskiy operated within the "8-Digits Team", an affiliate syndicate linked to INC and Lynx ransomware operations.

The group breached networks across six states, stealing over 50 terabytes of sensitive data, including 70 million medical files, to extort over $500 million in ransom demands. Khlynovskiy now faces up to 27 years in prison on multiple cyber fraud and extortion counts if convicted.

U.S. federal courts also sentenced 24-year-old Tyler Robert Buchanan to six years in prison for the theft of millions in cryptocurrency through multiple breaches. In custody since April 2025, Buchanan pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Buchanan and his conspirators targeted corporate employees across technology, telecommunications, and outsourcing firms through hundreds of SMS phishing messages. After tricking staff into giving up enterprise credentials, they executed SIM-swapping attacks to compromise cryptocurrency accounts, ultimately stealing over $11.6 million in digital assets before federal investigators dismantled the ring.

In Ukraine, police partnered with the FBI to arrest four members of an international ransomware group linked to over $40.5 million in ransom payments. The criminal network breached at least 28 corporate victims across logistics, energy, finance, and healthcare sectors worldwide.

To infiltrate corporate networks, the attackers deployed social engineering tactics combined with AI-generated voice calls to impersonate IT support specialists and steal network credentials. Law enforcement officers conducted 66 coordinated searches across 11 regions, seizing computers, mobile phones, bank cards, and nearly $370,000 in cash.

The Bad | Autonomous AI-Powered Pentesting Tool “ARTEX” Abused to Launch Global Cyberattacks

A FLASH advisory from the FBI went out this past week, warning that threat actors are deploying an AI-powered pentesting framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks across global organizations. Written in the Go programming language, ARTEX operates as an automated penetration testing suite that translates high-level attacker objectives into coordinated tasks executed by specialized software agents.

Rather than deploying its own machine-learning models, the framework integrates directly with commercial LLMs, including OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, DeepSeek, Grok, and others. These autonomous agents perform reconnaissance, discover software vulnerabilities, execute exploits, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data with minimal human supervision.

The FBI highlighted how ARTEX accelerates attack velocity, compressing intrusion timelines from initial targeting to privileged access to under three hours in multiple cases. The framework proves particularly effective at identifying overlooked perimeter weaknesses, such as exposed partner portals, unpatched legacy services, and misconfigured third-party application programming interfaces.

Although the original developer, Autumn-27, removed the primary GitHub repository in October, threat actors continue to distribute the software through community forks, archived mirrors, and a commercial edition dubbed “ARTEX PRO”.

The FBI report notes several high-profile intrusions driven by the toolset, including the October ConnectWise supply-chain breach by China-aligned group Storm-0940, which attempted unauthorized authentication across more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer tenants.

Chinese-speaking operators have also been observed pairing ARTEX with Claude Code to breach major South Korean financial institutions, while one espionage-focused actor targeted over 200 organizations across 14 countries.

SentinelOne customers are protected from ARTEX agents via Behavioral AI, which detects the shell spawned by a compromised web application and the reconnaissance tools the ARTEX agent runs, the escalation to root on a Linux host, and DLL sideloading on a Windows host.

The Ugly | Attackers Target Critical “Java4Shell” Flaw in OpenJDK Across Enterprise Applications

A critical memory corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK, dubbed “Java4Shell”, enables unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute arbitrary code in popular enterprise software, including Atlassian Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, and Keycloak. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938 with a CVSS score of 9.2, the flaw resides within the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding routine of the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine.

The issue impacts OpenJDK 17.0.6 onward, including versions 21, 25, and 27. However, exploitation strictly requires x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. Since Java applications decode Base64 data in authentication headers, tokens, and file uploads before authenticating users, remote adversaries can trigger the flaw without credentials.

A malformed Base64 string ending with an extraneous equals sign forces the decoder to write 62 fixed bytes past buffer boundaries. In controlled testing, researchers chained this overflow to expand adjacent memory arrays, reading server secrets via a technique called “JavaBleed” and redirecting program flow to achieve complete remote code execution (RCE).

The bug lacks a universal exploit payload. Instead, each target requires customized memory arrangement and precise timing. Researchers independently rediscovered the flaw in an hour using an AI coding agent and built a first working exploit two hours later; an earlier public bug report from June had gone unpatched.

While Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, threat actors have begun probing internet-facing infrastructure. Honeypots have logged reconnaissance traffic and blind exploitation attempts, though no successful in-the-wild exploitation has been confirmed.

CISA has also issued an advisory urging immediate patching. SentinelOne customers are protected against Java4Shell. SentinelOne continues to defend its customers against Java4Shell, with details found here.

Title: The New Analyst Learning Curve: Training and Retaining Talent in the Autonomous SOC
Context: Give each analyst a yearly rotation through incident response, threat hunting, or detection engineering
Full Text:
Ask a senior analyst how they learned the job, and closing false positives rarely comes up. That work mostly built alert fatigue. The learning happened in rarer moments: the real hit, the escalation that became an incident, the Tier 2 analyst walking you through what you missed.

Agentic investigation now clears much of that queue. For coverage, that's a clear win. For your bench, it removes the place where people learned. Earlier this year, we mapped where the analyst role is heading. This blog covers the leader's side: how to get your people there without losing what the queue used to teach.

Security comes from habits repeated in everyday moments. Analyst judgment is built the same way, through reps. Naturally, if AI removes those reps, leaders have to schedule the practice back in.

The Autonomous SOC can relieve the grind that drives burnout, but only for leaders who deliberately maintain the learning that used to happen naturally. The grind was also the learning curve, and organizations must prove it that they haven’t lost it.

Two Talent Problems, One Shift

By taking over triage, AI now affects retention and the talent pipeline at once, and each problem feeds the other.

Start with retention: in addition to shift work, after-hours pages, understaffing, and pay, repetitive work has driven SOC attrition for years. AI is supposed to relieve that repetition, but the early data is mixed: in ISC2's 2026 Rethinking AI's Impact on Cybersecurity Roles report, 48% of professionals using AI say it lowered their stress, while 32% say it raised it. That second group is more likely to report spending extra time validating AI output and deciding when to trust it. Without structure, AI moves the stress into validation work.

The pipeline shows a similar split: the same report found 56% say AI has reduced the need for entry-level roles, while 53% say it is creating new entry-level opportunities. Both can be true: the old entry-level job is shrinking and a different one is taking its place. And AI skills now top the list of skills needs in ISC2's 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, cited by 41% of respondents who reported a skills need. You can't hire your way out of a senior shortage if no one is coming up the ladder behind them.

The obvious objection: if AI handles triage, juniors don't need to learn it. ISC2's respondents disagree: 62% say AI has not reduced the need for foundational skills, versus 26% who say it has. Someone still has to recognize a wrong verdict, and that judgment used to come from triage.

The Capabilities At Risk

Reviewing an investigation is a different skill from conducting one. An analyst can become very good at evaluating an automated system's work without the independent expertise to see when that system is fundamentally wrong. The capabilities most at risk are the ones the old queue exercised without anyone planning it:

Approaching an unfamiliar problem with no verdict to start from

Forming competing hypotheses instead of testing the first one offered

Noticing missing or incomplete evidence

Recognizing when the premise of an investigation is wrong

Write these down. Every practice below should build at least one of them, and every metric should test whether they hold.

What the Job Is Now

Responsibilities are shifting at every level of the SOC.

Tier 1 analysts move from closing every alert to reviewing AI verdicts and escalating the ones that don't hold up.

Natural-language querying speeds up hunting, but writing and reading queries is how they learn the data: the schema, the parsing gaps, the missing logs.

The path out of triage runs toward detection engineering, where analysts write and tune the logic the AI depends on.

Workflow design and leadership reporting stay with SOC engineering, IR leads, and managers, who now also own the rules the AI works within.

Each new responsibility assumes judgment that analysts used to build by doing the old one. Training must supply it now.

Training: Rebuilding the Learning Curve

Training is also how autonomy gets earned, as we covered in our retrospective review of our Autonomous SOC Maturity Model. Partial Autonomy (Level 3) is built on how analysts conduct investigations independently, and how they review investigations: which AI results they accept, modify, or override. Trained analysts make their records trustworthy before the system acts alone.

Five practices a SOC manager can start this quarter:

Run blind investigations. Have analysts work a share of live alerts cold, before they see the AI's verdict. Replay past incidents the same way, with the verdict withheld. Then use the AI's evidence chain as the answer key. Additionally, expand peer reviews: Add in 5 to 10 AI-closed cases per analyst per week and run quality assurance. This keeps investigative skills sharp and teaches where AI is reliable and where it needs a human.

Schedule the reps. Purple teaming, atomic tests, replays of past incidents, and tabletop exercises put analysts in front of attacks where the answer is known. Put them on a fixed calendar so they survive a busy quarter. Emulated attacks also let you score what the AI missed and what the analysts missed, separately. Current threat intelligence keeps the techniques realistic.

Make the AI's work the curriculum. Have juniors trace agentic investigations back to the raw telemetry: what was gathered, what was compared, why the conclusion followed. In addition, review the misses: wrong verdicts expose exactly where the AI's reasoning broke. Ask why the AI missed and feed the answer back into your workflows.

Treat ownership as governance training. Stage people the way you stage automation: crawl, walk, run. Juniors start by reviewing verdicts, then own a low-risk automated workflow such as phishing response. From there, they expand by domain. Ensure they read generated queries, because they’re learning AI verifiability and governance.

Train analysts. Give each analyst a yearly rotation through incident response, threat hunting, or detection engineering. Teams without those functions in-house can co-investigate with an MDR or IR partner.

Retaining: Make the New Work Visible and Rewarded

Training without recognition just builds a better resume for your competitor.

Rewrite the career ladder. If promotion criteria still count alerts closed, you're rewarding work that AI now does. Promote on independent investigation performance, as well as hypotheses tested, AI misses caught, and detection coverage added.

Change what you measure. Measure independent detection rate on emulated attacks, and pair it with a rubric that measures blind investigation quality. In addition, run unassisted exercises on novel attack scenarios twice a year.

Protect the time you free up. If saved capacity is immediately backfilled with more queue work, you get the same burnout with better tools.

Give real governance authority. Analysts who set the boundaries the AI works within have a stake in the system, and that ownership is a reason to stay.

Training for the Work That's Here Now

In the Autonomous SOC Maturity Model, Partial Autonomy (Level 3) is where the work is now. Human oversight is moving from reviewing individual actions to governing a system's behavior within a defined scope. However, training programs can produce good-looking metrics while independent skill erodes for years.

As such, the idea of verifiability is more important than ever. Purple AI, for example, shows the evidence chain behind every verdict, so you can grade analysts against it, test it against emulated attacks, and see where each falls short.

Two questions belong on every security leader’s agenda:

Which capabilities are we preserving?

How do we test that analysts can perform independently?

We believe that expansion from Partial Autonomy (Level 3) to High Autonomy (Level 4) should occur only when independent human capability is shown to hold. Governance precedes autonomy, and proven human skill is part of that governance.

Title: The Path to AI Autonomy in the SOC
Context: In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents
Full Text:
Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027.

The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters.

The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it.

Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence.

Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum

The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents.

In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system.

Mapped onto security operations, the four stages look like this.

Evidence collection. Querying the SIEM and EDR, pulling process trees, enriching indicators, gathering identity and cloud context.

Analysis and verdict. Correlating what was collected, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether the alert is a real threat.

Response recommendation. Proposing what should happen next, such as containing a host, resetting credentials or closing the case.

Response execution. Actually changing something in the environment.

This split gives security leaders a cleaner set of choices. A team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system.

Human IN the loop vs. Human ON the loop

Once autonomy is split by stage, teams need a shared way to describe how much of it each stage gets. A useful vocabulary comes from researchers at the University of Washington, who define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays.

Level

Human role

What it means in practice

L1

Operator

The human directs and decides, and the agent carries out instructions

L2

Collaborator

Human and agent plan and execute together

L3

Consultant

The agent leads and checks in for expertise or preferences

L4

Approver

The agent works independently and asks for approval only in risky or predefined cases

L5

Observer

The agent acts on its own while the human monitors and can hit the stop button

The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart. Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is. A highly capable agent can still run at L2 if the stakes call for it.

Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic.

Enterprises evaluating AI SOC vendors should make sure that both models can be applied as appropriate, across their entire operations.

How to decide where and how much autonomy to grant an AI SOC

The levels mentioned above tell you what the options are. Deciding where each SOC action belongs takes a rubric, and three questions do most of the work.

Reversibility. If the agent gets this wrong, how quickly and completely can it be undone?

Blast radius. How many users, systems or business processes does the action touch?

Receipts. How strong and verifiable is the evidence behind the decision? An action backed by forensic proof of what was executed deserves more latitude than one backed by an LLM hunch about what looks suspicious.

Scoring real actions against those questions produces a map that most security teams will recognize.

The exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point. The rubric forces an explicit decision for each action, instead of a single policy that is either too loose for the dangerous actions or too tight for the safe ones.

When human approval becomes a rubber stamp

According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. It sounds like the safe choice, and in many cases it is. It also hides a failure mode that rarely gets discussed.

Human approval is only as good as the context the reviewer receives. When an approval step arrives without clear evidence or criteria, reviewers start clicking through requests to keep the queue moving, and oversight quietly disappears.

If the AI shapes how every investigation is framed, the human approving the final action is approving a conclusion they never saw being reached.

Only when the reviewer can actually check the AI’s logic and work along with hard, forensic evidence that conclusively points in one direction or another, is the approval actually worth anything.

In practice that means every approval request should show three things.

The evidence the agent collected and where it came from.

The reasoning that connects that evidence to the verdict.

What the agent checked and ruled out along the way.

A useful test if this is working, is time spent. If a reviewer cannot verify a verdict in a minute or two, the approval step is ceremonial and the team is paying for a human-in-the-loop without getting it.

Autonomy you earn, autonomy you lose

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications gives this approach a name. It extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks and letting that autonomy grow as it is earned.

Earning it requires criteria that are set before the pilot starts. Otherwise autonomy expands on vendor promises and gut feel. A practical set of graduation criteria for moving an action class up one level looks like this.

Measured agreement. Track how often the agent's verdicts match analyst review over a defined period and alert volume, and set the threshold in advance.

Dry runs first. Run new actions in a test mode that executes the logic but mocks every write, so the team sees what the agent would have done before it does anything.

A complete evidence trail. Every decision at the new level must be auditable after the fact, including what the agent looked at and why it concluded what it did.

A rollback path. Define how the action is undone and who owns that before expanding scope.

Autonomy should also move down. A drop in agreement rates, a major change in the environment such as a new EDR or cloud migration, or a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. Teams that only ever ratchet upward are building risk they cannot see.

Your SOC agent is an agent too

Every level of autonomy granted to a SOC agent has a second effect. It raises the damage that agent can do if it is wrong, manipulated or compromised.

Security leaders already feel this risk across the enterprise. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions.

The lesson for the SOC is that autonomy itself is a risk factor, scored alongside the vulnerability. Treat the AI SOC agent the way you would treat a new privileged identity.

Give it its own identity, never shared credentials.

Scope its permissions to the actions it is approved for at its current level.

Log every tool call, query and action in a form a human can review.

Watch it with the same detections you would apply to a new admin account.

A playbook for the next 12 months

The move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. Security leaders who want the capacity gains without the incident that sets their AI program back a year can start with five steps.

Inventory every action. List everything your AI SOC agent can do today, from read-only queries to response actions, and place each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric.

Automate investigation aggressively. Evidence gathering and analysis consume most analyst hours and carry the least risk. This is where full autonomy pays off first.

Gate disruptive response with real evidence. Keep approval on high-impact actions, and make sure every approval request carries proof a reviewer can verify quickly.

Write graduation and demotion criteria now. Agree on the accuracy thresholds, test periods and rollback paths before the pilot starts, so autonomy expands on data.

Govern the agent like a privileged identity. Scope it, log it and monitor it, because its autonomy is also its blast radius.

Crossing the trust threshold

Every SOC that adopts AI agents will eventually face the same question for each action. Is the agent's work trustworthy enough to act on without a human checking it first?

A helpful way to think about it is a trust threshold. Below it, AI assists analysts, and humans still validate every conclusion. Above it, teams can safely hand off execution and supervise outcomes instead of steps. What moves an action across that line is depth and proof. An agent that can show what actually executed, where it came from and what it did, gives a human something real to verify, and gives the organization a defensible reason to extend its autonomy. Forensic-level investigation, the approach Intezer’s AI SOC is built on, is what moves an action across that line.

That is what earned autonomy means in practice. The agent gets more authority one action class at a time, each step backed by evidence the team can inspect, and each step reversible if the evidence stops holding up.

Note: This article has been written and contributed by Zev Schonberg, PMM at Intezer.

CVE-2026-93637 (#22070) Is a rate-limit bypass in Zimbra's Network Edition GraphQL authentication endpoint, which lets credential-stuffing attempts skip the source-IP lockout counter that normally protects the SOAP login path.

Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

Title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
Context: Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers
Full Text:
Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community.

In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems.

“I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month.

Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI), rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

“I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added.

These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems.

Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility.

The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail. Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked.

Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis, told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards.

“We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.”

The math at stake

Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics:

Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers)

Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc.

“What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO.

Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science.

“The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.”

2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece

Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance.

“A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026, and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained.

AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978).

“The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added.

Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.”

Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen.

The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis.

Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’

Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis.

Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded.

Q-Day and LLMs

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography.

“We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.”

Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use.

“We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”

Title: Windows Event Log Cleared? Think Outside the Box
Context: Investigation Methodology and Findings During an investigation into a ransomware incident, Arctic Wolf found the threat actor cleared event logs, a technique frequently built...
Full Text:
The ubiquitous and dreaded “Event log cleared” event record often thwarts forensicators‘ analysis. However, new research by Arctic Wolf® Incident Response analysts indicates that clearing a Windows Event Log does not wipe the underlying Windows Event Log (EVTX) file. Instead, it leaves the “cleared” events behind; ironically, within the very file that was supposedly cleared.

The process is analogous to asking a child to clean his bedroom: rather than removing the mess, he sweeps it under the bed and calls the room clean. This article describes what our analysts found when they looked under the bed.

Investigation Methodology and Findings

During an investigation into a ransomware incident, Arctic Wolf found the threat actor cleared event logs, a technique frequently built into ransomware encryptors. This is not the anti-forensic advantage that ransomware operators assume it to be; log clearing often triggers Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) or Intrusion Detection System (IDS) alerting and is frequently the very action that allows these systems to identify an attack in progress or prompt an incident investigation.

In this particular case, the encryption binary did not execute without providing the correct password to run it. To reverse engineer the encryptor, analysts required locating the –pass <password> portion of the command line used to execute it. Triage of the domain controller showed that log clearing had affected several logs. Examination of one of the logs, System.EVTX, showed that the final log-clearing event occurred at 16:01 PST, with 104 events logged between 16:01 PST and the time of collection, 17:26 PST. These 104 event log entries were corroborated using Windows Event Viewer, Zimmerman Tools’ EvtxECmd, and Magnet AXIOM. In our testing, we didn’t identify any forensic tool that flags records left in EVTX slack space after a log is cleared. One tool we reviewed can parse events sequentially without relying on the file header, which may surface these records. However, to our knowledge at the time of writing, it doesn’t indicate whether records survived a clearing event or which records predate the clearing event a distinction that is important in investigations involving anti-forensics. Other forensic artifacts indicated that the encryptor had actually run around 12:53 PST, approximately three hours earlier; however, no evidence of this existed in parsed output from the System.EVTX log file.

The full forensic image was also analyzed for additional artifacts. A physical space keyword search for –pass returned the full command-line string for the encryptor, which had been renamed, somewhat unremarkably, to svc-host.exe. The location of this —pass artifact, however, was remarkable: rather than appearing in unallocated space (where cleared log remnants are typically expected), it was found inside the existing and allocated System.EVTX file.

The entry carried a timestamp of 12:53 PST, hours before the final log-clearing event and first reported entry in the System.EVTX. A separate, supposedly cleared, log entry also contained evidence of the threat actor’s use of netscan.exe and a leaked threat actor hostname.

Here’s the problem with that. Most forensic tools do not identify, alert on, or parse EVTX slack space. As a result, relevant data may be overlooked, particularly in ransomware investigations or other cases where log clearing is a common way to conceal activity.

Context

With the release of Windows Vista in 2007, Microsoft replaced the older EVT file format with the newer EVTX format. The new structure of EVTX files allowed for faster loading and querying. Each event is tagged with a sequential record number, and cryptographic protections make it difficult to fake new entries or remove individual entries without detection.

An EVTX file is always at least 68 KB in size: a 4 KB header, plus at least one 64 KB block containing the event data structures. The header specifies the starting and ending record numbers for the events contained in the log. The log may increase to become many gigabytes in size, but is always reset to 68 KB minimum. When a log is cleared, Windows truncates everything after the first 64 KB cluster and resets the first and last record numbers in the log. This does not mean that the remainder of that first 64 KB cluster is empty. In effect, clearing the log merely hides its remaining contents, where they remain, waiting to be found by anyone who knows to look. This means that until enough logs are generated to fill 64 KB, there will always be available data from the previous log file.

However, it is not as simple as just “carving” out the deleted records. To save space in the EVTX file, the file uses substitution templates to fill in repetitive data (hostname, event description, etc.) in each event record. Some unique data will be missing because of this, but very basic information is still available verbatim in the record. Additionally, it is possible to recreate some of these templates accurately, as the templates are mostly standardized by Microsoft.

Detailed Analysis of EVTX Files

For an analyst, forensic tools that parse data are essential to accomplishing work in an efficient and timely manner. But sometimes, manual review of the raw data is required to understand how the tools work and validate their output.

The below screenshot is the 128 byte EVTX Chunk Header (not to be confused with the EVTX File Header, which takes up the first 4096 bytes). All following screenshots and offsets are shown in decimal format.

Figure 1: 128-byte chunk header.

Analysts can speed up manual review by using a feature of X-Ways forensics called “Templates” which highlight areas of bytes based on a preset byte offset. This works well quite while still giving us easy access to confirm raw data from disk, but we still want to verify the results manually.

Figure 2: X-Ways forensics template for reading chunk headers.

The highlighted portions below show the starting and ending index numbers. (Note: all bytes are stored in Little Endian.)

Figure 3: At relative offset 8 for 8 bytes, the starting index number (1).

Figure 4: At relative offset 16 for 8 bytes, the ending index number (104).

Figure 5: Windows Event Viewer showing 104 events.

Opening the EVTX in Windows Event Viewer shows 104 events, as expected.

Figure 6: First allocated event record with identifier 2,635,913 (decimal, highlighted). Note Windows FILETIME timestamp at offset 16.

Figure 7: Last allocated event record with identifier 2,636,016 (highlighted). Note later file timestamp at offset 16.

Figure 8: First event record in free space. Identifier 2,635,767 (highlighted). Note the earlier timestamp than the first allocated event record, 2026-07-07 16:01:22.

Figure 9: Identifier 2,635,218 (highlighted). Shows netscan activity.

Figure 9 shows evidence of the second log clearing, since this record has an identifier of 2,635,218 and earlier timestamp (12:19:36 as compared to 15:00:48), even though it is later in the EVTA file (offset 53480 as compared to offset 43360). Note the netscan artifact of relevance – which took place BEFORE the clearing of the log, yet is still present and accessible within the EVTX file.

To confirm this hypothesis, analysts reviewed another EVTX file from another incident where log clearing occurred; in this case, the Windows PowerShell EVTX file. The review uncovered only one allocated record, both in X-Ways (Figure 10) and in Windows Event Viewer (Figure 11).

Figure 10: EVTX Chunk Header of a cleared Windows PowerShell EVTX file

Figure 11: Log clearing entry of a cleared Windows PowerShell EVTX file

The event log, figure 11, shows one record, as expected, with the log clearing command.

Figure 12: EVTX Record information of the one and only allocated entry, showing the log clear activity on 2026-03-06 00:54:21.

Figure 13: Last event record in file slack space, showing a timestamp of 2026-03-05 09:59:23, which is earlier than the single allocated record.

In total, there were 44 event records in this Windows PowerShell EVTX file, of which only one (1) was allocated. Interestingly, every single log entry was the same PowerShell clearing command

Systempowershell.exe -ep bypass -Command Get-WinEvent -ListLog * | where { $_.RecordCount } | ForEach-Object -Process{[System.Diagnostics.Eventing.Reader.EventLogSession]::GlobalSession.ClearLog($_.LogName) }

This shows the threat actor clearing the log file multiple times. Whether or not the threat actor deliberately filled the log file slack space with data is not determinable.

Conclusion, Impact, and Next Steps

Event records are key pieces of intelligence for incident responders and forensic analysts. In many instances, forensic analysts are no stranger to recovering deleted data. However, cleared EVTX files pose a challenge, as deleted but still allocated entries are not recovered (or flagged) by standard forensic tools or processes, to our knowledge. Yet there are still many methods to recover these entries, if they exist. All that is required is to learn how EVTX files operate (aka how a “child” operates) and how check underneath the digital “bed”.

While we built a proof of concept (PoC) Python script to carve and rebuild old records from an allocated EVTX file, industry standard tools should, at minimum, alert on EVTX files with possible old data. As a solution, we recommend some level of recovery and notation that a recovered record is a partial record and to place the parsed info within normal forensic output.

Title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way
Context: "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview
Full Text: The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023. "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them." Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime. "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption." Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering. Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained. Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network. "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life." At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play. Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content." Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements. "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device." If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success. But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky. Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose. "On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app. "And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app." Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. Title: No Straight Lines: The value of a different career journey
Context: Since our Sophos Women in Technology (SWiT) No Straight Lines: Rebuilding and Rising in Tech event, I've been thinking about how much value people gain from the parts of their...
Full Text:
Since our Sophos Women in Technology (SWiT) No Straight Lines: Rebuilding and Rising in Tech event, I've been thinking about how much value people gain from the parts of their careers that didn't go according to plan. Career changes, time away from work, and moves between different industries can sometimes feel like things that need to be explained.

I think we should look at them differently.

These experiences can build resilience, curiosity, judgment, and perspective. They can change how someone approaches a problem or understands a customer, colleague, or situation. Those qualities matter enormously in technology and cybersecurity.

At Sophos, we talk about simplicity, empowerment, passion, innovation and authenticity. For me, valuing different career journeys is part of putting those values into practice. It means recognizing potential alongside experience. It means giving people opportunities to grow. And it means acknowledging that someone's career history doesn't have to fit a conventional pattern for them to make an important contribution.

Helping people see what they bring

The other important part of this conversation is confidence. Very few people build it entirely on their own. Having supportive colleagues, managers, mentors, and role models can help someone see strengths in themselves that they might otherwise overlook.

That's why communities such as SWiT matter. They create opportunities for colleagues to connect, share experiences, learn from each other, and realize that they aren't alone in navigating an unconventional path.

I'd encourage all women across cybersecurity and in the professional world to think about that in their own teams. Who might benefit from some encouragement? Whose transferable experience could bring a different perspective? Where could someone be given an opportunity to take the next step?

There is no single route to a successful career, and the more we recognize the value of different journeys, the stronger our teams can become.

Title: Empowering Employees to Make a Difference: The Digital Café
Context: So, I contacted my local volunteer office and launched “Digital Café”, a community initiative offering practical, friendly support to people who need a helping hand with...
Full Text:
Sometimes, making a difference starts with spotting a problem and deciding to do something about it. For me, that moment came around two years ago when I read an article in my local community newspaper about the challenges many older people face when navigating an increasingly digital world.

Using a smartphone, joining a video call, or setting up a tablet might seem like everyday tasks, but for people who are less confident with technology, they can become frustrating barriers to independence and staying connected with family and friends.

I wanted to help. So, I contacted my local volunteer office and launched “Digital Café”, a community initiative offering practical, friendly support to people who need a helping hand with technology here in Nauheim, Germany. On the first Wednesday of every month, we hold an open drop-in session at my local community center. Visitors can bring along their smartphones, tablets, laptops and apps, as well as any questions they might have.

No question is too small. Sometimes, my fellow volunteers and I help someone understand a new device or get an app to work. Other times, the impact goes much further. Recently, I helped a woman who had been struggling to get her tablet working again. Fixing the technology meant that she could video call her granddaughter again. It was a simple example of how digital inclusion can help people feel more confident, independent, and connected.

Giving people the time to make an impact

At Sophos, we believe that when talented people are empowered to do meaningful work, we can make a positive difference both inside and outside the workplace. Our company values include Simplicity, Empowerment, Passion, Innovation, and Authenticity, helping define how Team Sophos works together and the kind of company we aspire to be.

The Sophos Employee Volunteering program gives permanent employees around the world up to 40 hours of paid volunteering time every calendar year, enabling us to support causes that matter to us. With manager approval, that time can be used flexibly, including in one-hour increments, for individual or team volunteering.

For me, that means having meaningful support from Sophos to turn something I care about into action. I think “Digital Café” is a great example of empowerment in practice. I saw an opportunity, took ownership, and made something happen. It also reflects the passion our people bring to creating an impact, and the authenticity that comes from supporting causes that genuinely matter to us.

More than technology

So, why call it a café? Because solving technology problems is only part of the experience. While visitors wait, they can enjoy free coffee and cake provided by other volunteers. We want it to be a welcoming space where people can talk, learn and connect, helping to take away some of the anxiety that technology can create.

Alongside the Digital Café is the Repair Café, where volunteers help give broken possessions a second life. From household appliances and bicycles to children’s toys, the initiative helps prevent usable items from being thrown away while promoting sustainability and reducing waste.

What began as an idea I had on my own has now grown into a dedicated team of five volunteers. The Digital Café has become a trusted part of the community, welcoming regular visitors who know there will be someone there to help when technology becomes frustrating. It’s also exciting to see the initiative attracting wider attention. The mayor of Nauheim has taken an interest in what we’re doing, and I’m meeting with him to explore further ways we can support digital inclusion in the community. Our wider efforts have also included a “Cybercrime in Everyday Life” seminar for senior citizens, supported by a former investigator from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Wiesbaden.

A culture that makes space for what matters

At Sophos, volunteering is one way we have the opportunity to make an impact beyond our day-to-day roles. The company’s volunteering policy reflects a commitment to the communities in which Sophos operates, as well as to employee health and wellbeing and a sustainable environment.

When I first read that newspaper article, I had no idea where it might lead. What started with an idea has grown into a community of volunteers helping people become more confident in the digital world. I couldn’t have done any of it without the support of the Volunteering Department in Nauheim.

Ultimately, the Digital Café isn’t really about smartphones, tablets, or apps. It’s about empowering people to stay independent, stay confident, and, most importantly, stay connected. I’m proud to work somewhere that gives me the time and support to make that difference.

Title: ARTEX, and the offensive tool powered by LLMjacking five months earlier
Context: The Sysdig TRT has a name for the kind of operator these tools enable: An agentic threat actor (ATA) is an operator whose attack capability is delivered via an AI agent rather...
Full Text:
On June 12, 2026, the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) watched someone build an autonomous hacking tool using someone else’s AI server. Then, in July, a similar tool called ARTEX appeared on GitHub. On November 13, the FBI released a FLASH saying a variety of threat actors have been running ARTEX against several business sectors.

To be clear, there is no proof to date linking these two offensive tools. However, they are similar in nature, have both been documented as using LLMjacking to power AI inference, and defenders can learn from both about why they shouldn’t underestimate their speed, cost, or ability.

The Sysdig TRT has a name for the kind of operator these tools enable: An agentic threat actor (ATA) is an operator whose attack capability is delivered via an AI agent rather than a human at the keyboard. ARTEX is the newest entry.

This blog covers what each tool did and what defenders can learn from putting them side by side.

What the Sysdig Threat Research Team documented in June

Over the summer, the Sysdig TRT saw someone using a misconfigured Ollama server as the reasoning engine to build an automated, multi-stage offensive tool. The actor wasn't chatting with the model or reselling access as seen in prior LLMjacking operations. Instead, they wired it into a pipeline that scanned a target, matched it to known vulnerabilities, wrote proofs-of-concept (PoCs), and tried to break in, with the model making the decisions at every step. The tool self-identified throughout the code as VAPT, shorthand for vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, so we dubbed the tool VAPT.

Because VAPT sent its full instructions to the model on every request, we captured the whole architecture: fingerprinting, vulnerability matching, web recon, PoC synthesis, SQL injection, credential extraction, privilege escalation, and an orchestrator that ran until it got command execution. VAPT was being rewritten stage by stage while the Sysdig TRT watched, and every target was a private practice range. We were looking at a tool in development, before it was potentially turned on real victims.

Due to LLMjacking, the Ollama server was free, unauthenticated, and unmetered. For an actor whose tool makes hundreds of model calls per attack, our blog said, "the economics are clear." When the cost of an attack drops to the cost of inference, and inference is stolen, offensive operations become free.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open source, multi-agent penetration testing platform written in Go. It turns the operator’s goals written in natural language into machine commands run by specialized AI agents, with minimal human involvement necessary beyond setting the objective.

ARTEX doesn’t have a model of its own. Microsoft describes its architecture as a planner agent to decide next steps and worker agents to run command tools, with all of the findings compiled in a shared graph of assets and vulnerabilities. A prominent ARTEX campaign analyzed by Amazon Threat Intelligence was powered by the large-scale theft of credentials used to access AI models. Attackers organized a self-sustaining LLMjacking operation in which stolen keys paid for the AI inference to drive further credential hunting.

Fortunately, the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) in the FBI FLASH read like an attack playbook every security team already knows:

Sub-second permission checks and dry-runs

Exploitation of SAML, XXE, SSRF, injection flaws, and hardcoded credentials

Web shells and open source remote access trojans (RATs) for persistence

Kerberoasting and DCSync for escalation

Residential proxies, Tor, and tunneling tools used for command and control (C2)

The FBI says ARTEX traffic is noisy, which means defense evasion techniques aren’t an issue. It’s the speed that can pose a problem. Some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, though according to Microsoft, most targeting attempts were unsuccessful. While other campaigns move faster with more success, three hours is nothing to brush off.

What VAPT has in common with ARTEX

The "authorized pentest" label is a master key. That framing recurred across VAPT's stages, and the operator likely used it as a wrapper to keep the model cooperative, even though the AI model was already abliterated, or had the guardrails removed. Whether VAPT was truly created for educational purposes or not, the compute engine used to build it was stolen. Therefore, the entire campaign was unauthorized.

The FBI FLASH says attackers favor models with a "lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing." Call the job a pentest, and many AI models stop asking questions. That's not one provider's bug, but a dual-use problem without a clean technical fix.

To that end, VAPT's first probes asked for an abliterated Llama-3.3-70B model. Its model list also included deepseek-r1:8b. The FBI says ARTEX operators gravitate to the DeepSeek Flash family because of its "balance of capabilities, relatively low cost, and lack of observable guardrails." Different models, but the selection criteria are the same: capable enough (they don’t need to be frontier models), cheap, and not likely to refuse a prompt.

VAPT's operator simply repointed a backend-agnostic tool at a free Ollama server in place of paid OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google APIs. ARTEX has no model of its own and plugs into at least six providers. In both cases, changing the engine is a configuration change. That's why "just block the bad model" isn't a strategy — it would require blocking all the models, and that just isn’t logical.

Another similarity is that neither VAPT nor ARTEX needs a novel exploit. There was no CVE in the VAPT operation, and the FLASH cites none for ARTEX either. The speed comes from chaining ordinary weaknesses without getting tired or pausing efforts. These AI-powered tools industrialize the boring stuff. And when pitted against human defenders, those who have to eat and sleep will always be at a disadvantage.

Lastly, both the tools and their fuel are sitting in the open. Researchers previously catalogued roughly 175,000 publicly exposed Ollama instances. And as of early November, researchers counted over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles, according to the FBI. One is a free engine. The other is the thing the engine drives. The attackers have the same hygiene problem as the people they target.

Where VAPT and ARTEX differ

VAPT (June)

ARTEX (July onward)

Who

One actor on residential IP space in India

A variety of actors

What it is

One actor's tool, iterated within a session

An open source project with thousands of forks, translations, and a commercial edition

Targets

Private practice ranges

Real organizations across many sectors

Where the compute came from

Documented. An exposed and unmonitored server

Not established

What defenders saw

The tool's full instructions, because the model server was one we could observe

The aftermath: bursts, dry-runs, new credentials, webhooks

The last row is particularly important. With VAPT, the Sysdig TRT saw the brain. With ARTEX, defenders mostly see what the brain did. Behavior-based detection exists for exactly this reason.

Cost is an important part of the story

Defenders can change many things, but the price of an attacker's tokens isn't one of them.

Sysdig TRT’s LLMjacking research has followed this cost curve since 2024. That May, we coined the term for attackers using stolen cloud credentials to reach a victim's paid AI models, leaving the victim with the bill, and modeled a worst case of up to $46,000 per day. By 2025, LLMjacking had matured into an industrialized black market. In June came the next step: exposed model capacity powering an offensive tool. The economics of compute theft can now fund the development of offensive capabilities.

One month later, ARTEX showed up, and the FBI's advisory reads like a footnote for LLMjacking:

Model choice followed price. DeepSeek Flash dominates attacker-controlled instances partly because of its "relatively low cost."

Resellers and gateways are in the picture. The FLASH's one domain indicator is an LLM API reseller used in the South Korean campaign, and it tells defenders to hunt for LLM gateway software (CLIProxyAPI, New API).

The FBI wants your AI bill. Among the evidence it asks victims for: token consumption patterns or API billing anomalies, unfamiliar LLM proxies or resellers in egress logs, and outbound connections to LLM APIs.

It’s important to note that it doesn’t say "stolen" credentials or access, because a reseller isn't proof of theft. However, LLMjacking is a natural fuel for tools like ARTEX, and the credential-theft half of one intrusion can supply the compute for the next.

During a recent incident in October, the attacker used a harness similar to ARTEX and ran up a bill of $740,000 in unauthorized spend on stolen AI keys.

Separately, but further proving the point about what offensive security costs, Calif says it spent under $200 in tokens to find and build the first exploit for Java4Shell.

The AI bill is telemetry that very few organizations pay attention to, or monitor in real time. An owner of an exposed model server sees elevated compute and an open port, not realizing it’s a multi-stage attack pipeline. A victim of stolen AI credentials sees an invoice. The FBI asking for token consumption in incident reports should be a pretty obvious hint about where defenders should be looking.

The challenge of “dual use” tools

Herein lies the struggle with many open source tools and attacks. ARTEX's developer said the tool was for authorized security testing within defined scopes. And the intent behind VAPT was unclear, because it could’ve been developed and used for legitimate activity, but stealing compute was illegal either way.

The attack and the pentest are the same software, pointed at different targets. The "authorized" label works on the model, the repository gets pulled after abuse reports, and the forks keep going. The FBI says ARTEX still circulates through forks, archives, translations, and a commercial version. A GitHub query on November 18 returned around 1,100 repos, a few of which had thousands of forks. But blaming open source software isn’t the answer. And the transparency of open source software helps defenders to better understand the signals created by the tools themselves.

The defender’s playbook against autonomous hacking tools

Defenders worried about VAPT, ARTEX, and whatever nefarious autonomous offensive tool may come next can follow these recommendations. For ARTEX specifically, the FBI FLASH includes IOCs to hunt for as well.

Treat AI infrastructure like a database. Don't leave model servers on public interfaces without authentication, and watch their usage. An exposed Ollama server is someone else's free engine.

Add the AI bill to your telemetry. Alert on token consumption spikes, unfamiliar API consumers, and billing anomalies, and know which credentials grant model access.

Treat AI-service credentials like cloud credentials. They're a high-priority target and a currency. Rotate and scope them, and keep them out of repos.

Run authorized agentic testing against yourself first, and treat any open-source pentest harness you run as hostile code: isolate it from production and enforce scope in configuration, not prompts.

Detect behavior, not models. You can't predict which model sits behind the next tool. What you can see is the pace: sub-second permission checks, bursts with small changes, sequential enumeration on partner portals, new identities probing other tenants, and servers reaching webhook.site or LLM APIs they never used before.

Vet indicators before you block. Cloud-hosted IPs can be reassigned, so make sure you verify the list and periodically review your block list. They don’t need to be permanently banned.

Conclusion

In June, the Sysdig TRT watched someone build an offensive tool on borrowed compute and aim it at practice targets. In November, the FBI described a polished, open source offensive tool in the field, run by a variety of actors against real organizations. There is no clear link between the two aside from the fact that both have been documented using LLMjacking and neither required much money, skill, or novelty.

For two years, the question was whether AI agents could hack. That’s settled: they most definitely can. The question now is whether an organization will notice if they’re the one paying for it.
