Title: Treat Your Honeypot Analysis Like Code: Git, Pull Requests and a Human Gate for AI [Guest Diary], (Wed, Nov 18th)
Context: Conclusion Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code
Full Text:
[This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Introduction When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat.

While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks:

An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [1]

A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [2]

A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [3].

Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them.

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.

Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].

AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with <sensor-ip>, and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].

The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.

A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.

A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.

Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.

Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.

Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. Title: Physical Penetration Testing: When Physical Access Became Network Access
Context: Figure 1: Physical Penetration testing attack chain showing how public information, access control gaps, workplace trust, and internal technical exposure can combine, with...
Full Text:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security specialists sharing lessons from authorized security testing engagements. Client information and selected operational details have been anonymized and generalized.

Physical security usually looks strongest from the outside. Cameras. Guards. Badge readers. Locked doors. Visitor procedures.

Each control may work exactly as designed. The harder question is whether they still work when somebody deliberately connects the gaps between them.

That is what a Sophos Physical Penetration Test is designed to examine. Rather than reviewing policies from a conference room, Sophos testers safely simulate an adversary attempting to enter a facility, move into sensitive areas, exploit workplace trust, and determine whether physical access can become digital access.

The following diagram shows the generalized attack chain assessed in this engagement, along with the places where alert employees, security personnel, access systems, network controls, and hardened devices can interrupt it.

Figure 1: Physical Penetration testing attack chain showing how public information, access control gaps, workplace trust, and internal technical exposure can combine, with detection opportunities at every stage.

The building was not the first target

The engagement started before anyone approached a door. The Sophos Red Team reviewed public information and studied how people moved around the facility. Public images revealed details about the property, its entrances, and the appearance of employee credentials. Onsite observation provided the rest: where people entered, how badges were carried, which areas were busy, and where an unfamiliar face might blend in. None of this required breaking a window or picking a lock.

A photograph shared for an innocent reason can reveal more than the person posting it intended. A badge image can expose its visual design. A building photo can show where reception sits. A normal workplace rhythm can reveal when entrances are crowded and attention is divided.

Individually, these details may appear harmless. Together, they can become a plan.

A valid badge does not always mean a valid person

Using information gathered during reconnaissance, the team demonstrated that access badge data could be captured and written to test credentials and cloned onto a fake badge. Those credentials allowed entry into parts of the facility and access to internal areas that should have required stronger validation.

Figure 2: Fake access badges created using badge data captured during reconnaissance, allowing the team to gain access to restricted areas of the facility.

Once a door accepted the credential, the environment largely treated the person carrying it as legitimate. That is an important distinction. A badge reader answers a narrow question: “Is this credential valid?” It does not necessarily answer the more important question: “Is the person presenting it authorized to be here?”

Employees encountered unfamiliar people moving through workspaces but did not consistently challenge them. Tailgating attempts also succeeded when people held doors or accepted a simple forgotten badge explanation. There was no dramatic confrontation. People were being helpful.

That is exactly why this type of penetration testing matters.

Inside, the trust boundary changed

After entry, the team identified unlocked workstations, unattended laptops, visible technical information, and gained access to internal network equipment. An authorized testing device placed beneath an unused workspace successfully established internal network connectivity.

Figure 3: An authorized testing device placed beneath an unused workspace.

That was the moment the engagement stopped being only a facilities issue. Physical access had become network access.

The assessment demonstrated that a person who entered the building could potentially reach internal systems without first defeating the organization’s internet facing defenses. The concern was not one specific port or one specific desk. The broader issue was that internal network access was being granted based largely on physical proximity rather than strong device authentication.

The team also encountered unattended and unlocked laptops in shared areas. These could provide an intruder with immediate access to applications, documents, communications, or a place to install persistence.

Once someone is inside, the workspace itself becomes part of the attack surface.

Encryption worked until another process failed

A test laptop provided another useful lesson. Full disk encryption initially prevented straightforward access to the device’s data. That control did its job. The team could not simply remove or mount the drive and read its contents. That's when the attack path changed.

Instead of attacking encryption directly, the testers evaluated the process used to recover the device. A believable support request resulted in the release of recovery information without sufficient identity verification. Combined with separate weaknesses in boot protection and privilege controls, that recovery information allowed the team to demonstrate a complete compromise of the test device.

The lesson is not that encryption failed. Encryption held. The recovery process around it did not.

Security controls rarely operate alone. Strong encryption can be undermined by weak recovery procedures. Strong endpoint protection can be undermined by insecure boot settings. Strong authentication can be undermined by a support process that trusts a believable story.

Some defenses did exactly what they were supposed to do

This was not a story where everything failed. The badge system generated alerts when cloned credentials were used in ways that did not match normal behavior. Security personnel raised their awareness, increased patrol activity, challenged a tester, confiscated the suspicious badge, and escalated the situation. Later attempts using invalid credentials were rejected, and additional security attention caused the team to abandon some entry routes. An employee disconnected the planted testing device, ending the team’s remote network connection. The employee may not have known exactly what the device was, but the action disrupted the attack path. These outcomes matter. A useful penetration test should not only document failures. It should identify the controls, decisions, and employee behaviors that interrupted the attack so those strengths can be reinforced.

The cheapest control may be a conversation

One of the clearest lessons from this Sophos Red Team engagement was that an unfamiliar person moving through a restricted workplace should not be able to rely on everybody assuming someone else has already verified them. Employees do not need to become security guards. They do need a safe, simple way to acknowledge unfamiliar people, offer assistance, and escalate concerns.

CISA’s “Power of Hello” guidance recommends observing suspicious behavior, initiating a polite conversation, evaluating the situation, and obtaining help when appropriate. Even a friendly “Can I help you find somebody?” can establish that a person has been noticed and may expose a weak pretext. Security awareness should make that response feel normal, not confrontational.

What organizations should take from this

This engagement was one anonymized example, not a claim that every facility has the same weaknesses. The broader lessons are widely applicable:

Protect badge information. Avoid publishing clear images of access credentials. Use badge technology that resists copying and limit each credential to the minimum areas required.

Require individual access. Employees, contractors, and visitors should authenticate or follow the visitor process rather than enter through ordinary courtesy.

Make polite challenges normal. Give employees simple language, a safe escalation path, and clear permission to report unfamiliar people or unusual activity.

Assume entry may eventually happen. Lock workstations automatically, secure sensitive documents, restrict internal rooms, and prevent unknown devices from receiving network access.

Harden recovery processes. Help desk and device recovery procedures should verify identity through trusted channels before releasing keys, resetting authentication, or granting elevated privileges.

Connect physical and cyber monitoring. Badge anomalies, visitor records, guard reports, network connections, and identity recovery events should contribute to a shared view of suspicious activity.

Test the whole chain. NIST guidance recommends structured security testing that includes planning, execution, analysis, and mitigation. Physical penetration testing adds value because it tests whether several individually reasonable controls can still be chained together.

The biggest lesson is not that organizations need more locks. It is that technology, process, people, and culture have to support one another.

A badge reader cannot challenge a convincing story. A locked door cannot protect an unattended laptop. Encryption cannot compensate for weak recovery verification. A network control cannot stop an unknown device if physical presence is treated as authorization. Layered security works only when the layers remain connected.

Want to know what happens when somebody tests your locks, your badges, your people, and the controls behind the front door? We're happy to help.

Title: Runtime security for Amazon EKS Auto Mode with Sysdig
Context: Runtime security adds an extra layer of defense against exploits that static analysis or vulnerability scanners may miss, such as zero-days
Full Text:
If you use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Auto Mode, you benefit from AWS-managed infrastructure, but you still need runtime security for your workloads. Amazon EKS Auto Mode lets AWS run your Kubernetes cluster infrastructure: compute, networking, storage, load balancing, and node patching. That removes a lot of toil. Because AWS operates the nodes for you in a managed model, nodes are identical, predictable, and immutable, with read-only root filesystems and strict security controls. This post covers what that means for runtime security, and how to deploy and use Sysdig Secure with EKS Auto Mode using Universal eBPF.

What changes with Amazon EKS Auto Mode

With standard EKS, AWS manages the control plane, and you manage the worker nodes. Auto Mode extends AWS's responsibility to the nodes and the core cluster capabilities:

Nodes are AWS-managed appliances: a locked-down, container-focused OS (Bottlerocket-based) with a read-only root filesystem and SELinux enforcement. Nodes are replaced regularly, so they never drift. See the Auto Mode documentation for the full list of managed components.

Shared responsibility still applies

AWS managesYou manage

AWS's security guidance for Auto Mode and best practices cover the AWS side. This post covers the last row: what happens inside your workloads at runtime.

Why Auto Mode needs a different agent approach

Auto Mode nodes don't allow kernel module loading for security reasons. Because Bottlerocket fully supports eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter), Sysdig uses eBPF as the primary mechanism for runtime security. A Universal eBPF driver embedded in the Sysdig Host Shield (agent) enables a real-time approach to monitoring system activity safely within the kernel using system calls as a source of truth.

Learn more about kernel-level security monitoring.

How to get started

Sysdig deploys as a Kubernetes workload, so it follows Auto Mode nodes as AWS adds and replaces them. Nothing runs on the host outside Kubernetes.

Where Sysdig complements AWS-native controls

Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, EKS control-plane logging, network policies, and Pod Security Standards are recommended in an Auto Mode design. They cover the AWS and control-plane layers. Sysdig complements these controls with in-depth cloud workload protection. With Sysdig, security teams can apply runtime policies, investigate process activity, monitor file and workload behavior, and correlate events with Kubernetes context.

Customizable detection rules are built on the industry-leading Falco engine. It allows you to monitor system calls to identify errant or suspicious events at the Linux kernel level. You can use the default threat detection rules in Sysdig Secure or easily customize rules to work with your unique threat model.

The dynamic, short-lived nature of container workloads in a Kubernetes environment means static scanning and other traditional security measures may not detect threats that emerge at runtime. You need runtime security-the ability to monitor behavior in real time to quickly identify and address security issues for workloads running on Amazon EKS Auto Mode. For example, a compromised container might spawn an unexpected process or open a network connection that no vulnerability scanner would flag in advance. Runtime monitoring catches that behavior as it happens, with full Kubernetes context such as cluster, namespace, and workload identity.

We recommend proper posture management, including thorough container vulnerability scanning. Runtime security adds an extra layer of defense against exploits that static analysis or vulnerability scanners may miss, such as zero-days. Runtime security matters for modern organizations because it helps protect workloads and data from unauthorized access, malicious or unintentional changes, and suspicious behavior that could indicate an attack.

Try Amazon EKS Auto Mode with Sysdig

The fastest proof of value is a small EKS Auto Mode cluster with Sysdig on Universal eBPF. Check that core detections and Kubernetes context work, then test the response and investigation workflows that matter to your team. Ready to get started? You can request a demo, check out the installation docs, or read more about Sysdig for Kubernetes here: Runtime-Driven Security for Containers & Kubernetes — A Practitioner’s Toolkit.

Title: Prompting GPT-Live for languages and regional accents
Context: Start with the right voice First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices
Full Text:
Even if a voice agent speaks Spanish, it can still sound off for the audience you’re building for. It might use an accent from a different region, choose wording that feels too formal, or read a price in a way a local speaker wouldn’t expect.

While the default options for GPT-Live can go a long way, there are additional considerations when building voice applications for audiences across languages and regions. Let’s look at voice selection and session instructions to get better results, using regional varieties such as Indian English, Spanish from Spain, and Emirati Arabic.

Start with the right voice

First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices. Some may already have a language or regional influence close to what you need: for example, Bossa and Tempo have a Brazilian Portuguese influence, while Nira is a Hindi voice. Test them with your own conversations before designing something new, as the built-in voices have high naturalness out of the box.

Use lowercase API names when selecting a built-in voice (for example, nira). The voice options guide has the complete current catalog.

If you need a more specific regional sound, you can use prompt-to-voice to generate a synthetic voice from a text description. Describe the region as precisely as you can, along with the pitch, pace, and vocal character you want. When generating a voice, you can use the script_hint field to add representative speech in the target language, and for a bilingual voice, include both languages in the sample text and describe the desired sound in each. Use original adult voices, and don’t impersonate real people. See the responsible-use guidance.

Eligible customers can also create a custom voice from a recording of a consenting speaker. Check the supported models and accents before choosing a recording-based voice. Before uploading, obtain the speaker’s express consent and secure the rights needed to use the recordings and the resulting voice in your application. The consent recording and reference sample must come from the same speaker. For any generated voice, make clear to listeners that they are hearing AI-generated speech.

Voice creation is ineligible for Zero Data Retention. See the data controls guide for the settings that apply to GPT-Live sessions.

Example: Hindi-influenced English with Nira

For an English-speaking agent serving users in India, set session.audio.output.voice to "nira" when creating the session, then add this prompt to the session instructions:

You are in a natural, clean English voice conversation. Speak fluent English in your natural Hindi-influenced Indian English accent. Keep that familiar rhythm throughout.

Example: Spanish from central and northern Spain

Suppose you’re building a shopping assistant for customers in Spain. Rather than asking for a generic Spanish accent, open the voice Playground and try this description in its prompt-to-voice workflow:

An original adult feminine voice, clear and lightly bright, with a medium pitch and gentle warmth. Speak Spanish with a natural standard Peninsular Castilian accent of central/northern Spain, with native Spanish vowels, consonants, stress, and sentence melody. Naturally distinguish s from z and c before e or i, without exaggeration. Use a moderately lively conversational pace, natural pauses, and varied intonation.

Pair it with a Spanish script_hint that gives the voice some ordinary connected speech to work with:

Hola, ¿qué tal? Estoy aquí para ayudarte. Podemos revisar las opciones con calma y elegir la que mejor encaje contigo. ¿Prefieres empezar por los colores o por las tallas? Esta chaqueta azul combina bien con unos zapatos cómodos. Acércate a la ventana para ver el color con luz natural.

This targets a particular variety of Spanish; the distinction described in the prompt isn’t universal across Spain or the Spanish-speaking world. With this prompt, you can generate a few candidates, keep the saved voice you prefer, and test it on a fresh sentence that wasn’t in the creation script until you’re satisfied.

Example: Emirati Arabic from Dubai

Arabic is another case where naming the language alone leaves a lot unspecified. For a conversational Dubai voice, an Arabic voice-design description might be:

صوت رجالي خيالي أصلي لرجل بالغ، بلهجة أهل دبي الإماراتية الحضرية المعاصرة. نطق الحروف وحركة الكلام وإيقاعه محليّان ومتناسقان، وتبقى الكلمات واضحة داخل الكلام اليومي المتصل. طبقة متوسطة تميل للانخفاض، ورنين دافي وصافي. يتكلم على مهله، والجملة تمشي كفكرة وحدة بنبر متنوع حسب المعنى.

The description asks for an original adult masculine voice with a contemporary urban Dubai accent, warm resonance, a slightly lower pitch, and connected, relaxed speech. Use a conversational Arabic script_hint as well:

هيه، شفت رسالتك. أنا هني صوب الحديقة، لا، أقصد صوب المواقف عند الباب الثاني. زين؟ المكان أهدى من اللي كنا فيه أمس. خذ راحتك، أنا توني واصل وما عندي شي مستعيل عليه. تبانا نتمشى شوي ولا نقعد؟ عادي، اللي يريحك.

In general, keep the voice design focused on sound. Managing details like whether the agent should answer an Egyptian caller in Emirati Arabic, switch into English, or confirm an order belongs in the session instructions, which we’ll cover later on.

Test the voice on what your application will actually say

But having a solid voice is only the starting point. Once you have a voice, you can build a small listening set with fresh sentences, realistic conversations, and the words or values your application handles most often to stress-test your voice.

A few edge cases are particularly useful to test:

Pronunciation in context: Include names, place names, product names, and specialized vocabulary. For Japanese, for example, give the agent a reading such as 承る（うけたまわる） and test it in a full support sentence. Or if your agent is pronouncing Lakshmi with a “my” ending instead of the intended “mee,” you can include guidance in the session instructions: लक्ष्मी — अंत में ‘क्ष्मी’, ‘क्ष्माई’ नहीं. For tonal languages, listen to important words in several sentence contexts.

Regional number conventions: The Indian system of numeration uses lakh and crore. One lakh is 1,00,000 (100,000), and one crore is 1,00,00,000 (10,000,000). For an English-speaking agent serving India, test whether ₹1,25,000 is spoken as “one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees” when that’s the intended convention.

Identifiers and corrections: Have a caller spell a fictional booking code, pause, and correct one character. Check that the agent waits for the correction and reads back the final code accurately. Test email addresses and other alphanumeric inputs your product accepts.

Mixed-language speech: Try an Arabic sentence containing an English product name and a price, then switch languages for the next turn. Check the spoken amount, currency, and product name separately from the accent.

For dates, amounts, and identifiers, validate what your application actually sends to the backend as well as what the caller hears. In many regions, 04/05 could mean two different dates, so it may be worth asking for clarification and reading the month back by name.

Prompt the agent for the conversation

Once you’ve chosen a voice, select it when creating the GPT-Live session. For a saved generated voice, set session.audio.output.voice.id to the returned voice ID. Put the agent’s role, language policy, delivery, and conversation behavior in instructions, and reinforce the original voice description there.

For a single-language application, write the instructions and examples in the language you want the agent to speak. Here’s a starting point for the Spanish shopping assistant:

Eres un asistente de compras. Habla en español de España, con acento castellano del centro y norte de la península, un ritmo conversacional y una entonación natural. Usa un tono cercano y respetuoso, sin sonar como un anuncio. Responde en español salvo que el cliente pida cambiar de idioma. Haz una pregunta cada vez. Si un nombre o una talla no están claros, pide que los repita. No confirmes precios, disponibilidad ni cambios en un pedido hasta que el sistema los haya verificado.

For a multilingual application, decide what should trigger a language switch and whether the underlying regional speaking style should remain fixed. Those are separate choices. For an Emirati Arabic and English assistant, first extend the earlier voice description with English delivery guidance, such as “In English, speak naturally with a light Emirati influence while keeping the same warmth and lower pitch.” Include representative English speech alongside the Arabic in script_hint, such as “I can check the available sizes for you,” before generating the bilingual voice. Then use a session policy like this:

Answer in the language of the caller's latest clear utterance. Switch between Arabic and English when the caller clearly switches. A short “OK,” number, name, or English product name inside an Arabic sentence does not by itself change the conversation language. When speaking Arabic, use conversational urban Emirati Arabic from Dubai, even when the caller speaks another Arabic variety. Prefer natural local wording where appropriate: شو for “what,” الحين for “now,” وين for “where,” and مب for negation. Keep the dialect coherent without exaggeration. In English, keep the same speaker identity. Use these as phrasing examples, not fixed answers: - Clarification: «تقصد العلبة الصغيرة ولا الكبيرة؟ وكم وحدة تبا؟» - Unclear name: «الاسم مب واضح عندي، ممكن تعيده أو تتهجّاه لي؟» Say amounts in the current conversation language and preserve their exact value and currency. Only confirm a lookup, price, or completed action when the backend supports that statement.

This example deliberately keeps the assistant’s Arabic dialect fixed while allowing English language switches. If your product should accommodate a caller’s requested dialect instead, write and test that policy explicitly. While voice descriptions and session prompts can steer an accent, they don’t guarantee that every reply will retain it, so test switches in both directions, including after a session reconnects.

Give examples of the register you want

Language and accent also leave the level of formality open. In Hindi, a courteous support agent might use आप and respectful verb forms. You can make that preference concrete in the session prompt:

ग्राहक से "आप" कहकर बात करें। सम्मानजनक भाषा और क्रिया रूपों का उपयोग करें। "हाँ, बताओ" की जगह "जी, बताइए" कहें। "तुम कैसे हो?" की जगह "आप कैसे हैं?" कहें।

The examples distinguish a casual “yes, tell me” from a more courteous equivalent. That gives the model a clearer target than simply asking it to sound professional. Use phrases a local support representative would actually say, and test them in context rather than translating an English script word for word.

For more on pronunciation cues, personality, greetings, and interruption behavior, see the GPT-Live prompting guide. The voice agent evaluation guide covers how to turn your listening cases into a repeatable evaluation as you change voices, prompts, or models.

Context: The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical
Full Text: Apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.” including at least one rated "critical." These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk. CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.” The earlier informational advisory urged users to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.” These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation said is very unlikely in real-world applications. Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here. The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites. While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26. Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers. The Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®

Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community.

Today, we’re announcing two open-weight model releases:

We’re introducing an updated version of Clairic. Since the preview, we’ve improved extraction from complex documents including images and PDFs (new!), with more reliable handling of tables, lists, and dates, and better grounding of answers in the source material.

We’re introducing Clairic-flash, a lighter, faster version of Clairic that delivers strong extraction and prediction performance in a compact, 9-billion-parameter model.

Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face.

We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef, Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community.

A new version of Clairic: redesigned after the preview release

Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data.

We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic.

Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. Title: A new critical Java hole illustrates the enterprise IT visibility problem
Context: “The same Java application and version can be vulnerable on a newer x86 server and unaffected on older hardware because the faulty decoder only runs when AVX-512 is available,”...
Full Text:
When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE).

With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT.

Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous. Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK x86-64 Base64 decoder that scores 9.2 in severity (Critical) under CVSS 4.0, Calif said. Oracle assigned it a lower rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1.

Calif explained in its post describing the issue that Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. “It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” it wrote. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution.”

It said that the corruption can be triggered by a string of just 64 “A” characters followed by a single equals sign (=); in older OpenJDK 17 versions, 128 “A” characters are required before the equals sign.

“Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the internet,” Calif said. “But one of Java’s biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers’ behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.”

Assessing the bug’s potential for exploit is complicated because triggering it requires a hardware accelerated decoding function that’s used on some x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. And fixing it requires patches from a lengthy list of vendors; just installing Tuesday’s patch from Oracle, which owns Java, is not going to do the trick.

Potential damage ‘extreme’

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, said the potential damage from an unpatched instance of exposed Java is extreme.

“The researchers were able to read Java heap memory before they achieved code execution, so an attacker may be able to steal tokens, credentials, or keys from those systems. That access can remain useful even after the vulnerable server has been patched,” Kenney said. “Any unexplained crashes on an exposed system should lead to a review of what secrets were in memory and whether they need to be rotated.”

But not every instance is vulnerable to this flaw.

“The same Java application and version can be vulnerable on a newer x86 server and unaffected on older hardware because the faulty decoder only runs when AVX-512 is available,” he noted. “That makes a normal software inventory less useful than it usually is. CISOs need to know the Java distribution and version, the processor underneath it, and whether untrusted Base64 reaches the decoder. Installing a newer processor can expose an application that was safe on the server it replaced, without changing the application at all.”

A further complication is that enterprises will also be running Java from a massive array of specialized vendors.

“Oracle released a fix for its Java builds, but enterprises also run Java from Amazon, Eclipse, Microsoft, Red Hat, and Azul, along with runtimes buried inside commercial products and containers,” Kenney pointed out. “CISOs should start with identity systems and software-delivery infrastructure, identify the runtime each one is actually using, apply the appropriate vendor fix, and restart or rebuild the workload.”

He also said that outbound connections need to be evaluated. “Researchers demonstrated that a Java program could be compromised by connecting to a malicious TLS server, even when it had no service exposed to the internet.”

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, agreed, pointing out, “the client-side exploit puts any Java process that connects to a malicious TLS server at risk: integrations, connectors, crawlers and batch jobs. Patch scopes built around internet-facing listeners will miss them.”

Lack of visibility a big problem

Mahapatra also stressed that many Java implementations can be hard to locate.

“Your SBOM [software bill of materials] can’t see the real exposure. Whether a service is vulnerable depends on the silicon underneath as much as the JDK version,” he said. “The same container image is exploitable on an Ice Lake or Zen 4 node and safe on ARM or older hardware, and autoscaling can move it between the two. For once, the organizations that refreshed their hardware are the exposed ones.”

But it is the lack of visibility that concerns practitioners the most.

The Java hole “exposes a blind spot in how enterprises identify, prioritize and validate vulnerabilities,” said Raj Annaladasu, staff customer success engineer at Palo Alto Networks. “Enterprise teams invest heavily in application code review, dependency scanning, and secure coding practices. Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerabilities can originate below the application layer, inside the managed runtime itself.”

“This is an important distinction: Java’s memory-safety abstractions do not protect an application from memory corruption originating inside a vulnerable native runtime implementation,” he said. “Applications may be using a standard Java API correctly while the underlying runtime implementation is vulnerable. This shifts the security boundary beyond application code and third-party dependencies to include the runtime, its implementation, and the hardware capabilities that influence execution.”

This means, he said, that exploitability depends on multiple conditions coming together: an affected Java runtime, the relevant CPU instruction capabilities, the vulnerable execution path being enabled, and attacker-controlled input reaching the decoder.

But, he pointed out, “one of the bigger challenges is discovering where Java is actually running. Runtime installations are often bundled inside third-party products, container images, appliances, custom runtime distributions, and application-specific directories. They may not appear as distinct entries in conventional software inventories. A clean application dependency scan or CMDB does not establish that the environment is free of vulnerable Java runtimes.”

Java hides everywhere

Given that there are going to be so many Java vendors, and so many hidden apps, at issue, the risk of a CISO missing a few is massive, noted Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research.

“Java4Shell is a big deal because a single missed server with Java is all an attacker needs, allowing someone who never logs in to read its memory, including personal data, private keys, and tokens,” he said. “From there, the attacker can run code on the server. If that server is an identity system like Keycloak or PingFederate, the attacker now owns you.”

And, he said, it’s highly unlikely that enterprise CISOs will catch all or most Java instances.

“Will a CISO miss one? The odds say yes. Java hides everywhere. Each Java instance needs its own fix,” Dickson said.

Its popularity is Java’s greatest weakness

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, said Java’s popularity is its biggest weakness.

“Java runs the back office of corporate America: logins, code pipelines, ticketing, internal wikis,” he said. “Java4Shell lets an attacker who hasn’t even logged in take over some of the most sensitive of those systems by sending a short string of text. If your company runs Java on modern servers, and almost every large company does, you’re exposed until you patch.”

He enumerated some examples: “Keycloak and PingFederate control who gets into your company. Jenkins and Artifactory build and store the software you ship. Jira and Confluence hold your roadmaps, incident notes and plenty of passwords people shouldn’t have pasted there,” he said. “Take over those and you aren’t breaking into one room. You’ve stolen the master key, the blueprints and the security guard’s notebook in one move.”

He added, “Java programs that simply connect out to the wrong server can be compromised too. That last one means firewalls and perimeter controls don’t fully protect you.”

However, he pointed out, “there’s one small mercy: the bug only fires on certain newer Intel and AMD chips. The catch is that those chips fill modern data centers and cloud fleets.”

Title: Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
Context: In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today
Full Text:
About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.

My plan today was to write a bit about attacks we are seeing against one of our Java-specific honeypots. But the results can be summarized in one sentence: We are seeing many attacks, but none that exploit Java4Shell (yet). Will it be an important issue? Probably. Should you patch? Sure. Will the world as we know it end? Maybe.

So why not go to "Yellow"? This is not a new question. Often people ask why we are on "Green" if they are seeing hundreds or thousands of attacks hitting their system each day. The Internet is a dangerous place. Shouldn't we be on "Yellow" (or "Orange") to reflect that danger? My answer has been: "Green" means the Internet is broken as usual. As long as the status is "Green", you should expect a normal "9-to-5" day. I have heard from organizations that have used our infocon to justify staffing and overtime, and I am well aware of the impact it may have.

The reason behind our conservative Infocon is that you can't be alert and "on guard" all the time. An alert status that is "high" all the time is meaningless and counterproductive. You must not treat these recent vulnerabilities as "emergencies". They are the "new normal". Treat them as such. You will not be able to patch nginx2shell across a large organization before the exploit is released. Instead of trying to do the impossible and fail, think beyond the vulnerability of the day. A new reality requires new procedures and techniques. Here are a few ideas:

Automate patching as much as possible, in particular for less critical systems. Traditionally, automatic patching had two significant drawbacks. First, you may crash a system because of a failed patch. Secondly, the patch may not be applied correctly, and you treat a vulnerable system as "patched". Select less critical systems that would be at the end of your patch priority list. I'd rather take a system down myself than have ransomware do it for me. Having a system possibly patched is better than being sure the system isn't patched. And of course, there should be some testing, but that can wait a bit longer. This responds well to the faster development of exploits.

Reduce your exposure. This should have been a priority years ago. But there are still too many systems connected to the internet that shouldn't be connected. Build a defensible architecture. The same is true for individual applications: reduce the "blast radius" by restricting which data and resources each application can access. And reduce your supply chain exposure. Do you get enough value from tools like Optimizely to justify the risk of them compromising your application?

Avoid chasing squirrels. Do not change your plan and drop what you are doing just because the world is going to end. The world may end, in which case, patching one more system is probably not going to make a difference. Whether the world ends or not, at least you will be well-rested to deal with it.

During my classes, I am exposed to security professionals from a wide range of backgrounds, working in different industries and countries worldwide. The one thing they all have in common is that they do not have enough time, tools, and sometimes skills to do their job. Making the job you can't do right now any more urgent won't help. Work on tooling and resources, and develop a plan for applying best practices at a sustainable pace. Embrace AI tooling. It is immensely useful for automation. It is even more amazing at helping you get organized. Many partitioners are afraid that AI will do more harm than good, and they are not wrong. But use it where it helps you most. Are you great at writing little scripts but horrible at tracking and inventorying them? Give AI the job you suck at and develop a rapport with your tools. But embracing automation does include embracing AI tooling.

Finally, I got a lot of positive feedback on the final "conclusion" of yesterday's podcast, so I am going to link to it directly here:

Title: MITRE Acknowledges Inaccurate Publication Timestamps in 87% of Its Recent CVE Records
Context: The findings come from security researcher Jerry Gamblin, founder of RogoLabs, an independent open source research lab focused on vulnerability intelligence
Full Text:
MITRE has acknowledged that a legacy publishing system is responsible for inaccurate timestamps in thousands of CVE records, following research showing that 87% of the organization's CVEs published over the past year were assigned a publication time of exactly midnight UTC. MITRE says the legacy system responsible for the problem will be phased out in the first quarter of 2027.

The findings come from security researcher Jerry Gamblin, founder of RogoLabs, an independent open source research lab focused on vulnerability intelligence. His projects include the CNA Scorecard, which evaluates the completeness of CVE records, and CNAPulse, which tracks vulnerability publishing activity across CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs). Socket has previously covered both projects and Gamblin's broader research into CVE data quality.

Analyzing CVE records published over the 52 weeks ending November 16, 2026, Gamblin found that 3,901 of MITRE's 4,509 CVEs (87%) had a datePublished timestamp of exactly 00:00:00.000Z. Across the other 425 CNAs, none of the 100,235 records carried that same timestamp.

The distribution creates the appearance that MITRE publishes hundreds of vulnerability records at precisely midnight on weekdays. In reality, those timestamps do not represent the actual time the records were published.

Publication Timestamps That Don't Match Publication Times #

The CVE Record Format defines datePublished as the date and time a CVE record was first published in the CVE List. Researchers and automated systems can use that field to track publication activity, measure delays, and analyze vulnerability reporting trends.

Gamblin first raised the issue on GitHub in July, calling for changes to CVE publication requirements and more accurate timestamps.

To confirm the discrepancy, he compared recorded publication timestamps with the first appearance of each CVE in the official CVE List's cves/deltaLog.json change log.

For 202 MITRE records published between October 19 and November 16, he found that 144 records stamped at midnight UTC had a median delay of 15.8 hours between their recorded publication time and their first appearance in the change log. The remaining 58 MITRE records, which carried other publication times, appeared a median of 4.6 minutes after their recorded timestamps. Records from other CNAs showed a comparable median delay of 4.5 minutes.

The comparison provides evidence that the midnight timestamps are placeholders rather than actual publication times. Gamblin also found that the dates themselves were accurate in the sample he examined.

“Timestamps are one of the few fields in a CVE Record that are supposed to be objective and machine-trustworthy," Gamblin wrote in his issue on GitHub in July.

"Right now, the largest single source of CVE Records is still shipping fabricated timestamps on 84% of what it published in the last 30 days, while every other CNA in the sample gets this right at 0%. Anything downstream that measures time-to-publish, time-to-update, or disclosure latency (EPSS, CNA scorecards, research like mine) is quietly built on bad data for the biggest chunk of the dataset."

Researchers tracking CVE publication delays could interpret the 15.8-hour gap as evidence that MITRE takes much longer than other CNAs to make records available. But because the midnight timestamps are artificial, that gap cannot reliably measure publication delays. The date may still be useful for daily reporting, but the timestamp cannot reliably establish when during that day a CVE record became available.

"For me the problem is uniformity more than precision," Gamblin wrote. "What breaks things is one field that means two different things depending on who published the record."

MITRE Explains the Legacy Publishing System #

Responding to Gamblin's findings on LinkedIn, Alec Summers, MITRE's CVE/CWE Project Leader, acknowledged the timestamp problem and attributed it to historical differences in MITRE's publishing infrastructure.

"Jerry – for clarity, this is a known historical timestamp issue that has been discussed previously, both directly and in writing," Summers wrote on LinkedIn.

Summers said MITRE publishes its CVE records through the same CVE Services API used by other CNAs, with the same validation and audit trail. However, different publishing workflows use different API endpoints.

He explained that one endpoint requires the client to supply a time value and that "because of concurrency issues in a legacy client architecture, a single predictable value (00:00:00) is best for system stability."

Summers confirmed that "Publications using that legacy architecture will be phased out in Q1 2027."

The transition is already underway. According to Gamblin's analysis, 97% of MITRE records published from 2023 through 2025 carried midnight timestamps, compared with 66% of records published so far in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Summers also addressed whether MITRE would correct historical publication timestamps.

"Modifying historical record publication timestamps, while possible, has not been highlighted as a demonstrated priority need by CVE data consumers," he wrote, adding that MITRE welcomes input on where improvements would provide the greatest value.

Gamblin, who participates in the CVE Program's Quality, Automation, and Consumer Working Groups, welcomed the Q1 2027 timeline but said he had not previously seen a documented commitment to fixing the issue. He asked MITRE to post the plan in the GitHub issue he opened in July so others following the discussion could track the progress.

CVE Publication Data Under Growing Pressure #

In his 2026 midyear analysis, Gamblin counted 35,364 CVEs published in the first six months of the year, a 49.5% increase over the same period in 2025. Meanwhile, VulnCheck found that 23.43% of known exploited vulnerabilities identified during that period showed evidence of exploitation on or before their CVE publication date.

As disclosure volumes grow and some vulnerabilities are already being exploited when their CVE records appear, accurate publication times become increasingly useful for reconstructing vulnerability timelines. MITRE's midnight timestamps can introduce hours of error into measurements of publication latency and comparisons between CNAs, making it difficult to determine how quickly vulnerability information became publicly available.

MITRE's planned transition should improve the accuracy of future records, but thousands of historical timestamps remain inaccurate. Researchers analyzing past disclosures will still need to account for those discrepancies.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief on How Java4Shell Turns Base64 Decoding Into an Enterprise Risk
Context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief on How Java4Shell Turns Base64 Decoding Into an Enterprise Risk appeared first on Cato Networks
Full Text:
Executive summary

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), disclosed on 17 November 2026, is a memory-corruption flaw in Java’s accelerated Base64 decoder. Malformed input can crash an affected JVM, and external researchers have demonstrated application-specific remote code execution. Exposure requires an affected JVM on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI and BW support, with the vulnerable decoding path enabled and reachable by untrusted input. Potential business consequences include service disruption, exposure of application secrets and access to connected systems.

Our Agentic CVE Researcher helped accelerate Java4Shell protection development alongside Cato security researchers. This response combines agent-assisted research with human expertise to shorten the protection window. Customers gain an additional layer of protection while they assess exposure and plan runtime updates.

How Java4Shell creates business risk

The flaw occurs when malformed Base64 input reaches the affected HotSpot decoder and an integer underflow causes an out-of-bounds heap write. Exposure requires an affected JVM, an enabled vulnerable intrinsic and an x86-64 CPU with the relevant AVX-512 features, including VBMI and BW. ARM systems do not execute this path. VulnCheck reproduced crashes, while reliable code execution required additional target-specific exploitation.

The business impact depends on the application’s privileges and connections. Crashes can interrupt sign-ins or transactions, memory disclosure could expose tokens and keys, and code execution may enable access to connected systems. Calif demonstrated exploitation against products including Keycloak, Jenkins, Jira and Artifactory in specific environments and described a client-side route involving connections to a malicious TLS server. These findings do not establish that every deployment is vulnerable.

As of its 17 November advisory, Talos had not observed exploitation in the wild. The reported research demonstrates potential impact, rather than evidence of widespread compromise.

How Cato shortened the protection window

Our Agentic CVE Researcher helped accelerate Java4Shell protection development alongside Cato security researchers. The workflow combines agent-assisted vulnerability analysis and protection generation with validation and researcher review.

This shortens the path from disclosure to protection on covered traffic.

For requests targeting a vulnerable Java service, Cato IPS can block exploitation attempts that match the deployed protection on inspected traffic. Inspecting malicious content inside HTTPS requests requires TLS decryption.

The upper flow explains the flaw and its possible outcomes. The separate Cato response shows how agent-assisted research helped add protection. Learn more about Cato’s Agentic CVE Researcher.

For private Java services, Cato firewall policies and ZTNA can restrict which users and systems can reach the application. LAN firewall segmentation can limit access from other local devices. These controls reduce the number of users and devices that can deliver malicious input to the service.

For the client-side route, restricting unnecessary outbound connections can reduce opportunities for a Java client to contact a malicious TLS server.

What this means for Cato customers

Cato IPS can block recognized exploitation patterns when the relevant protection is enabled and the traffic is inspected. Customers can focus on affected business-critical Java services and coordinate vendor-recommended runtime updates with their application owners.

Services outside that coverage may benefit from temporary access restrictions or earlier updates. If repeated JVM crashes or relevant security alerts occur, correlate them with application and network evidence to determine whether further investigation is needed.

Central protection supports distributed remediation

Java4Shell remediation spans application owners, runtime suppliers and deployment environments. Cato’s centralized architecture helps security teams distribute protections and enforce access policies across covered users, sites and cloud resources while application owners plan and validate runtime updates. The value is a shorter, more consistent protection window across inspected traffic. Confirming coverage and coordinating runtime updates completes the response, with centrally delivered protection helping manage exposure throughout the process.

Title: California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps
Context: "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said
Full Text: Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles. California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide. The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel. Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety." On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco. The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic. "The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said in the statement. Groveman said the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18. Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco. A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater. A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US. "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. "We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog, driving into telephone poles, and killing cats and dogs. ®

Title: Why AI-ROC Is the Future of Exposure Management
Context: The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading way attackers got in, while the median time to patch grew to 43 days
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Security teams have never had better visibility into their assets, vulnerabilities, and threats. What they lack is the speed to act on it. Frontier AI models are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than ever, attackers are using the same models to exploit them within hours, and most remediation still depends on scans, tickets, and change windows. Exposure management needs a new operating model that detects exposures as soon as they are disclosed, focuses only on what is proven exploitable, and remediates autonomously without breaking the business. That operating model is the AI-native Risk Operations Center (AI-ROC).

On October 13, 2026, Microsoft released the largest Patch Tuesday in its history, fixing 1,414 vulnerabilities. That is more than seven times the 193 vulnerabilities Microsoft fixed in October 2025. One of the new vulnerabilities was already being exploited, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) set a deadline of just three days to patch it.

At ROCon Americas 2026, we made the case that most organizations are focused on the wrong question. Knowing how many exposures you have is no longer useful on its own. What matters is how quickly you can turn those exposures into verified risk reduction.

The Vulnerability Surge Has Outpaced Remediation

Over the last twenty years, the security industry has gotten very good at finding things. Organizations now have more data on assets, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, threat intelligence, and alerts than ever before. The ability to fix what matters has not kept up.

Frontier AI has made that gap much wider. These models are not creating new vulnerabilities. They are surfacing flaws that already existed in code, and they are doing it much faster than before. The last two Patch Tuesdays, with 974 vulnerabilities in September and more than 1,400 in October, show how fast this is moving. Attackers have access to the same AI tools and are using them to weaponize new vulnerabilities within hours. In September, two of the vulnerabilities Microsoft disclosed were already being exploited before a patch was available.

The way most organizations remediate has barely changed. A scanner detects the vulnerability, a second tool adds asset context, a third ranks it, an attack simulation tool tests it, and a ticket is created in the hope that someone fixes it within a 30- or 60-day service-level agreement (SLA). Each of those handoffs adds time, and risk only goes down when the fix is actually applied. This process was not built for attackers who move in hours.

What the Surge Means for Security Teams

Remediation timelines are shrinking from weeks to days, but the resources to meet them are not keeping pace.

SLAs are moving from weeks to days. The 30- and 60-day SLAs most programs were built around no longer match the threat. Critical vulnerabilities now need to be patched in days, and mandates from CISA and CERT-In, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, can require remediation in as little as 12 to 24 hours.

Exploitation is how most breaches now start. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading way attackers got in, while the median time to patch grew to 43 days.

Budgets and headcount are not keeping pace. Only 15% of security leaders expect their budgets to grow by more than 10%. Hiring more analysts is not a realistic answer.

There are too many findings to fix. One large Qualys customer had 62.5 million findings. No team has the time or budget to work through that many.

The Ideal Operating Model for Exposure Management

None of this is a new problem. Exposure management still comes down to the same basics of visibility, prioritization, and remediation. What has changed is the speed at which each of them has to happen.

Detection must happen in real time. New exposures should be identified as soon as a vulnerability is disclosed, not after the next scheduled scan.

Prioritization must be based on proof. Risk scores tell you what could be dangerous. Teams need to know whether an attacker can actually reach and exploit the vulnerability in their environment.

Remediation must take hours, not a month. Low-risk fixes should be automated, and every fix should be checked to confirm it worked.

These steps also need to run on one platform. Every handoff between separate tools and teams adds delay, and that delay is the window attackers use.

Qualys calls this operating model the Risk Operations Center (ROC). When AI agents handle the time-sensitive work at each stage, it becomes an AI-native ROC, or AI-ROC.

How Qualys Operationalizes the AI-ROC

The Qualys AI-ROC brings this operating model together on the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management Platform. It pulls in every asset and exposure across cloud, on-premises, operational technology (OT), Internet of Things (IoT), mobile, and AI environments, enriches them with threat intelligence and business context, and then prioritizes and remediates the risk that matters. Three AI agents handle the work that has to happen at machine speed: Agent Insta for detection, Agent Val for validation, and Agent Sara for remediation.

AI-Speed Detection with InstaScan

With traditional scanning, a vendor has to write a detection signature, roll it out, and then customers have to rescan their environment. That can take a day or two before a team even knows it is affected. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta, monitors vendor advisories around the clock and matches them against the asset and software data customers already have. No new scan is needed. After the October release, Agent Insta customers had detections within five minutes.

Hyper-Prioritization with TruConfirm

Even after applying threat intelligence and business context, a large organization can still be left with hundreds of thousands of findings. TruConfirm, powered by Agent Val, tests whether those findings can actually be exploited in the customer’s environment, using production-safe payloads that never download malware. For the customer mentioned above, this reduced 62.5 million findings to 60,000 that were confirmed exploitable.

Zero-Day Remediation with TruRisk Eliminate

Detection and prioritization only matter if the risk gets fixed. Before launching TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence, we kept asking why teams were not remediating faster. Automation was not the blocker, since patch automation tools have existed for years. Confidence was. Teams did not know whether they were choosing the right fix, whether a patch would crash a business application, or whether compensating controls already covered the risk.

TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence is built to answer those questions and to be the system of record and system of action for cyber risk reduction. It takes prioritized findings from Qualys or third-party tools and recommends the right fix for each one. A patch reliability score shows how likely a patch is to deploy without issues, and integrations with firewalls and other controls show when a compensating control already covers the risk. Patching is not always the answer. If a company has moved from Zoom to Microsoft Teams and a Zoom zero-day is disclosed, the right action is to uninstall Zoom rather than patch it.

Agent Sara plans the rollout. Low-impact updates such as browsers and standalone utilities are patched automatically with no reboot required. Production workloads are patched in rings, starting in a lab environment, with health monitoring through partners like Dynatrace. If CPU, memory, or network indicators show a problem, Agent Sara stops the rollout and rolls the patch back. When a patch is not safe to deploy, Agent Sara applies a mitigation instead.

Trust Is Built Into the AI-ROC

As soon as agents start remediating, security and IT teams ask the same four questions. The AI-ROC answers each one with a setting the team controls.

What breaks if the agent gets it wrong? Every patch carries an AI reliability score based on real-world deployments. Dependency and downtime impact are known before anything is approved, and rollback is staged in advance.

Can we start small and prove it? Deployment waves let teams start with zero-touch automation for low-impact fixes, use ring-based rollouts for everything else, and keep tighter control over their most critical systems. Each team decides where to start.

How do I know why it did that? ROCky, the Qualys conversational AI interface, and every agent show their reasoning, including the threat, the affected asset, any compensating control, and the TruConfirm evidence behind each action.

Can I take the wheel back? Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback happens automatically if a service degrades, and nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated.

Policy, risk appetite, confidence thresholds, approval gates, and exceptions stay with the security team, and the agents work within those boundaries. Autonomy is not something teams have to take on faith. They control how much of it to use, and the program can grow with the environment instead of with headcount.

How the Three Agents Handle a Zero-Day

At ROCon, we walked through how the agents worked together on CVE-2026-81963, a Windows vulnerability from the September Patch Tuesday that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on the same day. Agent Insta detected it in the customer’s environment within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val confirmed it was exploitable on the customer’s assets. Agent Sara saw that the patch required a reboot and already had a low reliability score, so it deployed to the lab environment first. When health indicators showed issues, Agent Sara rolled the patch back and applied a temporary mitigation, reducing the risk without the patch ever reaching production.

What Comes Next for the AI-ROC

Organizations can adopt the AI-ROC in stages. The journey begins with AI-speed detection, then extends CTEM across every tool already in use, moves to autonomous risk elimination, and finally quantifies cyber risk in business terms for the chief information security officer (CISO), the chief financial officer (CFO), and the board. Each stage builds on the one before it, so teams see results early while working toward a fully autonomous program.

The AI-ROC will continue to grow with the attack surface. As applications, AI systems, and more advanced attack techniques create new kinds of exposure, they will come into the same platform, the same risk view, and the same agent-driven workflows.

Agentic ROC Studio and the Future of Agentic AI in Risk Operations

The next step is Agentic ROC Studio, a concept Qualys is building toward. Every security team has its own runbooks, its own tools, and its own way of working, and no set of prebuilt agents can cover all of it. Agentic ROC Studio is designed to let teams build agents around how they already operate. A team would describe what an agent should do in plain language, choose the tools it is allowed to use, and have it running in minutes, with no scripting required.

These agents would work alongside the Qualys AI agents for exposure, threat, patch, and compliance, and connect to third-party tools and agents across security, IT, cloud, and identity to run as one cross-domain workflow. That is where agentic AI in risk operations is headed: a digital workforce that takes on the repetitive work across the entire risk program, while the security team sets the rules and stays in the loop.

Conclusion

Frontier AI has changed the pace of vulnerability management. Record Patch Tuesdays have arrived for two consecutive months; attackers can weaponize new flaws within hours, and the SLAs most programs were built on no longer hold. Adding more scanners, more findings, and more tickets will not close that gap.

What closes it is an operating model built for AI speed. That means detecting new vulnerabilities as soon as they are disclosed, proving which ones can be exploited, and remediating them autonomously with safeguards that let teams trust the results. The AI-ROC brings all of this together on one platform, with AI agents doing the work at machine speed and security teams in control of every decision that matters.

Every tool on the market can tell you how many exposures you have. The organizations that stay ahead in the frontier AI era will be the ones that can answer a harder question: how quickly can we turn exposure into verified risk reduction?
