Title: From AI ambition to business impact
Context: They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning
Full Text:
Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs?

That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries.

Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams.

More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning.

The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together.

What this looks like in practice

Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations.

3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations.

Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees.

Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing. Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service.

KT, one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions.

Saint-Gobain, the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab.

Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same:

Begin with the value, not the technology.

Redesign the process, not just the task.

Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams.

Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one, so scaling doesn’t stall.

This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time.

New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact.

We’re holding ourselves to the same standard

If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to.

The real measure of success

The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build.

Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours.

Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company.

Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world.

Title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
Context: “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information...
Full Text:
Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC, commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain.

In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale.

What the research found

Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters.

Measurement is the next test. Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms.

Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks.

Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy.

“Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC.

AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings

Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses.

Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability.

Where scale stalls

66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them.

The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design.

Inside the Frontier Firm

IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause.

What they do differently comes down to five behaviors:

They invest ahead of plan. 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend.

They deploy AI broadly, across most of the business, not just a few teams.

They put agents to work. 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows.

They govern so they can scale. 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters.

They build skills everywhere. 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters.

At Bristol Myers Squibb, the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time.

Four disciplines for scaling AI value

The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off.

I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER. “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.”

Unlock model choice

Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data.

Redesign workflows around agents

Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters.

Govern decisions and actions

Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do.

Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.”

Measure and optimize value

Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest.

Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start.

Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch.

Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite

IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall.

What this means for business

The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation.

First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day.

Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business.

Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI.

The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next.

Get the full picture

Download the global infographic, The Real Business Value of AI, to see a summary of findings and benchmark your organization against Frontier Firms before your next AI investment review. Regional infographics are also available for Europe, Asia Pacific and the Americas. The full InfoBrief will follow.

Title: Apple’s HomeView Tries Face Authentication Without FaceID
Context: “This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post
Full Text:
Apple's HomeView, which debuts on Friday, is a smart home device—think of it as a an iPhone-Apple Watch hybrid sitting on your counter—that can be personalized for up to six people and connected to each of their iCloud accounts. Using ambient face and voice data, it is designed to seamlessly switch between users while maintaining each of their privacy. You can ask HomeView about your schedule for the day and what movie your friend recommended in a text, but you'll be stopped from asking about your roommate's travel plans or her texts from last night. The feature doesn't rely on one of Apple's battle-tested biometric locks, like FaceID or TouchID, though. Instead, it uses new “person recognition” technology built off of an Apple architecture for securing sensor data.

This is a key departure for Apple. On the one hand, the company has still been very careful to think about security and privacy comprehensively. Not only does HomeView check for your face and voice before accessing your data from iCloud, it is also designed like an Apple Watch to check that your iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView and has been recently unlocked (with FaceID or a PIN). On the other hand, expanding the architecture used to process biometric data and authenticate users creates more opportunities for mistakes and potential vulnerabilities. And when it comes to attempting to access users' Apple data, both law enforcement and exploit brokers consistently go to great lengths to attempt to break the company's on-device defenses.

FaceID is built for the use case where a person is staring at their device head-on from less than an arm's length away. It provides reliable security that’s difficult to defeat because it stores your biometric data on a special, physically isolated chip known as the Secure Enclave—first introduced in 2013 for the iPhone 5s. The architecture is so robust that Apple also relies on the Secure Enclave as the foundation of a device's entire encryption scheme. But Apple concluded that FaceID wasn't the best fit for the HomeView, because it needs to bounce quickly between users and relies on AI processing, which can't all be squeezed into the Secure Enclave.

As a result, HomeView uses Apple's recently announced Secure Exclave (note the “x”) to handle the video and audio data the device uses to evaluate who is in a room at a given time. Apple says it has actually been laying the groundwork for the Secure Exclave for a long time—early versions of the architecture were already in place for the iPhone 16 and 17 and MacBook Neo. Instead of being an entirely separately chip, the Secure Exclave is a dedicated, memory-protected space in recent Apple processors. It is in Apple's latest S11 chip for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, as well as the A20 Pro chip for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

Even though the Secure Exclave isn't based on the tried and true Secure Enclave technology, Apple argues that it is robust and expands the company's ability to secure a range of features, including improving the security of existing mechanisms. In a blog post on Thursday, the company even goes into some detail about how it used the mathematical technique known as formal verification to vet the “microkernel” designed for the Secure Exclave.

“This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post. “Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks.”

HomeView and the MacBook Neo also use the Secure Exclave to govern the indicator light that tells users when their camera or microphone is active. The goal is to isolate this process and the chain of command governing it to make it even more difficult for attackers to try to disable an indicator light when it should be on or stop it from coming on in the first place.

The HomeView's “person recognition” technology is simply not as comprehensive as FaceID, though, and it is possible that the technology is more susceptible to reconstructed 3D depth map attacks—and potentially voiceprint attacks—than FaceID.

Of course, you don't have to have a HomeView in your house. Or if you do, you can use it on guest mode or a less involved “personalized” mode that only incorporates things like your playlists for other users to access as well and doesn't access calendar or Messages data. But as Apple forges deeper into AI integration, HomeView's departure from FaceID provides insight into the scale of the changes Apple is planning.

Title: Lego Takes BrickLink Marketplace Offline After Detecting Unusual Activity
Context: In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to...
Full Text:
Lego Group has taken its BrickLink Marketplace offline after identifying “unusual activity” on the platform.

An update was posted on November 11 by the Danish toy firm which said, “Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.”

The company is currently investigating the activity and said it needs to “fully understand” what has happened before bringing the site back online.

“That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.”

It is not yet known how long the downtime is expected to last and when the service will be reinstated.

BrickLink is an online marketplace owned by Lego Group where independent third-party sellers can buy and sell individual Lego parts – like eBay for Lego. Lego Group acquired the online marketplace in 2019.

The Lego marketplace has previously found itself at the center of security issues. In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to internal production data. Lego resolved the issues after Salt Labs disclosed the issues to the toy firm.

In November 2023 BrickLink was taken offline for a number of days due to a suspected cybersecurity incident.

Professional Lego reviewer Jay Ong, who runs Jay’s Bricks Blog, covered the downtime and noted that users were prompted to update their passwords. However, in an email he received at the time of the incident, he was reassured that his BrickLink account had not been compromised.

Title: When Coding Agents Inherit Your Pipeline’s Permissions
Context: Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds
Full Text:
What you will learn

How coding agents borrow the permissions of your CI/CD pipeline, why enforcement is thinnest in those environments and how to scope agents to the task, treat pipelines as privileged identities and check each action at runtime.

A coding agent working in PocketOS’s staging environment hit a credential error, found an unrelated API token and used it to delete the production database and the backups stored alongside it.

Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds.

Most of the conversation about coding agents is about the code they write, but engineering and security leaders need to be able to say what an agent can set in motion, and whose authority it uses when it does.

Enforcement is thinnest where AI agents do their work

In Delinea’s 2026 Identity Security Report, Fall Edition, 2,254 IT and security leaders told us where AI access is checked at the moment of action, before the action runs. CI/CD pipelines came in at 35% and Kubernetes at 28%, the lowest of the six environments we asked about. And 47% of organizations lack enforcement at the moment of action across at least two of the six.

Those are the environments developers hand off to agents first, and they're where deploy roles, cluster permissions, and production credentials live.

The agent doesn’t need the prod credential

Say you ask an agent to bump a service in staging. It updates the deploy workflow and opens a pull request. On GitHub, a pull request from a branch in the same repo runs the workflow as modified in that PR. If the workflow can pick up the pipeline’s cloud role, and that role reaches prod as well as staging, the agent’s edit now has production authority behind it.

The agent never touched a prod credential. It borrowed the pipeline’s.

Over-scoped CI roles were a problem long before agents showed up. Workflows branch too, but someone wrote and reviewed every branch. An agent can write a new one and trigger it in the same session.

Permissions that were safe for a predictable job become much broader once the identity using them can improvise

Identity has to follow the action

Security teams already know how to limit privileged access. Agents need those same controls applied to each action because they decide what to do next on their own.

Scope the agent to the task, not the person who launched it. You might be allowed to query the production database, but your agent shouldn’t inherit that because you started it. A policy that can tell the two apart lets your query through and stops the same query when the agent sends it.

Treat the pipeline as a privileged identity. The deploy role is what actually touches prod, so it deserves the scrutiny you’d give an admin account: one role per environment, and a human review before anything reaches production.

Keep enforcing policy after access is granted. Authentication only checks who's connecting, so a command an agent runs 40 minutes into the session goes through unchecked. Access should exist only while the task needs it, and each consequential action should be checked against policy before it runs.

Where Delinea fits

Delinea extends Privileged Access Management from the point of access to the moment of action. For the connections it brokers, including databases, servers, Kubernetes and MCP tools, access is granted just-in-time for the task, and in a brokered session the credential is injected at the proxy so it never reaches the agent. Each query, command and tool call is checked at runtime, and one that’s out of scope doesn’t run.

Start with one agent-assisted workflow

Pick one agent-assisted workflow and trace it to production. List each identity it touches, from the agent to the runner to the deploy role to the cluster, and what each one is allowed to do. Then find the point where a production action from a staging task would be stopped. If the answer is “we’d catch it in the logs,” you’ve found your gap.

Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027: Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline

November 12, 2026

Kyle Koppe

BLOG

5 min.

Have you been wondering what the prevailing cloud security best practices for 2027 might be? Unlike years past, 2027 is set to center around the data-to-AI pipeline. Data platforms, AI services and autonomous agents now run side by side across multiple clouds and the data moving between them carries the most business value and the biggest security risk. Organizations planning their 2027 security programs need practices that protect that entire movement, not just the environments on either end.

TL;DR – A critical cloud security best practice for 2027 is going to center around securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system, with protection and access policies following data from collection through model training, deployment and agentic AI use.

Key takeaways:

Own the configuration. Under the shared responsibility model, organizations are responsible for securing the AI and data services they use and default settings need tuning to each environment.

Enforce through architecture. Policy-as-code, infrastructure-as-code and automated guardrails turn security strategy into controls that hold up at scale.

Start with a baseline and build from there. Assess, plan and engineer pipeline security as a holistic motion, starting from wherever you are and building toward a scalable architecture that’s ready for what comes next.

Six Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027

Data teams and AI teams often work on different platforms with different priorities. Similarly, security programs have traditionally treated data security and AI security as separate disciplines. Moving into the coming year, organizations that secure the pipeline end-to-end will allow protection and access policies to carry forward as information moves between environments. This strategy allows them to enable new AI workloads to come online quickly without sacrificing security.

By following six interconnected practices, organizations can strengthen each individual layer of the cloud environment and then connect them into a cohesive, policy-driven foundation.

1. Treat Shared Responsibility as an AI Practice

Under the cloud shared responsibility model, the customer owns the security configuration of services such as Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker and Google Gemini Enterprise (Vertex AI). These services ship with default settings designed for broad use. Organizations should review and tune access controls, content filtering and model permissions to match their own data, risk tolerance and compliance obligations.

2. Classify Data Before AI Consumes It

Sensitive data discovery and classification work best when they happen early. Data security posture management (DSPM) gives teams visibility into where sensitive information lives, who can reach it and how it moves, so they can apply protection before data reaches a model or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application.

3. Enforce Policy as Code

Documented policies only reduce risk when they are enforced. Policy-as-code and infrastructure-as-code let teams define security requirements once and apply them consistently across every environment, pipeline and deployment, which keeps controls aligned as cloud footprints grow.

4. Govern Every Identity, Human and Non-Human

AI workloads and agents act as identities in the cloud and they can accumulate permissions quickly. Mapping entitlements, enforcing least privilege and reviewing privileged access for data and AI administrators help limit the reach of any single account or agent.

5. Build Compliance Into the Architecture

AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and the CSA AI Controls Matrix sit alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS. Aligning architecture to these frameworks from the start creates audit-ready governance and reduces rework as new regulations take effect.

6. Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline as One System

This is the practice the others point toward. Before data reaches a model or agent, teams copy, combine and transform it across databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines. At each stage, organizations need to preserve data integrity, understand sensitivity and origin and limit access to sensitive information.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top cloud security best practices for 2027?

Key cloud security best practices for 2027 include owning the security configuration of cloud AI services, classifying data before AI consumes it, enforcing policy as code, governing human and non-human identities, building compliance into the architecture and securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system.

What is the data-to-AI pipeline?

The data-to-AI pipeline is the path data takes from collection and preparation through storage, transformation, model training, deployment and use by generative and agentic AI applications. It typically spans databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines across multiple clouds.

Why is securing the data-to-AI pipeline a cloud security best practice?

AI models and agents are only as trustworthy as the data they rely on. Securing the pipeline end to end preserves data integrity, tracks sensitivity and origin and keeps access policies in place as data moves between environments and new AI workloads are introduced.

Who is responsible for securing cloud AI services like Copilot, Bedrock and Vertex AI?

The customer is. Cloud providers secure the underlying infrastructure, but the customer owns configuration, access controls, content filtering and model permissions for AI services. Default settings are designed for broad use, not your risk profile.

What is policy-as-code?

Policy-as-code is the practice of writing security rules as machine-readable code that deploys automatically with infrastructure. It eliminates manual configuration and ensures every environment gets the same controls from day one.

What is DSPM and how does it support AI security?

DSPM continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud environments. For AI security, it identifies which data AI models can access, flags overexposed training sets and tracks data lineage from source to model.

Which AI regulations and frameworks should cloud security programs plan for in 2027?

Organizations should plan for AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, the CSA AI Controls Matrix and state AI legislation, alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS.

Claude Opus 5.5 is now the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. We recommend it as your daily driver for knowledge work, meaning the model you leave selected when you work with Claude on research, analysis, and writing or producing memos, reports, spreadsheets, and decks.

If you or your team have been using Sonnet for daily work and saving Opus for heavy analysis or complex projects, it’s worth reconsidering because a more capable model can finish a task by doing less work, which can then offset much of its higher price per token.

Here's how the current models compare:

On Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, higher-priced models use your limits faster. Pro plans and standard seats on Team and seat-based Enterprise plans don’t include Fable 5.2 in their limits outside limited-time launch offers, so it runs on usage credits.

Haiku 5.5 is our fastest and least expensive model, built for quick lookups and high-volume work like writing summaries and sorting data. This is our first Haiku model with effort controls, so you can ask for a more careful pass before switching to a larger model. It’s best suited to short, narrowly scoped tasks. For longer analysis, switch to Opus 5.5.

Sonnet 5.5 is faster and cheaper than Opus 5.5 for well-scoped tasks that have a clear brief. This could be asking Claude to turn finished notes into a polished document, or to build a deck using a slide template. At higher-effort settings, however, cost per task with Sonnet 5.5 gets close to Opus 5.5, so if you find yourself pushing Sonnet to Extra high or Max effort, consider switching to Opus 5.5.

Opus 5.5 is built for complex work that needs careful judgment, like research, financial analysis, and producing finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets. We share details on why we recommend Opus 5.5 for daily knowledge work later.

Fable 5.2 is best for your most demanding reasoning and long-running work, like deep multi-step research or coding that you can hand off to a large team of subagents that run for hours. For most knowledge work, start with Opus 5.5 and move to Fable 5.2 when a project’s scope and complexity calls for it. Fable 5.2 is available on all paid plans, though how it draws on your usage depends on your plan.

Whichever model you're on, if Claude didn’t do as well as you expected, try a higher effort first before moving up a model. If it had the context, clearly tried, and still got it wrong, move up a model.

Opus 5.5 does its best work on documents, research, finance, and charts

Opus 5.5 follows instructions precisely and stays in scope, so the spreadsheets, slides, and documents it produces often need little editing. It's careful with figures and sources, too. In one internal research test, Opus 5.5 wrote reports on a company's quarterly performance using only a saved snapshot of the web, in which the company’s earnings release was hard to locate. An automated grader checked every figure and quote against the pages in that snapshot, under a condition that the report would fail if even a single figure or quote was invented. Across effort settings, 16 of its 18 reports passed.

Its writing is clearer than that of earlier models, too. Opus 5.5 puts the most important information first, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it, and on longer tasks it says plainly what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you. That also makes its work easier to check, which we count as a safety benefit as well as a practical one.

John Ruelas, a staff software engineer at Ramp, said: “It writes like a good colleague, and follows our writing rules. A design spec came out usable with very minimal edits, and when it rewrote one of our prompts I preferred its version to my own.”

Financial analysis is another strength. Opus 5.5 reads dense filings, financial models, and charts accurately and keeps track of context across a whole project or deal. In another internal test, it analyzed a proposed merger between two fictional HR software companies, building a financial model in Excel and then turning it into an executive presentation on whether the deal made sense at its price. It finished in 63 minutes, compared with 93 for Opus 5 on the same task, at half the cost, with a more thorough model, and an easier-to-read presentation.

Frank Corrao, who leads central equity quant research engineering at investment firm Walleye Capital, said that at higher effort settings, Opus 5.5 “detected that the minute indexing in our own instructions was off by one and corrected for it, noting that this would cost it points with the grader. It was right, and no model we’ve tested had caught and acted on that before.”

Opus 5.5 is our best Opus model for vision. It reads dense documents, charts, screenshots, and diagrams accurately, which makes it reliable for pulling data out of documents. Even at its lowest effort setting, it read values off dense charts more accurately than Opus 5 did at its highest.

Getting more out of Opus 5.5

Each new model is a reason to retest what you hand to Claude and to drop prompting habits built for older models.

Try these tasks first

Ask for a finished file. If you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the spreadsheet or document rather than an outline to build from. More often than not, Opus 5.5 can get from your request to the finished file in one pass.

Have it check long documents. Give it a long plan, report, or deck and ask it to find mistakes and inconsistencies. Opus 5.5 catches details that are easy to miss in long documents, such as a chart in a deck that doesn’t match its source data.

Hand it a research question. Ask a question without a set answer and have it pull sources together, work through long documents, and write up what it finds as a memo, report, or deck.

Try visual work. Its vision gains carry over to design, so try it for prototyping an interface, building a website, or illustrating a concept.

Change these prompting habits

Connect Claude to your work files and systems. This is one of the most useful steps for getting output that fits your work, because when Claude can reach your files and systems through connectors, it can go get what a task needs instead of working only from what you paste in. On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner has to turn a connector on before members can use it.

Say what done looks like in your first message. Instead of prompting Claude with instructions one at a time, describe your goal, the finished output, and when you want it to stop and ask. Opus 5.5 carries long, multipart work through to the end better than Opus 5 did.

Delete “think hard” and “think carefully.” Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5, and it decides how much to think based on your request and the effort level. In our testing, removing those lines made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.

Start at Medium effort. Medium is the default for Opus 5.5, and on our coding and knowledge-work evaluations, Opus 5.5 at Medium matched or beat Opus 5 at High. Higher settings think longer and cost more without always producing better work, so move up to High when Medium stalls. To change the setting, click the model name next to the send button and choose Effort.

Attach the chart instead of retyping it. Share the chart, screenshot, or diagram itself rather than copying its numbers into the prompt. Workarounds built for earlier models, like transcribing a chart's values, may no longer be needed.

Name the styles you don't want. For design work, a general instruction like “avoid a generic look” tends to swap one default style for another. Naming specific patterns to avoid, such as a cream background or pill-shaped buttons, works better.

Give it your house style. Paste your brand or writing guidelines into the request, or point Claude to your best existing decks, for example in a Google Drive folder it can reach through a connector, and ask it to match them. Expect a few rounds before it's exactly right.

The effort finding held for early testers, too. Zimu Li, Member of Technical Staff at Factory, said, “Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model we’d default to at medium effort. In our testing it matched Opus 5 on high effort, while using 20 to 25% fewer output tokens.”

Testing Opus 5.5 on a demo project

Here's what all this looks like on one project we worked through in a demo. At a hypothetical retail company, revenue growth had slowed over the past year, leadership had four theories about why, and an analyst had a folder of material: spreadsheets of sales by store, PDFs from the latest leadership off-site, and other files. With Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, the prompt read, roughly:

Growth slowed a lot this year. Leadership has a couple of theories about why; they're in [my manager's] note. Everything I have is in the uploaded folder. Please test each of the four theories against the data and tell me which ones hold up.

The prompt doesn't tell Claude to think hard, and it doesn't say which file to check for which theory. It states the goal and what the final output looks like, and leaves the approach to Claude.

Claude found that the data didn't support any of the four theories, though one couldn't be fully ruled out. It then proposed an explanation that nobody had raised: new stores had opened too close to existing ones and were drawing sales away from them. The pattern was a little unclear with the stores listed by city, and clear once they were filtered by proximity to a new store. Claude backed the finding with a regression of the sales impact against that distance.

Next, Claude turned the analysis into a document that holds charts and interactive elements alongside text, including a slider showing how sales change with the distance between a new store and an existing one. A teammate reviewed the doc at the same time.

The manager then asked Claude to turn the doc into board slides that opened with the answer. For teammates who don't use Claude, docs export to Word, PDF, or Google Docs, and decks export to PowerPoint, PDF, or Google Slides.

To see the whole project, including the Q&A, watch the Opus 5.5 for Work session on demand.

Try Opus 5.5 on your own work

Pick something you'd normally split across several requests, like a research memo, a variance analysis, or a deck built from an existing doc. Give Opus 5.5 the files and a description of the finished result in one message, leave it at Medium effort, and compare the result with what you're used to getting from other models.

Full Text:
Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents is now available in private beta. Developers can build agents that work directly in their company's code and internal systems, and run those agents in their own environment.

Self-hosting is a new way to run Managed Agents, a suite of composable APIs for building and deploying autonomous agents. Managed Agents provides the agent harness, sandboxes, credential handling, and session history to get long-running agents into production.

Run your agent control plane in your own environment

We first launched Managed Agents as a hosted service on the Claude Platform, where Anthropic runs the infrastructure for you. For teams who needed their code to stay in their own environment, we added self-hosted sandboxes.

Since then, agents have become more capable and are taking on more critical work, like fixing broken builds, testing releases, triaging alerts, and working through your bug backlog. They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems. For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves.

With self-hosted Managed Agents, every part of the service runs in your own cloud or on-premise, including the harness, sandboxes, credentials, and session history. You operate the Managed Agents server, its database, and the workers where agents run their shell and file tools. Model requests go where you choose, whether that's Anthropic directly, your cloud provider (Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry), or your own gateway. Your developers still build agents with the same core APIs as the hosted Managed Agents service.

Session history is stored in your own database. If your organization has zero data retention (ZDR) in place with Anthropic, it applies to the requests sent to Claude in the same way as any other Messages API call.

Designed for agent security

When an agent runs unattended inside your code and systems, you can't rely on a person checking every step, so the limits have to be built into the system itself. That's why agent security starts with architecture, and why we designed Managed Agents around four principles. These principles apply whether Anthropic hosts everything, you host just the sandbox, or you host the whole service.

The brain and the hands are split

The harness (the brain) calls Claude, and the sandbox (the hands) is where the agent's code runs. They are kept separate by design. The agent's code runs in the sandbox, while the agent loop, session history, and vault secrets stay outside it. Separating them also means an agent doesn't depend on one sandbox surviving its whole run, sandboxes start only when a tool needs them, and session history lives outside the sandbox as an event log.

Credentials stay out of the sandbox

Vaults are designed to keep credentials out of the sandbox. For MCP tools and supported API calls, a proxy outside the sandbox adds the credential to the request. With self-hosted Managed Agents, you can also store credentials in your own secrets manager.

Network access can be limited

You can limit each environment to a list of allowed hosts, and requests to any other host are blocked. For an agent that fixes broken builds, that list might be just your git host and your package registry. When you host the sandbox yourself, you set the same limits in your own firewall.

Every session leaves a full record

Managed Agents keeps a record of every step an agent took, including the tool calls it made and what came back. The record exports over OpenTelemetry, so you can send it to the monitoring tools you already use and review agent activity alongside the rest of your systems.

We see an opportunity to fundamentally rethink the shopping experience. Through our work with Anthropic, we're bringing decades of J.Crew styling, merchandising and creative expertise together to help shape what’s next for customer behavior.”

Full Text:
When OpenClaw launched almost a year ago, it showed the world the capabilities of a persistent agent. Unlike regular codex sessions which involve a fixed goal and human steering, persistent agents run 24/7 with a broad scope and the ability to proactively take actions without user input.

While persistent agents are extremely capable, their real world deployment has been limited to date. These deployments present many novel challenges compared to traditional software. With traditional software, we have relied on configuration and code to be deterministic and for threats to come (mostly) from external attackers. Persistent agents can change their configuration and write arbitrary code to accomplish a goal. Attacks come from the inside when agents take misaligned actions.

At OpenAI, we currently have persistent agents deployed across the entire company, including hundreds of OpenClaw agents. This post covers some of the controls we’ve adopted to enable OpenClaw deployments at OpenAI.

Separate trusted and untrusted execution

In order to secure persistent agents, we needed to isolate trusted deterministic logic from un-trusted LLM execution. Trusted logic includes critical components like networking, identity, and sandboxing. This is traditional static code that, outside of software bugs, should behave as configured. Agents, the environment they execute in, and the code they write are considered untrusted. This is an environment where agents can dynamically generate code to accomplish a goal with no hard guarantees on behavior.

To support this in OpenClaw, we ended up implementing remote harness execution in the open source project. This enabled the OpenClaw Gateway to run in a separate container (and in our case, a separate cluster), from the agent harness.

By implementing the split, we could treat the gateway, the component that configured the agent, as trusted deterministic code and focus on sandboxing the agent workload as untrusted code.

Enforce hard security boundaries

Security boundaries for agent workloads are enforced through sandboxing, which limits the actions agents can take.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we used the following sandbox controls:

network: control what endpoints an agent can access - we used an organization-managed allowlist with explicit denials for restricted endpoints

workspace: control what files an agent can access - we only allowed writes to agent working directories

process: control what processes an agent can access - we relied on process isolation via codex linux sandbox

secrets: control what secrets an agent can access - we manage secrets through a credential broker so secrets are not visible to the agent

For our OpenClaw deployment, we used the built-in sandbox from the codex harness. The following are some of the settings we employed, divided between requirements.toml (restrict what options are available in codex configuration) and config.toml (actual codex configuration). Note that we also enabled some additional security controls - removing the ability to use danger-full-access mode and relying on cached web search which routes web searches through OpenAI’s own index for search queries.

requirements.toml

# Exclude unrestricted "danger-full-access" sandbox mode. allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"] # Permit cached hosted search, but not live hosted search. allowed_web_search_modes = ["cached"] # Require the managed network proxy. experimental_network.enabled = true # Prevent user-level configuration from expanding the domain allowlist. experimental_network.managed_allowed_domains_only = true # Allow only these destinations; replace with the workload's required hosts. experimental_network.allowed_domains = [ "github.com", "api.github.com", "codeload.github.com", ] # Explicitly block these destinations, including cloud metadata endpoints. experimental_network.denied_domains = [ "pastebin.com", "*.pastebin.com", "webhook.site", "metadata.google.internal", "169.254.169.254", ]

config.toml

# Select the permission profile defined below. default_permissions = "openclaw" # Use cached hosted search. web_search = "cached" [permissions.openclaw.filesystem] # Allow reads needed by the minimal runtime environment. ":minimal" = "read" # Allow reading and modifying the agent's workspace. "/home/dev-user/openclaw-workspaces" = "write" # Allow reading managed assets without modifying them. "/home/dev-user/read-only" = "read" # Prevent access to SSH credentials. "/home/dev-user/.ssh" = "deny" [permissions.openclaw.network] # Permit network access through the administrator-required proxy. enabled = true # Do not inherit an upstream proxy. allow_upstream_proxy = false # Keep the proxy's local/private-address guard enabled. allow_local_binding = false # Disable the SOCKS5 listener. enable_socks5 = false # Disable SOCKS5 UDP support. enable_socks5_udp = false # Do not permit proxy listeners on non-loopback addresses. dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy = false # Do not permit unrestricted Unix-socket access. dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets = false [shell_environment_policy] # Preserve default filtering of sensitive environment variables. ignore_default_excludes = false # Remove GitHub credentials from agent command environments. # This does not hide credentials stored in accessible files. exclude = [ "GH_TOKEN", "GITHUB_TOKEN", "OPENCLAW_GITHUB_BASIC_AUTH", "OPENCLAW_GITHUB_READONLY_BASIC_AUTH", ] [apps._default] # Disable apps unless individually enabled. enabled = false # Disable destructive app operations by default. destructive_enabled = false # Disable open-world app operations by default. open_world_enabled = false

Add model-based safeguards

All the controls we talked about so far are static in the sense that they rely on traditional deterministic code to prevent an agent from taking misaligned actions. As models get smarter, it’s critical that we also have defenses that scale with compute - aka other models.

With Auto-review, a second agent can monitor and approve the actions of a primary agent. Constantly requiring human review creates review fatigue where humans are trained to blindly accept all permission prompts. By using an LLM based reviewer as a filter, we reserve human attention for high value approvals. This is a feature that is natively supported in both OpenClaw and Codex.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we enforce auto review on all agent actions.

Split agent identity from user identity

When an agent takes an action, we need to be able to audit said action, give the agent access to resources, and distinguish whether that action was initiated by the agent or by the user. Agent identity gives us the means to do so. There are emerging specifications like WAG that give agents their own access to resources, and others like XAA that let agents act on behalf of the user through OAuth delegation. Note that agent identity is different from service accounts which provide separate API access for bots. The two should be used together - for example, your agent should act with its own agent identity and access third party services through service accounts which are linked to said identity.

For our OpenClaw deployment, each agent has a unique identity that is associated with a ChatGPT Service Account. This gives each agent its own inference credential separate from the user’s and allows teams to connect custom plugins to the agent. This also lets us audit agent actions and if needed, turn off inference.

Observe everything

Comprehensive observability lets operators understand the full lifecycle of agents - from how they were configured to what actions they took. With persistent agents, it’s critical that we have this coverage in order to trace and detect misaligned actions.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we log everything - every configuration change on the control plane and all turns from the agent. Because agent turns can contain sensitive information, these logs are locked down and only available to a select few individuals in the security team.

Closing thoughts

We are still at the beginning of the adoption curve when it comes to deploying persistent agents. The lack of established best practices makes it difficult to adopt agents in many enterprises today.

When we rolled out our internal pilot of OpenClaw at OpenAI, we witnessed a huge jump in both productivity and adoption, from both technical and non-technical teams across the company. We now have over 500 agents that run proactively in the background doing meaningful work - everything from automatically opening PRs in response to product feedback to continuously running data experiments on new features.

During OpenAI dev day, we announced OpenClaw Enterprise (OCE), an open source vendor neutral agent control plane. If you use OCE, you can launch an agent with many of the safeguards we talked about built-in when using the standard codex preset. Note the project is currently still in the pilot phase and that we plan to get to a 1.0 release by the end of the year.

We believe many of AI’s biggest gains in industry will come from persistent agents. By sharing what we’ve learned and building OCE in the open, we hope to make them safer for everyone to deploy.

Beyond the Kill Switch: Containing AI Agents at Machine Speed
Context: Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and...
Full Text:
AI agents can retrieve information, use tools, and trigger actions across multiple systems before a security team can assess their decisions. If an agent begins operating outside its authorized purpose, the organization must immediately contain the risk and determine which parts of the business process can safely continue. However, harmful actions unfold faster than human defenders can respond.

Closing this gap is a focus of Fortinet’s recent contributions to the World Economic Forum Centre for Cybersecurity’s Cyber Frontiers: AI and Cybersecurity initiative. Fortinet’s participation includes an in-person meeting in San Francisco last month and ongoing initiative workshops. Through this collaboration, we bring a practitioner’s perspective on translating agent governance into enforceable controls.

Effective containment requires AI-enabled security that detects signs of misuse and automatically triggers controls to restrict an agent’s actions. Enforcement must extend beyond prompts to the agent’s tools, credentials, active context, and stored memory. These controls must also give security teams time to assess an incident and choose an appropriate response. An agent kill switch remains an essential last resort when narrower interventions cannot reliably contain the risk. However, it must be designed to support business continuity, allowing it to stop an affected agent while safe, authorized work continues.

Here are critical steps every organization can take to secure their AI agent deployments:

1. Establish What an Agent Is Allowed to Do

Detecting misuse begins with a clear understanding of an AI agent’s legitimate role. Before deployment, organizations must define the agent’s identity, purpose, accountable owner, and authorized scope. This scope needs to specify which tools it can invoke, what information it can access, and which actions it can delegate.

With those boundaries established, AI-enabled monitoring can assess whether an agent’s activity remains consistent with its assigned task. That assessment must go beyond checking credentials: An agent using valid credentials and permitted tools can still request an inappropriate operation or access information unrelated to its purpose.

When monitoring detects a deviation, the first priority is to limit potential harm. Whether the cause is a compromise, faulty instructions, or a routine error, containment must begin before the uncertainty is resolved. Predefined intervention criteria should specify which actions to block, which permissions to restrict, and which cases require human review.

Defining those criteria beforehand requires an understanding of both attack behavior and legitimate operations. Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and linking those signals to proportionate controls.

2. Use Deception to Strengthen Detection

Deception techniques can generate useful detection signals. Fortinet’s deception technologies include deploying decoy assets and credentials to identify credential misuse and lateral movement. Agentic workflows can build on this approach: A canary credential or decoy tool outside an agent’s authorized task, for example, could reveal an attempt to exceed its scope. That signal could trigger a targeted restriction or pause while a person assesses the situation.

For threat researchers, the key question is how reliably these techniques translate into agent behavior. Testing should determine how to interpret the signal in context—including benign discovery and configuration errors—and what response is warranted. Agent-specific applications should also be validated before organizations rely on them for containment.

3. Contain Risk While Preserving Verified Work

Responses must address both potential harm and whatever remains trustworthy. Consider a hypothetical security operations agent investigating suspicious activity. If the agent recommends isolating a production system without verifying its business dependencies, acting on that recommendation could cause as much harm as the threat it is intended to contain.

Unless a preapproved containment policy authorizes an action, an approval gate should pause the isolation request before execution. This gives an analyst time to assess potential operational consequences. Authorized evidence collection can continue as long as the process remains secure and appropriately restricted. If the agent’s identity or working context may be compromised, move supporting work to a trusted process or analyst using trusted tools, and treat suspect evidence as untrusted data.

Graduated containment provides several ways to make that distinction operational:

Throttle authorized activity. Limit tool-call rates, concurrent tasks, execution time, and the number of retries or delegated steps. This constrains automation loops and creates time to investigate. Unauthorized actions or imminent harm require an immediate block or stronger containment.

Restrict permissions and connectivity. Remove write access, disable specific tools, or limit network destinations. Use task-scoped credentials with short lifetimes so you can withdraw authority without disrupting unrelated services. Read-only access also warrants scrutiny when sensitive information could be transmitted elsewhere.

Limit active context. The context window contains the instructions, history, and retrieved content supplied to the model for its next decision. The application can cap how much task data enters that window and restrict retrieval to approved sources. If context may be poisoned, preserve a snapshot and rebuild it from a trusted task definition and validated state. Simply shortening the window is insufficient: It can discard necessary instructions while leaving malicious content in place.

Restrict persistent memory. Stored conversation history, summaries, and retrieval records can influence later decisions. Limit the records an agent can read or write, separate memory by task or user, apply expiration rules, and quarantine suspect entries. Clearing active context does not remove poisoned persistent memory, and neither operation revokes the agent’s tool permissions.

Require additional approval. Hold higher-risk actions for review by an authorized person. Bind approval to the specific operation, target, parameters, and scope. A material change should require another decision.

Pause or isolate the affected work. Suspend the agent or a workflow branch, preserve evidence, and keep suspect outputs from reaching downstream systems. Continue other work only when its dependencies and controls can be independently validated; treat evidence from suspect sources as untrusted data.

These options can be combined according to the incident. They are not a mandatory sequence: Active compromise or imminent harm may warrant an immediate stop.

4. Enforce Limits Where Agents Act

A gateway model offers a practical way to enforce these restrictions. Agent requests to models, tools, APIs, and services must pass through control points that evaluate them before execution. A policy decision point then determines whether a request is allowed, requires approval, or must be denied. An enforcement point at the gateway, tool executor, or receiving service enforces that decision. Both must operate outside the acting agent’s authority.

Agent-aware enforcement should link each request to an identifiable agent, an accountable owner, a delegated task, and an authorized scope. It should evaluate the operation and its parameters, the destination, the resource’s sensitivity, and any delegation involved. In the security operations example above, this means setting separate authorization requirements for evidence collection and production isolation.

AI guardrails can inspect prompts, retrieved content, responses, and proposed tool calls for signs of injection, data leakage, or other policy violations. Tool authorization must still independently verify which actions are permitted. An agent’s claim that an action is safe or that approval has been granted does not constitute authorization. If required approval or policy checks fail, the affected high-risk action should remain blocked.

The architecture must also account for bypass paths. Blocking a single connector is ineffective if an agent can access the same function through another tool or delegate the task to an unrestricted agent. You must cover all relevant execution paths and verify authorization in the systems receiving requests. The agent application and storage controls should also manage context and memory restrictions; a gateway alone cannot enforce every aspect of the workflow.

This separation aligns with OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance, which recommends enforcing authorization outside the agent’s context, validating approvals for specific tool calls, and isolating and limiting memory.

Fortinet’s work on AI security reflects this architecture. FortiAIGate provides a runtime gateway with guardrails for prompts, responses, and agent tool traffic and adds automated AI validation, agent security, and real-time protection. These capabilities support independent inspection and policy enforcement. Organizations must also implement the task-specific permissions, memory controls, and continuity procedures described here.

5. Define Human Decisions Before an Incident

Automated enforcement enables timely intervention, but humans must still define the policies that govern it. Before deployment, teams should agree on which signals trigger restrictions, who can intervene, and when an incident calls for escalation or a complete stop.

Higher-risk actions that require approval should remain blocked until a decision is made. Escalation deadlines and safe fallback procedures should account for situations where no reviewer is available. Organizations should also test whether their staffing and escalation processes can handle the volume of decisions generated by agents.

Reviewers also need evidence to support a decision: what the agent attempted to do, which actions it completed, which restrictions are in effect, and which systems or data may be affected. Without that context, an alert can leave someone responsible for a decision they’re not equipped to make.

6. Design Your Emergency Kill Switch for Business Continuity

An emergency stop should revoke the suspect agent’s authority while preserving the underlying business process wherever it remains safe. This includes halting the affected run through the orchestration layer, revoking its task credentials and sessions, and propagating restrictions to child agents and delegated jobs. You should also block new tool calls at external enforcement points and cancel queued work. In-flight operations require explicit handling: cancel them where supported, determine what has already completed, and reconcile or compensate for completed changes where possible.

Continuity depends on having a tested fallback in place in advance. Keep unfinished work in a protected queue, and hand validated tasks to an analyst, a constrained playbook, or an independently trusted service. For example, a SOC can keep receiving and routing alerts while suspending the suspect agent’s response privileges. The fallback must not automatically inherit the same compromised context, memory, or credentials.

Keep checkpoints and action records outside the agent’s control so a replacement agent or analyst can distinguish completed actions from pending work and reduce the risk of duplicate execution. These records support a controlled handoff, but continuity also requires a tested fallback. A kill switch alone cannot keep the business process running safely. If no safe fallback exists, the affected process may need to be paused.

Before an agent resumes, responders should verify affected systems, address the root cause of the incident, and validate a trusted configuration, context, and memory state. A designated person should authorize restoration, and permissions should be returned incrementally where appropriate. Exercises should test the entire workflow, including revocation, delegated tasks, fallback operations, and safe resumption.

Turn Collaboration into Operational Guidance

Implementing such controls requires cooperation across the agentic ecosystem. Enterprises rely on model developers and tool providers for visibility and enforceable boundaries. Security researchers need operational feedback to evaluate detection methods. Policymakers need to understand where technical controls can support accountability and where gaps remain.

Cyber Frontiers brings together public- and private-sector perspectives on securing agentic AI. Through our participation, we share Fortinet’s operational experience while learning from organizations with systems, constraints, and consequences of failure that differ from our own. Comparing approaches helps clarify responsibilities and assess whether proposed safeguards can work when agents interact across organizational boundaries.

The practical value comes from sharing what organizations learn when those safeguards are tested: which observations warranted intervention, how quickly restrictions took effect, whether delegated tasks were halted, and what enabled safe operations to continue. Organizations can apply these lessons to test their own workflows before expanding agent autonomy. Those tests should demonstrate that controls can detect misuse, apply proportionate restrictions, and give an accountable person the evidence and authority to decide what happens next.

Learn more about the forum’s Cyber Frontiers initiative and its work to support secure adoption across the agentic economy.

Title: Node2Shell and eMudhra: 2 Unrelated Problems, 1 Node.js release
Context: js released a security update addressing CVE-2026-111497, a remote code execution vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decoder
Full Text:
What you will learn

Find out how Node2Shell and the eMudhra CA compromise differ, why Node.js 24.22.1 addresses both, why patching a host doesn’t fix old containers, and what each risk means for machine identities.

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released a security update addressing CVE-2026-111497, a remote code execution vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decoder. The same release updated its root certificates and added checks for blocked public keys following the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities.

The incidents are unrelated. Node2Shell involves memory corruption, while eMudhra involves CA private keys recoverable from public certificates. But both sit within components that applications trust without controlling: a decoder that handles external data, and a certificate authority that vouches for who is on the other end. One is about what happens when untrusted data reaches a vulnerable component. The other is about whether that data came from the service the application meant to contact.

Node2Shell: from compressed data to code execution

Node2Shell, as Imperva named the vulnerability, affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js to decompress HTTP traffic. When the decoder encounters an invalid block transition, it continues processing instead of rejecting the data, writing beyond the allocated buffer.

Imperva demonstrated remote code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image using malicious Brotli data in HTTP request bodies and responses processed by fetch(). The researchers needed several attempts to achieve code execution.

Not every Node.js application is exposed. A basic HTTP server doesn’t automatically decompress Brotli requests, but Express applications with compatible body parsers can. The built-in fetch() API also decompresses Brotli responses, creating another entry point.

Node.js fixed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1.

Exploitation has already moved beyond laboratory demonstrations

On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Researchers have observed exploitation attempts against vulnerable Node.js installations, although the publicly analyzed attempts have not established successful compromise.

The bigger issue is that Brotli isn’t specific to Node.js. The underlying bug is in Google’s Brotli library, which is used by other applications and runtimes, so other software bundling affected versions needs to be checked separately. Whether a particular application is exposed depends on how the library is integrated and whether untrusted data reaches the vulnerable decoder.

eMudhra: When a trusted CA key isn’t secret

Four days earlier, on October 17, a researcher reported that eight eMudhra intermediate CAs had private keys recoverable from their public certificates. Although the keys used P-384, their private values were smaller than 256, making recovery a matter of checking at most 256 possibilities. That wasn’t an elliptic-curve weakness.

According to eMudhra’s preliminary explanation, a mistake during an April 2025 key-generation ceremony led to a weaker set of keys being used. The keys remained recoverable for roughly 18 months. There is no confirmed exploitation, but they could have been used to issue forged certificates. Six intermediates were for TLS and two for code signing, and eMudhra says none issued end-entity certificates.

Chrome blocked the affected TLS keys on October 17, followed by Firefox. Google found no TLS certificates from the affected intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs before the block. That protected browsers, but many applications don’t receive browser blocklists.

Sectigo had also cross-signed all eight intermediates, creating alternative certificate chains involving the same compromised keys. It revoked those certificates on October 19, but clients without updated trust or revocation information could still accept an affected chain.

Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store, with distribution scheduled for October 27. This also affects legitimate certificates under that root. On October 22, eMudhra announced that it was leaving the global TLS certificate business, so organizations using its publicly trusted TLS certificates need a replacement plan.

Apple's response shows why updating trust isn't always straightforward. Apple began blocking the compromised TLS intermediates on October 19 and the affected root on October 23. Safari, Mail, and applications using Apple's security frameworks receive these protections automatically. But some macOS command-line tools, including curl and git, can still accept the affected certificates because they use a separate certificate bundle. Apple says a future software update will address this gap.

One release, both fixes

That brings us back to Node.js. Version 24.22.1 included the Brotli fix, TLS hostname-verification fixes, updated NSS root certificates removing trust in the emSign ECC Root CA - G3, and checks for blocked public keys.

Shipping a fix is only half the job. Trigger.dev updated its Node.js runtimes and removed trust in the compromised eMudhra CAs in v4.7.7, but existing deployments still need to be redeployed. The same applies to containers: patching the host doesn’t update an old Node.js binary or CA bundle inside an image.

What this means for machine identities

The two problems threaten credentials in different ways. Successful Node2Shell exploitation grants an attacker code execution inside the application process, putting credentials accessible to that process at risk.

With eMudhra, an attacker who can redirect a connection and present a forged certificate accepted by the client could impersonate a trusted service. This could expose authentication tokens sent to that service. But the same trusted connection could also be used to deliver malicious content to the application.

For example, the attacker could return a Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable Node.js application. If the application processes it through the affected decoder, the certificate compromise could provide a delivery path for Node2Shell.

There's no public evidence that the eMudhra keys were exploited or that this combined attack has occurred.

What's next?

In the next blog of this series, we will look at whether the two vulnerabilities can be combined into a working attack chain. Can a forged certificate be used to deliver a malicious Brotli response to a vulnerable Node.js application? What conditions would make that possible, and where would the attack fail?

We'll also investigate the broader impact of the Brotli vulnerability. Node.js is one affected implementation, but the underlying library is used elsewhere. The question is which other applications expose the vulnerable decoder to untrusted data, and whether the impact goes beyond what Imperva demonstrated.

Our next blog will focus on what happens after a successful compromise, particularly the risks to application credentials, service accounts, and other machine identities.
