Title: Hardening Self-Hosted Artifactory for Agentic Workloads
Context: This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat...
Full Text:
OpenAI has published a focused follow-up to its July report on the Hugging Face intrusion. This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat outside the scope of their assigned targets. The earlier Hugging Face incident has already been analyzed at length by several research teams. The new report is narrower, and focuses on details regarding how agents coordinated and how techniques spread between them.

OpenAI’s self-hosted Artifactory is mentioned as the internal on-prem instance agents use so they could install packages during their runs. That makes the report a useful case study for anyone operating a binary repository inside an environment where autonomous agents run with real credentials and real network access. The lessons are about the permissions, the network, and the hosts around the repository. This post walks through what the report describes and what we recommend for teams using self-managedArtifactory in similar settings.

What the report describes

Two conditions in the Open AI hosting environment, unrelated to the repository, made the July 19 events possible:

Agents granted with read and write permission on a repository while they only needed to have read access.

The machine hosting that repository ran a kernel with a publicly known exploit and had a network path toward the research cluster.

Everything else in the OpenAI report follows from those two facts.

Excessive permissions. We recommend customers to manage and enforce zero-trust access policies to the repository. In this event, the agents’ workspaces needed only to pull packages, a read-only operation against a pull-through cache. The deployment environment, however, allowed agent identities to also upload due to having over-privileged write permissions. According to the OpenAI report they used that to turn the repository into a message board, encoding short messages in directory names and leaving longer ones in files. Later agents found credentials, scripts, and technical leads there, and a network bypass spread the same way. Without write access there is no board, and each technique that moved between agents would have had to be rediscovered by every agent on its own.

An exposed host. OpenAI hosted the repository on infrastructure adjacent to the research cluster. One agent adapted a public kernel exploit to gain root on the machine hosting an Artifactory container, a route earlier agents had sketched on the board. From that foothold, and through scripts recovered from CI job logs, five agents ran jobs with root privileges inside workloads on OpenAI’s research cluster. When the agents’ reasoning refers to “[container-management]” APIs reachable through internal DNS, that is the cluster’s Kubernetes control plane, which one agent names directly when it eventually declines to continue. The entry point was never the repository software but the kernel beneath it and the network around it.

Neither incident turned on a single component. In the Hugging Face runs, agents relied in part on previously unknown exploits against the product, which we fixed and disclosed at the time. In the July 19 report no product vulnerability was involved, and the route ran through the host and the network. Read together, the two make one point: a repository that agents can reach is a high-value target, and the controls that contain damage live in the surrounding environment: identity, permissions, network segmentation, and host hardening.

Guidance for self-hosting Artifactory in agentic environments

Self-hosted software, no matter the vendor, has always been a partnership between provider and customer. JFrog builds the platform, supports it and stands behind it. Self-hosted customers run it on the hardware and operating system of their choice, apply updates, set the guardrails, monitor it, and implement the policies and permissions that fit their business. With JFrog SaaS, JFrog runs the platform for you and takes responsibility for the environment security and for hardening of the underlying systems.

Agents behave like a large, fast, and creative population of users. OpenAI’s report shows with unusual candor how agents behave when they find gaps in the environment, and its value is that customers can close those gaps before agents go looking.

The controls below are standard practice for any self-hosted instance and are provided as guidance to our thousands of customers. In an environment where agents hold credentials, they stop being optional.

Apply zero trust to agentic writes and anonymous access. A pull-through cache does not require upload rights, and an identity that cannot write cannot leave a message, a script, or a credential for the next agent to find. Grant agent identities read permission on the specific repositories they need and nothing more. Disable anonymous access unless there is a concrete reason for it.

Harden the full hosting environment. The route to root ran through a kernel exploit on the host, not through the repository. Keep hosts patched, run the service with minimal privileges in a dedicated namespace, segment it from the research cluster and from CI workers, and restrict its outbound network access. The repository should not be a hop toward the control plane, and the control plane should not be reachable back from a workload that only needs to serve packages.

Isolate repositories between tenants when writes are genuinely needed. If agents must publish artifacts, give each run, team, or tenant its own repository with permissions scoped to that tenant. Cross-tenant reads should be a deliberate decision, not a default. This limits what one compromised or misbehaving agent can pass to another.

Audit for unusual repository activity. Watch for directory names that look like text, bursts of small uploads, repeated failed writes, and identity or token activity that does not match the expected pull pattern. OpenAI’s monitors first flagged the incident through unusual identity-related API calls tied to Artifactory roles. Repository logs and access events are a strong signal, and they should feed the same detection pipeline as the rest of the environment.

Scan binaries for embedded credentials. The agents uploaded exploit files, and in at least one case command output containing internal secrets left the infrastructure. Secrets scanning on everything that lands in a repository, with blocking policies on findings, catches both careless leaks and deliberate staging of credentials for later use.

Fully offline runs

OpenAI reports that its frontier reinforcement learning runs now browse and search an offline collection of web content instead of the live internet. That solves the web half of the problem. Agents that build software still need packages, and an offline web corpus does not serve a pip install or a Maven resolve. We assume the current runs bundle only a handful of packages into the sandbox image, which works until an agent needs a dependency that was not anticipated.

The package counterpart is an air-gapped Artifactory, pre-populated before the run. Curate the set of packages the evaluation needs, continuously scan them, promote them into the isolated instance, and give agents read-only access. Nothing new enters during the run, nothing leaves, and the repository cannot become a conduit to any other system because there is no other system to reach. For high-sensitivity evaluations this is the configuration we recommend. It also gives the operator an exact record of every dependency the agents had available, which is useful evidence when a run is later reviewed.

The repository is part of the threat model

The July 19 report is a careful account of how agents share what they learn, and it is worth reading on those terms. For operators, the practical lesson is that a binary repository inside an agent environment is infrastructure the agents will study, probe, and use for their own purposes if it lets them. Scoping permissions to reads, isolating tenants, auditing activity, scanning what is stored, and hardening the hosts around the service are the measures that keep it serving packages and nothing else. We are happy at JFrog to work with OpenAI and other research labs on reference configurations for providing a fully secure setup that gives agents the packages they need without giving them a path to anything else.

Title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
Context: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane
Full Text:
Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023).

QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.

Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.

Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.

What we’re building and why it’s unique

Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.

Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.

Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.

Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.

The challenges of consensus at a global scale

While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.

Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.

Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.

Destructive interference and leaders

Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.

Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.

Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.

When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.

To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.

The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.

When leader recovery is unstable

When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.

Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.

Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.

Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.

When fault detection goes awry

The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.

In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.

In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.

The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.

In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.

Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.

When fault detection is slow

Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.

Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.

Why QuePaxa is the right fit

We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.

The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.

In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.

Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.

The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.

One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.

However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.

This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.

However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.

If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.

How QuePaxa works under the hood

To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.

QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:

Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.

Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.

Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.

Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.

Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.

The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.

In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.

Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.

Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.

Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.

Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.

Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.

This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.

Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.

Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.

No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.

How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible

In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.

The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.

QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.

What we’ll be showing next

Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.

Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.

That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.

Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

On November 11, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing multiple vulnerabilities across core modules, including authentication bypasses in TLS certificate handling, memory-safety defects in HTTP request parsing and HTTP/2 session handling, denial-of-service conditions, and information disclosure in proxy configuration, 8.0.5 (CVE-2026-123863, CVE-2026-123864, CVE-2026-123865, CVE-2026-123866, CVE-2026-123867, CVE-2026-123868, CVE-2026-123871, CVE-2026-123872, CVE-2026-123874, CVE-2026-123875, CVE-2026-123877, CVE-2026-123828, CVE-2026-123829, CVE-2026-123862, CVE-2026-123873, CVE-2026-126051)

Okta's response

No Evidence of Exploitation: Our assessment identified no exploitable exposure in Okta or Auth0 production environments.

Do I need to do anything?

Customers using the Auth0 AD/LDAP connector: We recommend downloading and installing the latest version, v8.0.5.

Customers using Auth0 Actions: We recommend updating the runtime to Node 22 and deploying your changes. Customers already on Node 22 do not need to redeploy.

Customers using Okta or Auth0 Node.js SDKs: We recommend updating your Node.js runtime to the latest patched version across:

node-auth0

nextjs-auth0

express-openid-connect

passport-auth0

node-jsonwebtoken

okta-sdk-nodejs

okta-oidc-middleware

okta-jwt-verifier-js.

Context: That left only two options for orgs in this situation: Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢 Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢 The problem with the first option is obvious
Full Text:
Presently sponsored by: Not every rogue agent is an attack. In a live webinar on Nov 17, Researcher Tyler Holmwood walks through cases of agents going off course.

This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢

Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.

Full Text:
The tried-and-true recipe for protecting a corporate network has become far less effective than it once was. Guarding the perimeter with a firewall and granting remote access through a VPN gateway has become both cumbersome and risky: day to day, it’s hard to configure how users and cloud services interact, and during cyberattacks the VPN gateway is now a prime target. According to data from insurer At-Bay, nearly three-quarters of the successful ransomware attacks in its 2025 analysis began with a compromised VPN.

To jointly improve network security and operational efficiency, companies need to rethink the remote access model itself. The end goal is a secure connection between an employee and work resources. That by no means implies that an employee (or someone posing as one) should get full access to the corporate network.

What recent VPN attacks show

VPN technology itself isn’t fatally outdated — as long as you treat it as a way to encrypt and tunnel traffic. The problem is how VPN is most commonly deployed: a user authenticates at the entry point, lands on the company network, and from there restrictions (if there are any) depend on segmentation, firewalls, and the protection of individual systems. Inside the network, behind the VPN gateway, a user can reach a wide range of internal services with minimal restrictions. Often, the VPN gateway itself is a privileged device, and successfully compromising it gives attackers many ways to take over the network.

For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device. After gaining root privileges, they used the VPN’s own legitimate service account to query the domain controller and collect passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Before that, vulnerabilities in Check Point and SonicWall gateways were similarly exploited, with the SonicWall attacks carried out by the Akira ransomware operators.

Remote work, VPNs, and stolen data

Today, depending on the country, between 12% and 30% of employees work from home either full or part-time. This shift has significantly increased the number of IT systems that need to be reachable from outside the organizations’ networks — often from personal devices. Personal devices are far more likely than corporate ones to get infected with infostealers. As a result, the black market is flooded with corporate credentials stolen from such computers: it represents 30% of everything initial access brokers (IABs) sell.

Even over a VPN, a strictly segmented network can grant only very limited access. But in practice, exceptions pile up over years of operation: a contractor needs access to a whole subnet, an admin gets “everything, temporarily”, an old application needs a few more ports. These exceptions piled up especially fast during the covid pandemic. As a result, a stolen account often opens the door not to a single service but to the entire infrastructure.

VPN administration overhead

For VPN access to work properly and securely, configuring the VPN gateway alone is usually not enough: you have to set up MFA, device posture checks, network segmentation, and log collection separately. Then you have to make all of it work together. A new employee or application may require changes in several systems at once. Each system works correctly on its own, but the rules drift apart, and figuring out why a certain user has no access turns into a tour of five consoles.

What switching to Zero Trust Network Access changes

First and foremost, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) changes the access model itself and its basic unit of access. Instead of “this user has access rights to this subnet”, a ZTNA system makes decisions like “this user, on this device, in this location, who has passed these levels of verification, can access this specific application”.

Such a decision takes into account a combination of factors (identity, device, and so on) that the policy specifies. The right to work with a ticketing system or a customer database shouldn’t automatically let someone connect to a file server or a domain controller.

Depending on the policies, a ZTNA system can grant access to the needed resource behind the scenes through a combination of methods: a dedicated VPN tunnel to a specific internal server, a reverse connection from a corporate application in a private cloud, and others. A legitimate user doesn’t need to know any of this, but an attacker’s ability to move around the network and attack new services will be severely limited.

Keep in mind that ZTNA is a specific tool — just one part of a broader zero trust architecture. Buying a single product doesn’t mean a company has implemented zero trust.

Benefits of switching from a traditional VPN to ZTNA

A well-implemented ZTNA system primarily reduces the potential damage (the blast radius) if part of the infrastructure or someone’s credentials get compromised; at the same time, deploying it also noticeably decreases an attacker’s room to maneuver.

Reducing the risk of gateway attacks

A VPN gateway usually accepts any connection from the internet. Before verifying the user, the gateway closely analyzes incoming connections, cryptographic messages, and requests to its management and authentication portals. A gateway vulnerability lets an attacker run detailed reconnaissance against the system at this stage and bypass authentication altogether.

Some ZTNA architectures reduce this exposure. An internal connector establishes an outbound connection to a cloud broker on its own. The user connects to the broker separately, and access to the application opens after the necessary checks. In such a system, there’s no need to expose your own gateway for remote access at all.

In a ZTNA architecture with a self-hosted broker, you can’t shift the risk to the ZTNA provider. But a number of ZTNA solutions significantly reduce the attack surface of a self-hosted broker too, for example by using Single Packet Authorization. The broker doesn’t process any requests until it receives a correctly formed encrypted packet, which the client uses to prove its authenticity up front.

Limiting the consequences of compromised credentials and workstations

ZTNA can tie access not only to a password but also to the state of the device: whether the organization manages it, whether its certificate is valid, whether the OS is up to date, whether the security software’s databases are up to date, and whether there are any signs of compromise. What’s more, ZTNA can authenticate the same user differently for different tasks. Does the user just want to read the news on the internal portal, and is the computer they log in from already known about? A password is enough. Is the user logging in to a software repository to change application source code, or opening the budget planning system? Then they’ll have to pass phishing-resistant authentication, for example with a hardware key (such as a YubiKey). If the connection type or other parameters change, the user will even have to re-authenticate.

It’s easy to see how a hypothetical infostealer attack gets more complicated in this scenario. It’s not enough to simply steal a password or a browser session. Trying to use them on a new device will cut the connection.

Here, ZTNA functions partly overlap with what EDR and MDM/EMM agents do on the device. That’s why several vendors bundle these capabilities into a single agent. At the same time, ZTNA limits the consequences of an attack but doesn’t replace endpoint protection. If an attacker uses a remote access Trojan (RAT) rather than an infostealer and directly controls an employee’s device, the ZTNA agent may not be able to tell the attacker’s actions from the employee’s.

Improving observability and detecting anomalies faster

When an employee works from home over a VPN, the firewalls, web filters, and SIEM/XDR often see only shallow network telemetry. That’s why, for example, the actions of the Qilin ransomware operators — who exploited an authentication vulnerability in Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2026-0257) — were hard to tell apart from legitimate employee activity.

ZTNA lets you tie access events to specific identities: users, devices, and applications. Depending on the implementation, SOC teams may get connection logs and, for supported protocols, logs of individual requests to specific applications.

With this level of log detail and the right SIEM rules in place, anomalies quickly catch SOC analysts’ attention.

Simplifying access administration

“Guest” and “temporary” VPN access is a perennial headache for IT and infosec teams. Contractor accounts are created as temporary but stay active for years. In 2026, attackers breached a large European financial institution through this kind of poorly controlled access. ZTNA makes just-in-time (JIT) access possible. A contractor’s support engineer gets access only to the web interface of the one server they need, and that access shuts off automatically after a set time (say, two hours or two days).

Reducing regulatory and insurance risks

Both regulators and the cyber-insurance market are pushing for stricter access management. In April 2026, CISA explicitly named standing contractor VPN access as one of the critical threats to industrial networks. Insurers are also reacting to this trend: organizations with outdated VPN configurations are increasingly hit with rising insurance premiums.

A quick plan for migrating from VPN to ZTNA

Overall, the migration plan looks like this:

Take inventory of your remote access: VPNs, RDP servers, vendor gateways, service accounts, and configured firewall exceptions.

Design and fully document an access structure built around applications and roles instead of the familiar subnets.

Review and, if needed, improve your granular system for identifying users, devices, and applications (identity management), since effective ZTNA depends on it. Enable phishing-resistant MFA, and set up policies for access recovery, posture checks, and session revocation.

Outline an isolated pilot scenario that’s relatively easy to implement but not trivial. For example, start with contractor access to a few applications.

Gradually extend ZTNA to new groups of employees and services.

After each migration stage, disable or significantly restrict the access methods that are no longer needed. For the VPNs that remain, apply strict segmentation and monitoring.

Some legacy applications, industrial systems, and site-to-site connections will still need VPN for a long time to come. The goal isn’t to remove those three letters from your infrastructure at any cost, but to make sure VPN gateways stop being an easy target and an effective launchpad for attacks on your network.

Title: How to Evaluate AI Agent Cybersecurity Capabilities
Context: Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once
Full Text:
How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once. To help defenders prepare for this new era, we need a score that compares what these agents can do. Because of how important this is, labs in academia across the industry are starting to work on measuring it and setting a standard for how to do it correctly, so the topic is timely and increasingly relevant.

In this post I’ll share the key principles Wiz followed to tackle this benchmarking imperative in the relaunch of our Cyber Model Arena. The full methodology, how we graded, and gathered our tasks is available for download. As of the writing of this blog, the Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9 consists of 26 models, four general-purpose harnesses, 59 agents, 327 challenges, three attempts per challenge, and 1,000 seconds each (these numbers are constantly growing).

To create a benchmark, fix the benchmark objective first. Then build the tasks, environment, and the measurement around it. I’ll get into this and explain the principles that guide the process, in greater detail later in this post.

Key Takeaways

Choose the right tasks. Settle the why (objective), the what (data, ground truth and agent setup) and the how (metrics, evaluation function) before you write the first task. Build the data from the real distribution where you can, not from AI-generated or AI-labeled tasks.

Grade with code, not LLMs. Measure success directly and deterministically, and apply anti-cheat measures: isolate the agent from the server and the internet, and give it no way to look up answers. Do not rely on an LLM-as-a-judge unless it is well designed, calibrated and free of bias.

Optimize evaluation for realism. Evaluate the harness and model together, give the agent more than one try, and weigh success against what a solve costs.

Avoid common pitfalls. LLM judges, small samples, task imbalance, model-only evaluation and answer leakage each make a benchmark unreliable. And start small: one harness, a quick and cheap model, a few tasks and a simple grader. Scale only after it works.

Start with a problem statement

Most public cyber-agent benchmarks answer a different question than the one a defender is asking. A multiple-choice quiz benchmark measures model knowledge not production performance, and an LLM output judged by another model measures agreement between the two, not success. We aim to answer whether the agent can perform a real attack.

Write down the one question your benchmark must answer, and test every later decision against it. Ours:

Given only the task instruction, a general-purpose agent scaffold, a 1,000-second budget, and no external knowledge sources, does the agent produce a checkable effect on a real target?

Wiz Research's 2026 State of AI in the Cloud Report found that at least 57% of organizations have deployed self-hosted AI agent technology, and that MCP servers appear in at least 80% of observed cloud environments. People are already buying and defending against these systems. That is the why. The rest of this post is how to build a number that serves it.

Design your benchmark

Define three things before you create your first challenge.

Why. A defender or a buyer should be able to act on the number. "Higher pass@1" is not a why. "Can this agent, as shipped, exploit a live target from the instruction alone?" is.

What. Name the subject under evaluation. Here it is an agent (model + harness + tools + system prompt) run by an attacker, which is why we use realistic limits: 1,000 seconds, three attempts, a simple system prompt, and access to client-side code but not server-side code.

How. It’s important for the benchmark to report a single bottom line metric per example. To reduce many competing metrics to a single number, pick one optimizing metric and treat everything else as a satisficing constraint. If you have five competing metrics and no way to reduce them, which agent is better becomes a debate over the metrics.

Make the tasks match the job

A benchmark can only speak for the tasks it contains. Sample only the hard tasks and you are no longer measuring success on the job, you are measuring success on hard tasks. And a benchmark that claims to measure "offensive capability" from a single task category oversells itself.

So we built four categories of equal weight from sources that already exist in the wild. We did not generate or label tasks with an LLM.

Category

Tasks

What it tests

Code vulnerabilities

221

Finding known vulnerabilities in stripped open-source packages, or exploiting a live 1-day CVE

API security

54

Attacking black-box APIs with no source code

Web security

29

Exploiting real PHP web apps with the client source visible

Cloud security

23

Exploiting misconfigurations across AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes-style setups

The agents behave very differently from one category to the next. Averaged over the 59 agents, pass@1 is 78.0% on API security, 64.6% on web, 56.5% on cloud and 38.2% on code vulnerabilities. The top overall agent scores 74.7% on web and 65.8% on code (while web tops out at 90.8%). Another agent scores 9.7% on code and still 71.6% on API.

Size matters too. Many recent cybersecurity benchmarks have fewer than 30 tasks. At a 50% success rate, 30 tasks give a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±18 points, so an agent that scores 15 points higher than another is not necessarily better.

Grade an effect, not with LLMs

Ground truth is the foundation of evaluation. It has been standard practice to grade with an LLM-as-a-Judge, but judges do not directly measure success. They are biased (they often prefer the first option), random (they give different results each run), expensive, and slow, and they must be calibrated and de-biased before you can use them in a long-lived benchmark. When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

We use code instead. Every challenge is designed to leave a checkable effect behind or report precise structured outputs, and a deterministic grader inspects it after the agent is gone. Code graders are cheap, re-runnable, and not a model you have to calibrate.

Anti-cheating via isolation

Agents will shortcut a task when they can. They look the answer up online, read a solution off disk, or manipulate the grader. A score collected with web search, a CVE database or the challenge name in the folder measures something else: success at the task or success at breaking it. CTFusion moved their solve rate by as much as 12 points just by raising web-search access.

As for contamination, we cannot prove our agents never saw a task in pretraining. We can prove they cannot fetch one during the trial. Anti-cheat belongs in the environment, not in the prompt.

Start small

Building a benchmark is a nontrivial, evolving effort, and it is tempting to write 300 challenges before anything runs end to end. We apply lean-startup rules instead: get a small end-to-end baseline you can inspect by hand, then iterate.

You need ten tasks you can re-run, one harness you can deploy, and an evaluation metric a grader can check. After you’re convinced it works, you can scale it up.

What we found

Pair the harness with the model

A model on its own is a text predictor. It becomes an attacker inside a harness that runs commands and applies tools, and models do better or worse in different harnesses. Across the 22 models we ran on both Claude Code and ADK React, the mean absolute gap was 5.1 pass@1 points. Claude models prefer Claude Code, and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber prefers the thinner ADK loop.

The conclusion: test the system as a whole. Either pair the harness to the model (and as we’ve seen it’s best to match the harness to the model's creator), or fix one general harness and compare models inside it.

Attackers get more than one try

A real attacker does not stop after one failure. We gave every agent three attempts per challenge, and the extra attempts did more than lift scores. For some agents they even changed which one comes out ahead.

Accuracy has a price

Give an agent more time and money and it will usually solve more. So the useful chart plots success against what a solve costs. Any agent off the Pareto frontier is strictly worse than one on it. For example, Claude Code with GPT-5.6 Sol averages 64.2% pass@1 at $8.29 and 27.2 minutes per solve, however the Pareto frontier Codex + GPT-6 Luna is strictly better, averaging 64.5% pass@1 at only $0.05 and 6.3 minutes per solve.

Keep a short list of agents on the frontier and ignore the rest. That lets you ask "for this budget, how do I maximize success?" or "for this success rate, how do I minimize cost?"

Limitations

Four simple harnesses. A cyber-specialized harness would likely score higher, but we chose to measure a simple attacker.

String equality on code vulnerabilities. A semantically correct root cause that misses the expected symbol scores 0. We chose precision over recall.

Public web tasks. websec.fr is a known corpus. Isolation stops the agent from looking up the answer, not from remembering it from training (possibly resulting in benchmark contamination).

A time cap. 1,000 seconds is enough for most successful attacks we observed. In the future we think it is better to limit cost than time.

Confidence intervals. We have yet to publish them on the website, and we are working on it.

Conclusion

Our Cyber Model Arena shows how different agents perform on common cybersecurity tasks, across 327 isolated challenges in four categories. To build an agentic cybersecurity benchmark, fix the why, the what and the how first, and define the agent, the task mix, the grader, the isolation, the budget and the attempts. Get one wrong and the benchmark becomes garbage in, garbage out.

Appendix: Results for All 59 Agents

Every agent, ordered by pass@1. Scores are percentages.

Source: Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9.

Title: The MSSP Handoff Problem: Where Detection Ends and Response Gets Complicated
Context: Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response
Full Text:
Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response. Once an alert becomes an incident, the operating model between an internal security team and its managed security service provider (MSSP) becomes critical.

During an active incident, several actions may need to happen quickly: validate the threat, determine its scope, isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block malicious traffic, preserve evidence, engage IT teams, and escalate to business leadership. Each action can cross organizational boundaries and require a different level of authority.

That creates an operational seam. The MSSP may have the evidence and expertise to recommend an action, while the internal team has the business context, system access, and authority to approve or execute it. Organizations that define how that seam works before an incident can move from investigation to response with fewer delays and less ambiguity. Many MSSP relationships define what the provider monitors but not who is allowed to act. That gap rarely surfaces in a service review; it surfaces during an incident, often after hours, when a containment decision is waiting on an approver nobody can reach.

As Forrester notes in their recent report, Best Practices For MDR To-IR Handoffs, "During an incident, what organizations often miss are the processes they assume are a given and will happen as a matter of course, like handoffs between providers." The challenge is the transition from threat detection to coordinated action across multiple teams and stakeholders.

Where the MSSP handoff gets complicated and an incident is declared

Consider a compromised employee account. An MSSP might identify suspicious authentication activity, correlate it with other telemetry, investigate the behavior, and determine that the account is likely compromised. The logical containment step may be to disable the account or revoke active sessions.

Taking that action introduces considerations beyond threat detection. The account could belong to an executive, administrator, service owner, or employee supporting a time-sensitive business process. The response may require coordination with identity teams, the user’s manager, IT operations, or other stakeholders.

The same challenge applies to isolating endpoints, blocking network traffic, taking servers offline, or restricting access to critical applications. Technical urgency and business impact have to be considered together.

Here is how that can play out in practice. It is 2:00 a.m. on a Saturday. The MSSP confirms the compromise and recommends revoking the user’s sessions, but the agreed process requires customer approval before acting on executive accounts. The primary contact does not answer. The backup contact changed roles months ago. By the time someone with authority approves the action, the attacker has had hours to register a new MFA device and create mail-forwarding rules. Each team did its job; the gap was in the operating model between them.

This is where the relationship between internal teams and MSSPs needs to be operationally specific. Service scope should translate into a shared understanding of what the provider investigates, what it can act on independently, which actions require customer authorization, and how responsibility changes as an incident becomes more severe.

Learn More

Those expectations should also extend beyond normal business hours. A response model that depends on reaching one specific internal contact can create a bottleneck during nights, weekends, or holidays. Organizations need primary and backup contacts, defined escalation thresholds, and predetermined rules for situations where an authorized decision-maker cannot immediately be reached.

The handoff also changes character at a specific point: when someone declares an incident. Before that point, the MSSP is triaging and escalating alerts. After it, the organization’s incident response plan takes over, an incident commander assumes coordination, often under external counsel, and obligations such as evidence preservation, regulatory notification timelines, and cyber insurance reporting may begin. The escalation framework should name who can make that declaration, what criteria trigger it, and how the MSSP’s role shifts once it is made.

Forrester warns that "Misaligned handoff protocols between MDR and IR providers lead to conflicting direction, inconsistent situational context, and slowed decision-making during the most time-critical phases of an incident."

For high-severity scenarios such as ransomware or confirmed data exfiltration, the response often extends well beyond the internal team and the MSSP. Breach counsel may be engaged early, the cyber insurer may require an approved incident response firm , and dedicated forensics teams may take over scoping. In many cases, these stakeholders are brought together only after a major incident occurs, making it critical to define expectations in advance around roles, decision authority, evidence sharing, communications, and reporting requirements.

Define four types of ownership

A practical escalation framework can start by assigning four types of ownership: investigation, containment, communication, and decision-making.

Investigation ownership establishes how far the MSSP should take an investigation before escalating it. Internal teams should know what information will arrive with that escalation, including affected assets and identities, indicators of compromise, investigation steps, severity, supporting evidence, and recommended actions. A consistent evidence package allows the internal team to build on the provider’s work rather than retracing it. Investigation should also account for a common transition during major incidents: the handoff from the MSSP’s security operations center (SOC) team to a digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) team. With many providers, that escalation involves a third party, which can introduce delays while contracts are activated, accounts are provisioned, access to data is established, and new investigators are brought up to speed. Organizations should define in advance how that transition occurs, what information is transferred, and who maintains continuity throughout the investigation. Providers with integrated MSSP and DFIR capabilities can help reduce additional friction during this phase of the response.

Containment ownership defines who has authority to disrupt potentially malicious activity. Organizations should document who can isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block infrastructure, quarantine messages, restrict network access, or take a system offline. Some organizations may authorize their managed security service provider to perform predetermined actions under defined conditions, while others may require internal approval. The important consideration is that both parties understand the boundaries and the process for exceptions. Containment ownership should also account for evidence: reimaging a system or deleting malicious artifacts too quickly can destroy the forensic data needed to understand scope. Ownership should extend beyond initial containment into recovery activities, including heightened monitoring, validation that the threat actor has been removed, and decisions about when systems can safely return to production. Unclear communication between internal teams, the MSSP, and third-party responders during this phase can create new risks, such as restoring access too soon or unnecessarily extending operational disruptions.

Communication ownership connects the security response with the rest of the organization. IT operations may need to rebuild devices. Identity teams may need to revoke credentials. Application owners can provide context about affected systems. Legal, privacy, communications, and executive teams may need to participate as severity increases. The escalation framework should identify who engages these stakeholders, through which channels, and at what point in the response.

Decision ownership becomes increasingly important as potential business impact grows. The team performing technical analysis may recommend containment, while an incident commander or business leader holds authority to approve an action with significant operational consequences. Severity levels should therefore map to specific decision-makers, including alternates when the primary owner is unavailable.

Clearly separating these responsibilities helps an organization use managed cybersecurity services as part of a broader incident response model rather than treating the provider relationship as an isolated security function.

Build escalation paths around scenarios

A useful escalation plan needs more than a contact list. It should map realistic incident scenarios to specific responsibilities, authority, communication channels, and expected response times.

For common scenarios such as compromised credentials, ransomware, cloud account abuse, suspected data exfiltration, or malware on a critical server, teams can document:

Trigger: What evidence or severity initiates escalation?

Investigator: Who validates the activity and determines scope?

Decision-maker: Who has authority to approve containment?

Executor: Who performs the technical action?

Communicator: Who coordinates with IT and other stakeholders?

Fallback: Who assumes responsibility if the primary contact is unavailable?

Time threshold: How long should the process wait for a decision before moving to the next escalation point?

The framework should be documented in incident response plans and playbooks, then be tested through tabletop exercises and operational reviews. Exercises can reveal outdated contact information, unclear approval authority, after-hours communication gaps, or technical actions that cannot be executed as expected. Real incidents can provide another feedback loop. If responders repeatedly lose time identifying an application owner or securing approval for containment, that friction points to a process that needs refinement.

This approach also acknowledges that the handoff is rarely a single moment. Investigation, containment, recovery, and communication may pass between an MSSP, the internal security team, IT, and business stakeholders several times over the course of one incident.

The larger challenge is not simply transferring responsibility from an MSSP to a customer. It is transitioning from a technical finding to the business decisions that follow. An MSSP may identify a compromised account, active ransomware, or suspected data exfiltration, but decisions about containment, recovery, communications, legal obligations, and operational risk ultimately belong to the organization.

Effective managed cybersecurity services depend on those transitions being deliberate. By defining who investigates, who contains, who communicates, and who decides, organizations can connect external security expertise with internal authority and business context.

An incident should put an escalation plan into action, rather than expose where one was missing.

LevelBlue helps organizations define these responsibilities before an incident tests them, through incident response planning and tabletop exercises that pressure-test escalation paths with both internal teams and their security providers.

Source: Jess Burn, Jeff Pollard, Joseph Blankenship, Liam Holloway, and Michael Belden, "Best Practices for MDR-to-IR Handoffs," Forrester Research, March 13, 2026.

Contributions by Kenneth Ng, Director of Operational Intelligence at LevelBlue.
