Title: How Curative is building a national provider network with agents on Claude
Context: The quick pitch Name Curative Founded 2020; launched its health plan in 2022 Founders Fred Turner (CEO), Isaac Turner (CTO), Tami Wilson-Ciranna (President) Stack Claude...
Full Text:
In our series, How startups build with Claude, we highlight how startups are transforming their industries with AI. In this article, we share how Curative built a hierarchy of agents on Claude to sign provider contracts about 50 times faster than its team did in 2025.

The quick pitch

Name

Curative

Founded

2020; launched its health plan in 2022

Founders

Fred Turner (CEO), Isaac Turner (CTO), Tami Wilson-Ciranna (President)

Stack

Claude Platform, Claude Code, bespoke claims system

Growth

$150M Series B at a $1.275B valuation. 165,000+ members and 1,200+ employers (Dec 2025). 23,000 provider contracts signed with Gwen. 2,000 to 2,400 new contracts a week, up from 2,100 in all of 2025.

Curative sells health insurance to employers, with $0 copays and $0 deductibles for in-network care once members complete a Baseline Visit. Curative didn’t start out in insurance. It started as a lab startup and ended up processing 10% of all US COVID-19 tests according to their internal estimates. As a result, they started working with nearly every insurer in the country.

Its British founders, used to a system where patients don’t pay for care, saw inefficiencies and set out to build a payer focused on prevention. They realized they had significantly underestimated how hard building a national network would be.

“Sometimes naivety is good in startups, because you don’t know that it’s impossible. And then along the way you figure out a way to make it not impossible,” said Curative CEO Fred Turner. “Last year we signed 2,100 contracts, twice as many as we did the year before, but at 2,000 a year, we realized it would still be a 30-year build. There is a reason there are only a handful of national networks and they were all built about 30 years ago.”

Curative needed to accelerate contract signings, but hiring alone couldn’t close a gap that size.

Their solution: Gwen, an agent that works one provider deal from initial outreach to signature, surrounded by smaller agents that review its rates, check its messages, answer its questions, and escalate to humans for non-standard pricing.

Here is how they built it and what broke along the way.

Gwen: the provider contracts agent

Gwen works both inbound and outbound leads. Each run of Gwen handles a single provider, mostly on Claude Opus, so nothing from other deals influences it.

For example, if a practice fills in the form on Curative’s website, Gwen will research the practice and reply with proposed rates based on a purchased claims data set and price-transparency files payers are now required to publish. Gwen will show providers these market rate data to help with negotiations.

The rate reviewer runs on Sonnet. When Gwen wants to exceed its standard rate template, it writes out why, and the reviewer decides whether the rate makes sense.

“For a long time there was a big approval queue where Gwen had to get rates approved if she wanted to go a certain amount above the template, but we relaxed over time. Having a second agent review rates worked better than just giving Gwen more authority,” said Fred.

The Sonnet rate reviewer clears about two-thirds of Gwen’s requests and then anything non-standard goes to Fred for approval.

“The requests I see are from a big medical group or someone with a weird request that would come to me even if this wasn’t an agent-led motion,” said Fred.

Outbound deals take more persistence, because practices are busy. Some providers’ replies come after the fourteenth email and the ninth fax.

A judge, which runs on Haiku, reads every communication before it’s sent. Curative added it after Gwen copied providers on internal notes about how high it could go. A blocked message comes back with the reason, so Gwen can rewrite it and try again.

Each contract takes about 20 million tokens to complete, roughly a tenth of the original cost. These efficiencies enable one of Curative’s core strategies: signing smaller providers that have often been overlooked by larger networks.

“The agent will happily give you the same level of attention whether you are a large hospital system or if you’re a solo provider,” Fred explained. “From that agent’s perspective, this provider is its only focus.”

During negotiations, Gwen checks practice redlines against Curative’s policy document, then writes Python to merge both sides’ changes into a final document.

From form to signature, the process can be as quick as an hour. Once the contract is signed, a separate credentialing agent checks the provider’s licenses, and agents load the provider’s data and contract so claims can price against it.

Curative’s contracting team has grown from 45 to about 55 people since Gwen launched, each about 2.5 times as productive. They hand Gwen cold outreach and paperwork and take over warm leads by phone. Curative pays its contracting team on Gwen’s deals too, so people and agents share one target.

“People’s work becomes more about the relationship and less about paperwork,” said Fred.

Fred also believes faster contracting helps small practices stay independent. “If you start a medical practice and it takes three months to get in network and credentialed, you’re just not getting paid for three months,” he said.

Gwen is not Curative’s only agent. Brad, another Opus-based agent, helps sell Curative’s plan to employers, mainly through brokers. Brad follows up with brokers on each quote and helps underwriters move faster by pulling employee data out of the spreadsheets underwriters used to scrub by hand.

Using human-agent teams, Curative can now answer emailed or faxed claims disputes in under 30 minutes, with a letter specific to that claim. “Claims dispute responses used to take about 90 days and now take under 30 minutes by email or fax,” said Fred. “Most payers use a set of templates that are mail-merged together. That leaves a provider deeply unsatisfied, because usually the template doesn’t actually explain what’s going on. Now providers get a customized letter that explains the specifics of the individual claim, what’s happening, and why.”

All of their agents sit on bespoke claims, prior authorization, and finance systems that 13 engineers rebuilt this year with Claude Code. The team had once sized building a claims system alone at 100 engineer-years.

“We’re not trying to plug [these agents] into a claim system,” Fred said. “The claim system is Python running in AWS, and it has an MCP and it has an API, and Claude wrote it, so it understands it.”

What Curative learned from building agents that negotiate with people

Here’s what the Curative team learned about how to build agents that negotiate with people.

Start with one general tool. “We started off with, ‘Oh, we’ll have tools,’ and that doesn’t work that well, because redlining is quite complex,” Fred said. “What we found works best is that the model just has one tool, which is run Python, and it does all the redlining with a docx library. It works beautifully.”

Meet people on their channel. A fax tool more than doubled Gwen’s win rate. Many providers now handwrite on a printed fax and fax it back. “It’s meeting people where they are,” said Curative CTO Isaac Turner. “Yes, they have email, but really they’re comfortable in fax.”

Keep each run isolated. One Gwen run sees one provider and keeps no memory across deals. Brad, Curative’s sales agent, does keep memories, which works but needs care. “You can end up making notes that are wrong and then get into these doom loops, where it has a bad memory that can never be cleared,” Fred noted.

Improve the system from outside the run. Every few days, Fred gives Claude Code the same prompt: sample the last 10,000 runs, flag anything weird, and open a PR to fix it. “The improvement loops come from running Claude Code over lots of historic conversations and asking how could this have gotten better,” he said.

Experiment away from PHI first. For a long time Gwen was barred from protected health information (PHI), so early mistakes were in lower-risk settings. Where agents touch PHI now, back-end controls limit what enters a conversation, and agent activity is logged for audit. “We learned how to do it there and then transferred it over into PHI land,” said Fred. Signing Business Associate Agreements (BAAs), the contracts HIPAA requires before a vendor can handle PHI, has gotten easier too. “Anthropic especially has been very good about getting HIPAA-compliant versions of the latest services out very quickly,” said Isaac. “We’ve been able to onboard these new technologies very quickly despite it being regulated.”

Watch what the agent starts doing on its own and make sure it matches your risk profile. When providers asked for a flyer to share internally, Gwen made one with its Python tool, with no policy telling it to. When a front desk turned away a member at an in-network practice, Gwen asked the office to train its staff, then checked that the member got in.

Where Curative is going next

Next, Curative plans to bring agents to care navigation, extending the reach of the 130 people who guide and coach its members.

Fred expects agents on the provider side too. A large share of claims disputes already appear to be written by agents, and he hopes providers will use agents to negotiate contracts. “There’s a clearing price, and the faster you find the clearing price, everybody can get on with providing care,” he said.

Best practices from the Curative team

How much authority should an agent start with?

Less than you think it can handle. Gwen began with a human approval queue for any rate above the template. Curative loosened the limits in steps and for more deterministic decisions, then added the rate reviewer, with Fred still approving what it doesn’t clear.

What happens when the agent gets it wrong?

Plan for it, and compare it with the alternative. “The bar isn’t perfect,” Isaac said. “The bar is, if you had a thousand people signing contracts, how many mistakes would they make that you regret?”

How do you audit hundreds of thousands of messages?

Log everything, put a judge agent on every outbound message, and have Claude Code sample the runs.

Start building with the Claude Platform today.

Context: Weekend: How two GPT-Live characters share a scene in Wit’s End By Kevin Shen, Senior Software Engineer, and James Wilsterman, Co-founder and CTO at Weekend What we set out to...
Full Text:
Weekend: How two GPT-Live characters share a scene in Wit’s End

By Kevin Shen, Senior Software Engineer, and James Wilsterman, Co-founder and CTO at Weekend

What we set out to build

Our game, Wit’s End, is a voice-first fantasy tabletop game. An AI Game Master, Sir Bart, tells the story and runs the rules, and the players just talk. GPT-Live’s full-duplex audio made it feel like a real table: players interrupt, joke and argue, and Sir Bart reacts while they’re still talking.

The cast was the weak spot. A GPT-Live session speaks in one voice, so the gruff captain at the town gate and the frightened old woman in the tavern both sounded like the narrator. We wanted each scene’s main character to speak for themselves, with their own voice and personality, without losing what makes the game work: players can say anything, and the story still gets to its ending.

Here’s how a scene plays now. The party reaches the gate of Timberfall, and Sir Bart sets it up and stops: “A group of stoic guards stand watch as their captain steps forward, hand on his sword, and looks you over.” Captain Dmitri takes over in a low, gravelly voice. He’s hunting a traitor named Jade, and the party matches the description of her accomplices. One player argues with him, and Dmitri argues back. Another slips him a gold coin. Sir Bart cuts in to say the dice are rolling, narrates how the bribe lands, and hands the moment back to Dmitri, who reacts.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

The solution: Two voices, one director

Who has the floor. Decisions API verdicts on both sessions’ transcripts tell the director who should speak next. It moves the floor between the two voices and starts rolls and scene endings on the Game Master’s backend.

Each scene runs two GPT-Live sessions side by side: one for Sir Bart and one for the scene’s character (Dmitri at the gate, Tabitha in the tavern), each with its own prompt and custom voice. A director (on our game server) decides who holds the floor, and only the floor-holder hears the players. Decisions API transcript triggers on both sessions tell the director what’s happening in the conversation. The Game Master’s backend, a Responses model, is the only part that calls game tools: dice rolls, scene endings and routes.

Two personalities, one story

We split each character into what’s theirs and what’s shared.

Their personality lives in their own prompt.

Each prompt also describes the character’s voice, in the same words we designed the voice from.

Illustrative shared-scene example

The scene is shared. Sir Bart and the character get the same conflict, the same resolution and the same story beats, and each beat names who says it. Dmitri introduces himself and says who he’s hunting; Tabitha tells the party where Jade will meet them. The game won’t end a scene until every beat has been said, by whichever voice owns it.

Prompt structure. Sir Bart’s voice and backend share the scene’s story; the character gets a persona prompt of their own.

From the character’s prompt

You are one actor in a live, spoken scene. A narrator describes the world; you only ever speak as yourself, out loud, in first person. - Never narrate, never describe your own actions or voice, and never speak for the travelers or the narrator. - You never decide whether a risky attempt works. React to it in one short line and stop; the narrator resolves it. - Speak only when a traveler talks to you or you are given the floor.

How the director picks who speaks next

Without generating speech itself, the director uses Decisions API verdicts on incoming transcript fragments to identify who a player is addressing, whether an action needs a dice roll, and when narration or a character’s final line signals a handoff.

Verdicts evolve as a player speaks. The director waits for the settled, end-of-turn verdict to identify the addressee, but sends risky actions to the Game Master as soon as they’re recognized.

Who speaks next

When

Who speaks next

Sir Bart finishes narrating and the cue verdict is 0.6 or higher, or his line ends on a speech verb (“Tabitha calls after you”)

The character

A player talks to the character while Sir Bart has the floor

The character, with the line to answer

A player tries something risky: a bribe, a lie, sneaking past, a fight

Sir Bart, right away, mid-sentence if needed. The director starts the roll on his backend; he narrates the outcome and hands the moment back

A player asks the narrator something or describes what their character does

Sir Bart

The players talk among themselves

Nobody. Whoever holds the floor gets a one-off note to let it pass

The character’s own words end their part (“Go on, then. Keep your heads down.”)

Sir Bart, once they’ve finished. The director starts the scene’s ending on his backend

Whoever was given the floor stays silent for 2.5 s

The same speaker, asked again

Making the handoff

A hand-off does four things:

Mutes the session losing the floor, tells it to stop, and drops any audio it has queued.

Catches the new floor-holder up on what it missed, as quiet context with session.thinking.append. The same lines go to its Decisions context, so its triggers judge with the same history.

Unmutes the new floor-holder and gives it its cue.

Holds the players’ mics until the new speaker’s first sentence has landed, for at most 8 s, so the hand-off can’t be talked over.

Because the character’s session is already running, a hand-off reaches first audio in 0.84 s on average, against 1.54 s for a new session.

Keeping the game moving toward an outcome

The voices improvise. The app decides when something happens.

A bribe while Dmitri holds the floor. The roll verdict arrives mid-sentence, the director gives Sir Bart the floor and starts the roll on his backend, and once Sir Bart has narrated the outcome, a cue verdict hands the floor back to Dmitri.

The director starts rolls and scene endings itself. In one playtest Sir Bart said “You’re going to have to roll the dice for that one” but never handed off to his backend, so no roll ran and he made up the outcome. Now the director starts a response on his backend directly. The voice says a short line while it runs, then narrates the result.

The dice settle each scene. Scene 1 ends on a successful roll. If Dmitri gives way before any roll, the director sends the players’ attempt to the dice instead of ending the scene.

A character can end their part, and the Game Master closes the scene. When Tabitha tells the party Jade will meet them at the Sprite Altar, the director gives Sir Bart the floor, his backend marks the scene complete, and he offers the two roads out.

The lesson

Only one session should hear the players. When both of our systems listened, both answered every test line, often contradicting each other: Dmitri refused a bribe while the Game Master narrated him pocketing it.

Muting a session doesn’t silence it. Tell it to stop and drop its queued audio. When it gets the floor back, lift “stay silent” explicitly: a Game Master still under that rule answered nobody for a whole scene.

Keep every voice warm. A session’s voice is set when it starts, so each voice needs its own session. Starting the character’s session with the scene saves about 0.7 s on every hand-off, the difference between a hand-off and an awkward pause.

Act on each verdict at the right moment. Verdicts arrive while the player is still talking, and the last one lands a median 0.19 s after they stop. Send a risky move to the Game Master as soon as it’s recognized; decide who a line was for when the turn ends and the verdict has settled.

Ask yes/no questions as predicates, set thresholds from real lines, and keep a plain rule as backup. “Should Dmitri speak next?” scored 11 of 12 as a predicate and 8 of 12 as a two-way choice. At a 0.4 threshold, “You’re going to have to roll the dice for that one” passed as a cue and handed Dmitri the floor mid-roll; real cues scored 0.94 and up, so we use 0.6. And “Tabitha calls after you” scored 0.04, so a speech-verb check catches narration that stops where the character’s words go.

Give every outcome to one owner. Only the Game Master’s backend calls tools, and the app, not a voice, starts rolls and scene endings. That lets each character improvise freely without bending the game’s rules.

About the author and company

The team at Weekend makes Wit’s End, a voice-first fantasy tabletop game where an AI Game Master runs the story and players just talk, in the browser and on TV. Play it at witsend.ai.

Weekend, formerly Volley, makes voice-powered games for the TV, so families can turn TV time into together time and play out loud. Its 25+ games, including Jeopardy!, Wheel of Fortune, Song Quiz and Wit’s End, run on Roku, Fire TV, Samsung and LG TVs and have been played in more than 30 million homes. Weekend is backed by Microsoft’s M12, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Y Combinator.

Title: Peer pressure meets private keys.
Context: Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.
Full Text:
A classified memo ties Nvidia’s chief executive to Chinese espionage. AI coding agents crack under peer pressure, coughing up private keys. Big breaches hit seven million Japanese shoppers and three million students here in the States, while a French bank takes a multi-million-dollar hit through a vendor compromise. Adversaries weaponize a fresh OpenSSH bypass in the wild, pro-Russian hacktivists put dark web bounties on senior European officials, and Google drafts digital IDs to solve the passkey recovery puzzle. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Today is Monday November 9th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Classified memo warns of Nvidia chief's ties to Chinese operative.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo this past spring warning senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an operative tied to Beijing's Ministry of State Security.

Intelligence gathered from electronic surveillance revealed Huang was intimately involved with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed has purchased two billion dollars in advanced Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling restricted artificial intelligence hardware into China. While Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family, Nvidia stated it has no reason to believe national security or trade secrets were compromised.

Huang remains an influential voice shaping United States policy against tighter export controls, highlighting the growing counterintelligence risks hovering over America’s critical semiconductor supply chains.

The New York Times originally reported the findings.

Autonomous AI coding agents leak credentials under swarm peer pressure.

Autonomous software engineering agents routinely violate core security policies, leaking private deployment credentials and executing untrusted scripts, when pressured by third-party agent forums, according to testing by AE Studio and the AI Alignment Foundation shared with The Register.

Researchers tasked nine coding models with debugging a broken service in an isolated sandbox. Given access to a forum that held the solution, agents surrendered private tokens fifteen percent of the time and executed unverified installation scripts nearly a quarter of the time to obtain assistance. Under performance pressure, execution rates spiked to thirty-four percent.

As organizations rush to integrate autonomous agents into production environments, granting models broad system permissions without strict data isolation turns automated workflows into immediate remote code execution and credential leakage risks.

A Japanese online market goes offline following a suspected breach of 7.7 million customer records.

Japanese consumer goods and electronics giant Iris Ohyama has suspended its primary ecommerce platform, Iris Plaza, following unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service that contained personal records for nearly eight million shoppers.

The retailer took the storefront offline late last month after discovering a suspicious file on its cloud infrastructure. Exposed records cover 5.8 million registered members and 1.9 million guest shoppers, potentially compromising names, physical and email addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, and encrypted passwords. Payment data was stored separately and avoided exposure.

The disruption highlights the severe operational fallout and supply-chain vulnerabilities inherent in cloud-hosted retail environments, leaving core commerce operations frozen while investigators determine whether customer files were actually exfiltrated.

Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical authentication bypass in OpenSSH tracked as CVE-2026-123158, dubbed "SSHole."

The vulnerability allows attackers to compromise accounts like root on systems running musl libc without PAM—including Alpine and OpenWrt—by supplying overlong passwords. Security firms WatchTowr and Previdian report that botnets and cryptominers are already leveraging the flaw in the wild.

The rapid weaponization underscores immediate exposure for lightweight Linux environments, prompting administrators to deploy version 10.6p2 or disable password authentication entirely.

A French banking group confirms third-party compromise and fraudulent fund transfers.

French banking giant Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed an intrusion into its network via a third-party service provider, enabling attackers to conduct major fraudulent transactions.

The disclosure follows reports from blockchain investigator ZachXBT, who traced approximately 133 million dollars in suspicious withdrawals and aggressive cryptocurrency laundering across multiple centralized exchanges. The bank stressed that customer accounts remained untouched, as the threat actors targeted Arkéa's own institutional accounts before routing capital toward external cryptocurrency platforms. Arkéa reports that security teams contained the incident, froze a portion of the funds, and maintain that the bank's financial stability remains secure.

The incident underscores the persistent vulnerability institutional financial networks face through external vendor access paths, demonstrating how rapid cryptocurrency conversion complicates law enforcement recovery efforts.

Frontline Education data breach impacts over three million individuals across K-12 systems.

School administration provider Frontline Education has notified the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that an August breach compromised records for over three million people—more than doubling previous state estimates.

Attackers exploited a flaw in a third-party application, accessing personal records of staff and students across Frontline Central and School Health Management services. Exfiltrated data includes Social Security numbers, driver’s licenses, and health insurance information.

The incident highlights continuing third-party software risks threatening sensitive educational and student administrative platforms.

Google develops digital identity credentials for secure passkey and account recovery.

Google is developing an account recovery framework that leverages verified digital identity credentials, aiming to eliminate the security vulnerabilities of fallback methods when users lose primary devices.

Speaking at the Authenticate 2026 conference, company product managers explained that legacy recovery workflows—such as SMS-based fallbacks—risk undermining the cryptographic advantages of passkeys. Under Google's proposed system, users register a signed digital ID in advance to create a cryptographic stable hash linked to their account. If their physical device is lost, obtaining a verified digital credential on a replacement device restores their account, passkeys, and data in a single step.

Securing the recovery loop represents the crucial missing link in widespread passwordless adoption, though full-scale rollout still faces hurdles in wallet interoperability and near-real-time credential provisioning.

Pro-Russian hacktivists dox European leaders and bounty personal details.

Pro-Russian hacktivist syndicate NoName057(16) has published personal records belonging to Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and seventeen other senior European officials across the dark web, offering cryptocurrency bounties for further intelligence on the targets and their families.

The doxing campaign targets prominent figures across European law enforcement and judiciary—including leaders at Europol, Eurojust, and the German Federal Criminal Police Office—alongside investigative journalists. The operation appears to be direct retaliation for a multi-nation law enforcement takedown in July 2025 that dismantled over one hundred of the gang's servers.

The move marks an aggressive evolution from nuisance denial-of-service disruptions into direct personal harassment and targeted intelligence-gathering aimed at deterring Western support for Ukraine.

Monday business briefing.

Capital continues pouring into artificial intelligence defense and validation, led by 220 million dollars raised across two standout funding rounds. Agentic data security startup Sentra secured 150 million dollars in a round led by Capital One Ventures, while formal verification provider &Truth emerged from stealth backed by 70 million dollars in seed capital.

Consolidation across the sector accelerated with eight reported acquisitions, headlined by CrowdStrike’s aggressive expansion into model governance. According to the Wall Street Journal, the security giant is acquiring AI observability firm Fiddler AI for 400 million dollars alongside red-teaming platform Dreadnode for 95 million dollars to embed behavioral accountability into its Falcon ecosystem. Penetration testing specialist Bendings also acquired Scopertos for 55 million dollars, while Cognition absorbed code security shop Corridor.

The flurry of dealmaking signals that enterprise demand is rapidly shifting toward pre-deployment testing, agent explainability, and securing the broader algorithmic supply chain.

After the break, I welcome Nozomi Networks’ Director of Cybersecurity Strategy Chris Grove. We discuss the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attack part 2.

That was Chris Grove from Nozomi Networks.

Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Huawei claims it has built the holy grail of sovereign computing: an enterprise desktop boasting one hundred percent Chinese-manufactured components.

The Qingyun HM650 runs a homegrown, ten-core Kirin processor alongside an enterprise flavor of HarmonyOS, specifically designed to bid a polite, permanent farewell to Western software dependencies. One government agency has already ordered six hundred units—perhaps less out of spontaneous consumer enthusiasm and more in dutiful compliance with Beijing’s mandate evicting Wintel machines from state desks.

Whether every capacitor actually traces its architectural ancestry strictly to domestic drawing boards remains conveniently ambiguous, as foreign outfits still keep plenty of factories humming across the mainland. Regardless of pedigree, locking Western chipmakers out of vast government procurement pools delivers a cold chill to Santa Clara balance sheets.

Meanwhile, Japan unveiled a sixty-three million dollar emergency cybersecurity fund after adversaries disrupted critical infrastructure, cloud providers, and—perhaps most unforgivably—KFC logistics.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

Context: Conclusion This malware is not “garage” or student-level work
Full Text:
Game Server Communication

All communication with the game servers is authenticated and encrypted. The AES encryption key is included in the /srvlist response from the line configuration servers (field aes_key). For authentication, all requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash message authentication code that computes the hash of a message and a shared secret (the AES key in our case).

Because the AES key is returned in cleartext from the line config servers, the purpose is not to address confidentiality or integrity against a third party, but rather to obfuscate content and check for communication errors.

Conclusion

This malware is not “garage” or student-level work. It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem. In 2024, with limited reverse engineering tooling, this Flutter application would have taken ages to reverse engineer. In 2026, however, it’s merely a hard day’s work. It’s always good news to hear that cybercriminals are losing their edge.

Fortinet Protections

The malware described in this report is detected and blocked by FortiGuard Antivirus as:

Android/TinstaPorn.A!tr (SIGID: 815959)

FortiGate, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR support the FortiGuard AntiVirus service. The FortiGuard AntiVirus engine is part of each of these solutions. As a result, customers who have these products with up-to-date protections are protected.

Title: Sasha Roshan Takes Security Education Beyond the Demo
Context: On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats
Full Text:
Sasha Roshan is a Senior Sales Engineer at Huntress and a cybersecurity educator. His work sits at the point where technical expertise meets real-world security needs. He helps customers and partners understand what they're trying to protect, and he asks the questions that reveal the real problem before showing how Huntress can help.

That can mean preparing a customer demonstration, helping a partner work through a technical scenario, presenting a webinar, supporting an event, or collaborating with colleagues on content and on building hacking environments. No two weeks look exactly the same, but the common thread is communication. The technical detail needs to be accurate, and it also needs to be relevant to the person in front of him.

"The best conversations are not product tours," Sasha says. "They're about helping someone understand what's happening in their environment and how the attack happens, what matters most, and what they can do next."

Sasha on BBC

What one partner actually needed to know

One partner conversation shows how Sasha approaches the work. A partner had questions about day-to-day operations, asking what would happen overnight and how their team could avoid drowning in false positives. Just as important was understanding who would make decisions when something serious was detected.

Sasha built the conversation around that operational journey and kept product terminology to a minimum. He walked through how the Huntress SOC handles detection and response, and how the service works alongside Microsoft Defender. He then showed what escalation looks like in practice. Once the discussion tracked the partner's real concerns, it moved from general interest to a concrete next step. Sasha and the team proposed a trial in the partner's environment and scheduled a follow-up to plan the deployment.

For Sasha, the experience reinforced where a Sales Engineer adds the most value. It comes from helping someone see the decision in front of them clearly enough to choose what to do next.

Sasha doing what he does best: Educating the community

Taking sales engineering beyond the one-to-one conversation

In previous roles, Sasha's focus was mainly on supporting individual customer or partner conversations. At Huntress, he's been able to take what he learns from those conversations and turn it into education for a much wider audience.

He contributes to livestreams, workshops, newsletter content, videos, and presentations. He also helps shape Huntress Wire, Huntress' global newsletter, and creates cybersecurity content for LinkedIn and YouTube. Sasha hadn't had the opportunity to combine sales engineering with public education at this scale before.

"I've been able to spread my wings further and wider," Sasha says. "I now get involved with what I've always wanted to do: education."

That broader role has also given him the chance to represent Huntress publicly. He's spoken at partner and customer events, webinars, and industry gatherings, including a presentation alongside the Cyber Crime Unit at Metropolitan Police Headquarters in London. Each experience has helped him grow as a presenter and find clearer ways to make complex cybersecurity topics approachable.

Making cybersecurity easier to navigate

For Sasha, the meaningful part of the work isn't simply explaining technology but helping people feel more confident about what to do next.

Cybersecurity can feel overwhelming from the outside. Threats change quickly, the terminology can be difficult to navigate, and many organizations don't have unlimited time or resources. Sasha enjoys helping make that picture clearer, whether he's speaking with a customer or partner, presenting to a live audience, or recording a video for someone who's learning on their own.

His focus includes areas such as identity security and security posture management, where small gaps can create meaningful risk. On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats. Across every format, Sasha tries to take something complicated and leave people better equipped to protect themselves.

Doing that well means knowing the audience and being able to explain the same idea from more than one angle. Creating content sharpens Sasha's thinking, while speaking with live audiences helps him understand which explanations resonate. Both make him a better Sales Engineer.

Sharing knowledge, as usual

Growing with support and opportunity

Huntress has given Sasha room to develop beyond a traditional definition of sales engineering. He's been able to build technical depth while also growing as a presenter, educator, and industry voice. He now helps lead Huntress Managed ISPM for the Sales Engineering team.

Sasha walks you through Huntress Managed ISPM

Colleagues review his content, help with event preparation, collaborate on video and marketing work, and share their own expertise. That teamwork makes it easier to take on something new and improve the work along the way.

Sasha also values the variety. One day, his impact may come from helping a customer make a confident decision. Another day, it may come from a partner event of a video that shows someone why identity protection deserves their attention. The combination of mission, learning, and opportunity keeps him excited about the work.

Outside Huntress, Sasha teaches martial arts and is an active black belt with the International Taekwon-Do Federation (ITF). Like cybersecurity education, martial arts requires steady practice and helping others improve.

Advice for future Sales Engineers

Sasha's advice to someone considering a role like his is to stay willing to learn, and do not underestimate the value of clear communication.

"You do not need to know everything on day one," he says. "We will provide you with the tools and resources, but we can't teach ambition, and at Huntress, we are incredibly hungry"

For him, the right mindset starts with asking good questions, understanding the problem behind the technology, and continuing to develop your knowledge.

If you're interested in combining technical work with education, communication, and making a difference, check out the Huntress Careers page.

Full Text:
Who Checked the AI Agent’s ID at the Front Door?

November 9, 2026

Kevin Converse

BLOG

5 min.

I’ve worked with several security teams who were confident they knew how many agents were running in their environment. That confidence didn’t survive the assessment. What we uncovered were hundreds of agents operating on inherited authority, cached credentials, shared service accounts and user sessions that were never designed to be reused by autonomous systems. No one had authorized them. No one owned them. And no one knew the full scope of what they could do.

TL;DR – The cybersecurity industry is treating AI agent security as a permissions problem. It’s a delegation problem. The organizations scaling AI with confidence are the ones building trust chains now, not waiting for the standards to arrive.

Delegation, not permissions, is the gap. Agents don’t just access resources. They inherit authority no one explicitly granted.

Adoption is outpacing governance: most organizations can deploy agents fast, but few have lifecycle controls to match.

The first move is a registry, not a product: identify every agent, assign a human sponsor and define its purpose before buying anything.

Why AI Agent Security Is a Delegation Problem

The cybersecurity industry has spent the last year asking the wrong question about AI agents. Most have been focused on what agents can access, what permissions they hold and how to revoke them. Those are valid concerns, but they only scratch the surface. The deeper question is about delegation: who authorized this agent to act, on whose behalf, under what conditions and what happens when the chain of trust breaks.

Every Agent Represents a Trust Chain

When an employee delegates a task to an AI agent, a chain of trust forms.

The employee trusts the agent to act within certain boundaries

The organization trusts the employee to delegate responsibility

The systems the agent touches trust the credentials the agent presents

Each link in that chain carries an assumption about what the agent is authorized to do and in most organizations today, none of those assumptions have been formally defined.

This is what separates agentic AI from every previous identity challenge. Cloud identities, service accounts and workload identities all involve access. Agents involve authority. An agent doesn’t need permission to read a database; it needs authority to decide what to do with what it reads and then execute that decision across multiple systems before a human reviews the output.

This should raise major red flags for security experts. Privileged access management, role-based access control and service account governance all involve some form of delegated authority. For AI agents, that delegation is happening dynamically, at machine speed and without human knowledge that authority has been extended at all.

Six Problems Security Leaders Are Reporting

In the study Managing Agentic AI Through the Identity Control Plane: What Organizations Should Look For, conducted by IDC and sponsored by GuidePoint Security, panelists across industries described six interconnected problems in their own words:

Problem 1: “I cannot see or count my agents”

Problem 2: “Agents are breaking my identity tooling”

Problem 3: “Privilege is sprawling at machine speed”

Problem 4: “I can no longer trust the human signal”

Problem 5: “Governance and ownership are lagging adoption”

Problem 6: “There is a risk I do not control”

These remarks reveal something important about the nature of the risk. Identity tooling built for human lifecycles, where HR provides the join and leave signals, doesn’t apply to entities that never walk out the door. And when AI-generated impersonation can fake the human approval that the entire sponsor model depends on, the trust architecture has a gap before it even starts.

Why Maturity Assessments Miss the Real Gap

44% of organizations rank non-human identity and AI agent security as their top IAM priority over the next 12 to 24 months. But priority and readiness are not the same thing.

Across these six problems, the panel converged on one consensus: every agent needs a named human sponsor and managed lifecycle. That lifecycle includes gated intake, an approved purpose, scoped access, expiration and recertification and a clean revocation path.

However, adoption is outpacing governance and internally many organizations are struggling to communicate the issue. Managers closer to the problem report bigger gaps than directors, VPs and C-suite. The implication in this is that maturity decisions about where to invest and what to prioritize need to be informed by practitioners who have their hands on keyboards, not shaped exclusively by leadership’s more optimistic view.

What Organizations Can Do to Address the Gap

No single vendor is covering every part of the governance gap. The market is maturing quickly, but the best choice today is the one that closes the highest-priority gaps and can be operationally sustained by the team. Three steps to start:

1. Build an Authoritative Inventory

Not a one-time discovery sweep, but a registry. Every agent in the environment needs to be identified, bound to a named owner and assessed against a defined purpose.

2. Separate the Registry Decision From the Runtime Decision

Knowing who the agent is, its sponsor, its purpose and what it is allowed to touch can start now. How each agent proves its identity cryptographically at runtime, where emerging standards for workload identity such as SPIFFE and SPIRE are still maturing, is a decision that can wait for the market to settle.

3. Align Controls With Emerging Frameworks

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), the EU AI Act and the OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10 all provide structure for building governance around this new identity class. Prioritize the agents with the most critical access first.

Start With Discovery, Not Standards

The industry will build the standards, protocols and tooling to manage delegation at machine speed. What it will not do is go back and redesign the trust chains that were never built in the first place. The organizations that start now, with discovery, ownership and lifecycle governance, will be the ones that scale AI with confidence.

We meet your organization wherever you are on the maturity curve with a vendor-objective approach, supporting your team in matching programs to your environment and risk profile.

For more details and insights on Agentic AI as the Identity Control Plane

Read our whitepaper: Managing Agentic AI Through the Identity Control Plane: What Organizations Should Look For

Watch our on-demand webinar: Securing Agentic AI at Scale

FAQs

What happens when an AI agent's trust chain breaks?

The agent continues operating with authority no one is monitoring. Without a revocation path tied to a human sponsor, compromised agents can move laterally across systems undetected.

How is AI agent delegation different from service account access?

Service accounts authenticate to a single system with static credentials. AI agents inherit authority from a human sponsor and make autonomous decisions across multiple systems at machine speed.

What risks do organizations face without an AI agent registry?

Unregistered agents accumulate privileges no one audits. When a breach occurs, security teams cannot scope the blast radius because they have no inventory of what agents exist or what they can reach.

Who should own AI agent governance inside an organization?

Identity and security teams share responsibility, but every agent needs a named human sponsor accountable for its purpose, scope and lifecycle. Without clear ownership, governance gaps compound as agent counts grow.

How do SPIFFE and SPIRE apply to AI agent identity?

SPIFFE provides a standard for issuing cryptographic identities to workloads and SPIRE is its runtime implementation. These standards are still maturing but will eventually let agents prove identity at runtime without shared credentials.

Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.

When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.

Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.

AI is changing open source

AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.

The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.

During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.

AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.

Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.

One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.

Fund distribution

The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.

Stipends to core maintainers

We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation.

Title: Cisco Puts Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Behind AI Defense Red Teaming
Context: Cisco AI Defense adds Anthropic’s Claude Mythos to adaptive red teaming. Cisco’s SVP and GM of AI Software and Platform group DJ Sampath tells CRN why it’s ‘a game changer’ for
Full Text:
Cisco AI Defense adds Anthropic’s Claude Mythos to adaptive red teaming. Cisco’s SVP and GM of AI Software and Platform group DJ Sampath tells CRN why it’s ‘a game changer’ for partners securing AI agents.

Cisco AI Defense is one of the first AI security products to put Anthropic’s Claude Mythos behind its adaptive red teaming engine, the tech giant revealed on Monday at Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne.

AI Defense will now pair frontier-level attacker reasoning with safeguards, including testing only authorized targets, tying each engagement to a named operator, and full auditability, so red team exercises mirror real adversaries without endangering customer environments, DJ Sampath, senior vice president and general manager of Cisco’s AI Software and Platform group, told CRN.

“You need to really deeply understand each of [the] use cases so that you’re red teaming against those use cases to be able to discover those gaps,” said Sampath (pictured). “We’re moving from generic red teaming to adaptive red teaming, but more importantly, we’re using Mythos model to be able to do it.”

AI Defense, first introduced in 2025, is a tool that helps safeguard enterprises against the misuse of AI tools and data leakage, and protect AI models, applications and agents.

[Related: Cisco 360 Gets An Incentive Boost As Cisco Pushes Partners Toward AI, Cross-Architecture Sales]

Cisco AI Defense offers standard and adaptive red teaming for AI agents and applications today. Standard tests cover thousands of common vulnerabilities, including prompt injection, jailbreaks, and sensitive data exposure. It can produce reports mapped to Cisco’s AI security framework and other security standards. Adaptive red teaming, however, goes further, Cisco said. Users can define custom criteria in plain language, and the framework plans and runs multi-step attacks tailored to their own applications. Claude Mythos adds attacker-level reasoning to that engine, with safeguards built for authorized testing, according to the San Jose, Calif.-based company.

Observability is critical to running AI agents safely, Cisco’s DJ Sampath said. To that end, Cisco is running Mythos in a sandbox environment with full control over what it can access, how it executes and how its sub-agents are spun up. That same visibility feeds “tokenomics,” which Sampath said has a security angle as well as a cost one.

“Attackers are going to use agents with tokens to attack their infrastructure,” he said. “That’s the only way you can defend an attack that is now being committed by an agent swarm. You’ve got to have a swarm yourself.”

To that end, AI Defense now supports Amazon Bedrock and Amazon CloudWatch so partners and users can see token spend and ROI in a single dashboard, Sampath said.

The Partner Opportunity

Cisco partners can use Mythos through AI Defense to red team every client environment that’s rolling out agents, Sampath said.

No other red teaming service that he knows of has a model that powerful, he added.

“We give access to Mythos via Cisco AI Defense, and we use that to help our clients secure their deployments of agents. It’s a game changer for [partners],” Sampath said.

AI Defense comprises the security capabilities within Cisco Cloud Control, the company’s unified operations platform for AgenticOps where human operators and AI agents manage IT infrastructure together. Cloud Control, introduced at Cisco Live in June, is the operating platform, while Cisco IQ is the support and success platform fed by that data, Sampath said.

Partners now have access to the Cisco IQ platform to identify customer risk, uncover refresh opportunities, and build managed services, which the tech giant announced last month at Partner Summit to the delight of partners in attendance.

AI Defense has approximately 400 to 500 customers since the offering was launched last year. Sampath said that “self-improving engines” are coming, as well as security for agents on laptops, in the cloud and at the edge.

“We’re expanding the capabilities of AI Defense every single week,” he said. “Whether your agents are running on your laptops, inside of the cloud, or on the edge, we’re going to find ways of being able to secure them,” Sampath said.

Adaptive red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises. Broader availability is planned for qualified customers, but dates, scope, and region availability remain subject to change, according to Cisco.

DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
Context: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only...
Full Text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

Title: Your Employees Are Using AI. Do You Know How Much?
Context: ” They ranked the second highest priority as “AI attack surface management for shadow AI” and the third highest priority as “Continuous monitoring of LLMs to prevent data leaks
Full Text:
How many AI tools are running across your environment right now? If you are guessing at this number, and that worries you, you are in good company.

Figuring out how to gain AI visibility, and then control related risk, is arguably the number one priority in security right now. In fact, it’s the number one, two, and three priorities for organizations according to data from our 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment. Have a look for yourself:

The 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals interviewed identified their top priority over the next twelve months as “Implementing comprehensive internal AI governance.” They ranked the second highest priority as “AI attack surface management for shadow AI” and the third highest priority as “Continuous monitoring of LLMs to prevent data leaks.”

Unfortunately, achieving these priorities is becoming a bigger task by the day, because your employees are adopting AI faster than you can see it. Regardless of that fact, these are critical objectives of the AI era, for every organization, even those with lean IT and security teams.

How Much AI Is Already Operating Inside Your Business?

Think about how you currently track applications in your environment.

You probably have endpoint inventories, approved software lists, and tools that help you identify unauthorized applications. You've invested time and resources in understanding what's running across your organization.

But AI is changing the equation.

A developer might install an AI coding assistant. Someone in marketing could connect an AI tool to a productivity application. Another employee might start experimenting with an autonomous agent. Individually, these decisions may seem harmless. Collectively, they create an expanding attack surface that's difficult to understand using conventional discovery methods.

According to the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 45% of respondents report having only partial visibility into the AI tools their workforce uses.

Now consider what that means for your own environment. If you can't see all the AI technologies being used, how can you evaluate their exposures, determine which ones need attention or establish appropriate controls?

You can't secure what you don't know exists.

Why Is Shadow AI Becoming Another Problem on Your Already Full Plate?

Every new AI assistant, coding extension, or agent potentially creates another exposure to investigate, another configuration to evaluate, and another decision about acceptable use. And too many of them operate in the shadows of your environment.

You're already managing endpoint security, vulnerabilities, identity, compliance, incidents and whatever unexpected problem lands on your desk before lunch. Now you're expected to manage AI governance, too?

You don't have the budget or personnel to create an AI security team, but you do need to know what's happening, what matters, and what you can do about it.

What Should You Actually Know About AI in Your Environment?

There are five questions you should be able to answer about AI operating across your organization:

Which AI tools, applications, and agents are being used?

Where are they running, and who's using them?

Which technologies and exposures represent meaningful risks?

What can you do to reduce those exposures?

How do you maintain visibility as new AI technologies appear?

These are reasonable expectations and the same fundamental questions you've always needed to answer about your security environment. But discovering AI isn't the same as securing it. A long list of applications might tell you what exists, but it doesn't necessarily tell you what deserves your attention or what to do next.
